messages.subject: Re: choice of priors in stan
messages.subject_clean: choice of priors in stan
messages.body_plain:
I've found half-Cauchy fine in many cases, but with non-linear models, it is easy for a variance parameter to be weakly identified, due to ceiling/floor effects. In those cases, something like an exponential prior or half-Guassian works much better, because both have much thinner tails than the Cauchy.

I think Daniel Simpson likes exponential priors for scale parameters, based upon a subtle argument having to do with constant penalty with distance from a base model with variance = zero. http://arxiv.org/abs/1403.4630

On Tuesday, June 30, 2015 at 9:28:32 AM UTC-7, Linas Mockus wrote:
> Hi,
>
> What are recommended choice of priors in stan?  I always struggle with variance - should it be half-cauchy or uniform if I know that variance is different from 0?  I gathered that for very small variances it is better to use half-cauchy.
>
> What about neg_binomial_2 with hierarchical scale parameter phi: neg_binomial_2(mu,phi[i])?  I am always confused if phi~gamma(loc_phi,scale_phi) or phi~lognormal(loc_phi,scale_phi).  If I use lognormal I should use  normal prior for loc_phi and half-cauchy (or uniform) for scale_phi?  It would be great having a cookbook with  recommendations on which priors for parameters/hyper-parameters work or don't work in stan since we don't have to worry about conjugateness.
>
> Thank you,
> Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampler diagnostic parameter questions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sampler diagnostic parameter questions
messages.body_plain:
“Essentially the only parameters that contribute to integrals lie on a hyper surface in parameter space“ . . .
Exactly!  That’s the intuition behind my paper with Roberts and Gilks:  with Metropolis you have to crawl along the surface of a sphere.

> On Jun 30, 2015, at 4:40 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Unfortunately we’re overdo for a serious rewrite of the manual,
> especially given our rapidly evolving understanding of subtle
> theoretical MCMC issues.  I have everything collected into
> slides, but turning it into text will have to wait until I have some
> free time.  But I’ll summarize the results here.
>
> MCMC is just a method for numerically estimating integrals,
> which is hard in high dimensions because of something called
> concentration of measure.  Essentially the only parameters
> that contribute to integrals lie on a hyper surface in parameter
> space and if we want to estimate integrals then we need to
> find that hyper surface and then explore it.  That’s exactly
> what a Markov chain does — eventually we have a series
> of states distributed across the hyper surface, { y_{n} }, that
> we can use as a grid for doing really simple quadrature,
>
> \int dy p(y) f(y) ~ 1/N sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(y_{n})
>
> Everything relies on our being able to find and then explore
> the _entire_ hyper surface (which we call the typical set).
> This is incredibly hard to determine theoretically so we’re
> left with a bunch of necessary but not sufficient diagnostics
> to identify when we’re not exploring everything.
>
> All of these apply only to samples — because we dynamically
> adapt sampling parameters in warmup those samples will
> behave very differently.  Again, ignore anything you see
> in warmup.
>
> Traceplots:
>
> The characteristic way pathologies manifest is the Markov
> chain getting stuck in the boundary of a pathological region
> of parameter space.  If you run long enough you’ll literally
> see the chain get stuck for long periods of time.  You can
> also compare chains to identify multi modality and other
> problems.
>
> R-hat:
>
> If our Markov chain can explore the entire target distribution
> then any realization of it should look the same.  R-hat
> essentially performs an analysis of variance on a bunch of
> chains (and subsets of chains) looking for any deviations.
> The more chains you use the more sensitive you’ll be to
> potential pathologies.
>
> n-divergent:
>
> Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has a unique diagnostic — regions
> of the typical set that are hard to explore induce particular
> numerical divergences that we can capture and report.  This
> is much more sensitive then looking at trace plots! If
> you see any divergences in sampling then you have to be
> careful.  For a few divergences you can increase the target
> acceptance probability, but for any nontrivial number of
> divergences you’ll probably have to consider tweaking your
> model to use stronger priors or different parameterizations.
>
> In RStan you can grab the divergences with
>
> fit <- stan(file='model_name.stan', data=input_data,
>            iter=2000, chains=1, seed=4938483)
>
> count_divergences <- function(fit) {
>  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
>  sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
> }
>
> Finally the treedepth issue is not so much a diagnostic of a
> bad Markov chain but rather a safeguard we’ve built in to
> avoid infinite loops caused by ill-formed posteriors which
> require the sampler to explore all the way to infinity in back
> (requiring an infinite tree depth an infinite time).  Sometimes
> your sampler will need to explore beyond our default safeguard
> value, in which case you have to increase it manually — this
> doesn’t effect the validity of your results, just the performance
> of the algorithm.
>
> I like looking at a histogram of the treedepths,
>
> hist_treedepth <- function(fit) {
>  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
>  hist(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'treedepth__']))[,1], breaks=0:20, main="", xlab="Treedepth")
>  abline(v=10, col=2, lty=1)
> }
>
> Technically the sampler tries one more step after maxdepth
> which is why you might see it exceed that value by one.  I
> can never remember the indexing and ordering to state whether
> you should see maxdepth or maxdepth + 1 but in the end it
> doesn’t really matter as the bad behavior (histogram saturating
> at a large value) is pretty obvious.
>
> On Jun 30, 2015, at 5:00 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>>
>>> On Monday, June 29, 2015 at 10:15:46 PM UTC-4, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
>>> ...
>>
>>> Finally, I'm not finding much documentation on how to interpret the sampler diagnostic parameters.
>>>
>>> Unfortunately, these things are better explained in the CmdStan manual
>>>
>>> https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/download/v2.6.2/cmdstan-guide-2.6.2.pdf
>>
>> Now that's something I understand how to fix!  I'll move the discussion
>> over to the Stan manual and just leave a reference in the CmdStan manual.
>> Here's the issue tracker link:
>>
>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1508#issuecomment-116940132
>>
>> - Bob

messages.subject: problems with implementing custom functions
messages.subject_clean: problems with implementing custom functions
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues!

I am trying to implement several custom distributions, such as one of the skewed t distributions.
I am totally new to stan, so I started with an attempt to implement a very simple model for fitting parameters of the exponentially distributed data. However, I quickly got stuck because three different methods I played with return inconsistent results, and I really want to know why, and what am I doing wrong. Details below.

I used three different ways, all of them were mentioned in the stan reference manual (2.6.2) - two functions (chapter 42.5. Exponential Distribution) and one method which is based on the log probability (chapter 16. Custom Probability Functions).

In sum, my model looks like:

> model < -
> “data {
>   int<lower=0> N;
>   real y[N];
> }
> parameters {
>   real lambda1;
>   real lambda2;
>   real lambda3;
> }
> model {
>   y ~ exponential(lambda1);
>   increment_log_prob(exponential_log(y, lambda2));
>   increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);
> }”

Sample from the exponential distribution and code for fitting lambdas (all in R):

> y <- rexp(10000, 1.648721)
> mcmc_samples <- stan(model_code = model,
>                   data = list(N = length(y), y = y),
>                   chains=9, iter=30000, warmup=20000,
>                   verbose = F, refresh = -1)

I did not set the bounds for lambdas, in result stan() function returned a lot of warnings. One of them:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::exponential_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Inverse scale parameter is -1.8615:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine, but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Of course these steps are common but the results are extremely confusing. Simple built-in functions fitted the parameter of the exponentially distributed data amazingly close to the origin parameter. However, the parameter fitted by the third method fell way far from the original value:

> mcmc_samples
Inference for Stan model: model_simple.
9 chains, each with iter=30000; warmup=20000; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=90000.

          mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
lambda1   1.64 0.00 0.02   1.61   1.63   1.64   1.65   1.67 34237 1
lambda2   1.64 0.00 0.02   1.61   1.63   1.64   1.65   1.67 34367 1
lambda3  11.18 0.06 7.97   1.25   5.34   9.37  15.09  31.43 15047 1
lp__ -10134.47 0.01 1.30 -10137.85 -10135.06 -10134.13 -10133.52 -10132.99 18477 1

Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Wed Jul  1 00:51:11 2015.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).

What am I doing wrong? Why do the methods return such different results?
And how do I implement a custom function correctly?

Thanks a lot,
Philipp

If I understand correctly, the best practice for sd prior:
- half-cauchy woks fine for sd
- if we know that most of sd < 2 then we scale the model:
real <lower=0> sd;
y~normal(mu,2*sd);
sd~normal(0,1)
- use exponential
- what if we know that sd is concentrated around 1?  Then half-cauchy may not be most efficient.  I don't know if it is true or not but I found sd~uniform(0,2) to be more efficient than half_cauchy.
- what prior should be used for neg_binomial_2 scale parameter? Is it gamma or lognormal or something else?  What should be the hyperpriors?

Thank you,
Linas

On Tue, 30 Jun 2015 21:47:33 -0400, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

>

In those cases, something like an exponential prior or half-Guassian works much better, because both have much thinner tails than the Cauchy.
> >
> > I think Daniel Simpson likes exponential priors for scale parameters, based upon a subtle argument having to do with constant penalty with distance from a base model with variance = zero. http://arxiv.org/abs/1403.4630
> >
> > On Tuesday, June 30, 2015 at 9:28:32 AM UTC-7, Linas Mockus wrote:
> > > Hi,

If I use lognormal I should use  normal prior for loc_phi and half-cauchy (or uniform) for scale_phi?  It would be great having a cookbook with  recommendations on which priors for parameters/hyper-parameters work or don't work in stan since we don't have to worry about conjugateness.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problems with implementing custom functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philipp,

The first thing you should do is to declare your parameters with constraints. Instead of lambda1, lambda2, and lambda3 being declared as real, they should really be declared as real<lower=0>.

On Wed, Jul 1, 2015 at 5:49 AM, Philipp Upravitelev <uprav...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear colleagues!
>
> I am trying to implement several custom distributions, such as one of the skewed t distributions.
> I am totally new to stan, so I started with an attempt to implement a very simple model for fitting parameters of the exponentially distributed data. However, I quickly got stuck because three different methods I played with return inconsistent results, and I really want to know why, and what am I doing wrong. Details below.
>
> I used three different ways, all of them were mentioned in the stan reference manual (2.6.2) - two functions (chapter 42.5. Exponential Distribution) and one method which is based on the log probability (chapter 16. Custom Probability Functions).
>
> In sum, my model looks like:
>
> > model < -
> > “data {
> >   int<lower=0> N;
> >   real y[N];
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real lambda1;
> >   real lambda2;
> >   real lambda3;
> > }
> > model {
> >   y ~ exponential(lambda1);
> >   increment_log_prob(exponential_log(y, lambda2));
> >   increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);
> > }”
>
> Sample from the exponential distribution and code for fitting lambdas (all in R):
>
> > y <- rexp(10000, 1.648721)
> > mcmc_samples <- stan(model_code = model,
> >                   data = list(N = length(y), y = y),
> >                   chains=9, iter=30000, warmup=20000,
> >                   verbose = F, refresh = -1)
>
> I did not set the bounds for lambdas, in result stan() function returned a lot of warnings. One of them:
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::exponential_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Inverse scale parameter is -1.8615:0, but must be > 0!
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine, but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>

If you constrain the parameters as mentioned, this should work better.

>
> Of course these steps are common but the results are extremely confusing. Simple built-in functions fitted the parameter of the exponentially distributed data amazingly close to the origin parameter. However, the parameter fitted by the third method fell way far from the original value:

This one is simple. You need a for loop. The current code:

    increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);

is only incrementing the log probability by the likelihood of the Nth element of the data.

It should look like:
    for (n in 1:N)
      increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[n]*lambda3);

If you wanted to be more efficient, you'd simplify the algebra and take the log only once, maybe sum the data in transformed data and multiply once too.

>
> > mcmc_samples
> Inference for Stan model: model_simple.
> 9 chains, each with iter=30000; warmup=20000; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=90000.
>
>           mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
> lambda1   1.64 0.00 0.02   1.61   1.63   1.64   1.65   1.67 34237 1
> lambda2   1.64 0.00 0.02   1.61   1.63   1.64   1.65   1.67 34367 1
> lambda3  11.18 0.06 7.97   1.25   5.34   9.37  15.09  31.43 15047 1
> lp__ -10134.47 0.01 1.30 -10137.85 -10135.06 -10134.13 -10133.52 -10132.99 18477 1
>
> Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Wed Jul  1 00:51:11 2015.
> For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
> and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
> convergence, Rhat=1).
>
>
> What am I doing wrong? Why do the methods return such different results?

Hopefully that explains it. Let me know if that fixes your problem.

> And how do I implement a custom function correctly?

Just to clarify, this is a custom probability distribution. You could also write this as a function.

Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problems with implementing custom functions
messages.body_plain:
Right.  To follow up on what Daniel said, you want to replace
this:

>   increment_log_prob(log(lambda3) - y[N]*lambda3);

with

  increment_log_prob(N * log(lambda3) - sum(y * lambda));

with y declared as

  vector<lower=0>[N] y;

Declaring as vector lets you do vector arithmetic, like multiplying
by a scalar.  Putting the bounds in does error checking on the data
when it's read, which is not required, but is helpful for catching errors.

It's critical that you have the constraints in the parameters
as Daniel stated --- Stan will not sample efficiently (including
perhaps not at all) when you have parameters that have values that
match their declared constraint but have 0 density in the model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
messages.body_plain:
This isn't a non-centered parameterization (aka Matt trick) issue.
There's simply no way to constrain mu and sigma so that
normal(mu, sigma) falls in (-5,5).  The best you can do is make it
unlikely that you fall out by taking mu in (-5,5) and taking sigma
small enough that it's unlikely to fall outside.

If you really need a value in (-5,5), you can scale and translate.

  theta <- 10 * inv_logit(alpha) - 5;

This guarantees that theta is in (-5, 5) no matter what alpha is, so
you can have

  for (n in 1:N)
    theta[n] <- 10 * inv_logit(mu_theta + theta_raw * sigma_theta) - 5;

It's a different regression, though --- mu_thtea and sigma_theta now mean
something different.

- Bob

P.S.  I think you meant theta_raw ("raw" as in uncooked).

> On Jun 30, 2015, at 4:41 PM, Steve Bellan <steve....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob. I doubt it would be multimodal since the fits to smaller data set seem to easily identify the posterior, I don’t see how increasing data size could lead to more posterior modes.

It depends on the data and how it's drawn.   What looks
like an "outlier" in a small data set might become a well-delineated
mode in a bigger data set.  Especially if one mode's much
higher mass than the other.

> I’ll definitely run longer. As for (a) and (b), my impression was that increasing delta (the target acceptance rate) automatically reduces the step size (which is adaptively tuned by NUTS), and that therefore I can do both (a) and (b) just by tuning this parameter. Or were you suggesting to explicitly set the step size through some other way, like switching to an HMC algorithm?

Not quite.  There is an initial step size (a), which then gets
adapted based on the target acceptance rate (b).  Changing the
target acceptance rate has no effect on the initial step size.
Usually if you need a higher acceptance rate, you want to start
with a smaller step size so you don't run too far into the tail
during warmup by taking too-big steps.  It'll mainly cut down on
warnings and make convergence smoother and less variable across
chains than anything else.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: BUGS Example Vol 2 Stagnant Problem
messages.subject_clean: BUGS Example Vol 2 Stagnant Problem
messages.body_plain:
I have tried to develop an extension to Bob's continuous version of the Stagnant model, for a simple case of an intercept and one covariate (data are 17 countries observed over ~50 years, N=854). It runs fine and converges quickly but I'm not confident that it's doing what I expect it to do. Here is the STAN code:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    real time[N];                    // time variable
    real<lower=0> lincr[N];     // y variable
    real sud[N];                     // x variable
}
parameters {

    real <lower=0> alpha;
    real beta[2];

    real gamma[2];
    real <lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=5, upper=45> cp;      // change point

}
model {
    real mu[N];
    alpha ~ normal(0,5);
    beta ~ normal(0,5);

    gamma ~ normal(0,5);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

    for (i in 1:N)

        mu[i] <- alpha +

          if_else(time[i]<cp, beta[1] + gamma[1] * sud[i],
          beta[2] + gamma[2] * sud[i]) * (time[i] - cp);
    lincr ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

And the results:

Inference for Stan model: pris_cp_nox.
3 chains, each with iter=1000; warmup=500; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=500, total post-warmup draws=1500.

            mean se_mean    sd      5%     95% n_eff  Rhat
alpha      4.574   0.001 0.032   4.520   4.627   627 1.004
beta[1]   -0.019   0.001 0.010  -0.038  -0.006   373 1.012
beta[2]    0.012   0.000 0.002   0.008   0.015   611 1.005
gamma[1]   0.010   0.001 0.015  -0.010   0.037   424 1.012
gamma[2]  -0.015   0.000 0.002  -0.019  -0.012   387 1.009
sigma      0.477   0.000 0.012   0.457   0.497   659 1.004
cp        13.036   0.174 2.928   7.985  17.687   282 1.014
lp__     209.159   0.116 2.147 205.152 211.945   345 1.015

My understanding is that alpha is the adjusted mean of Y, the betas are estimated differences in the mean before/after the change point, and gammas are before/after estimates of the effects of sud (a standardized measure). This could be wildly wrong since I don't really get the original Stagnant example.

I want to extend this further into a multilevel model (random intercepts with country-level predictors), and would welcome any feedback and suggestions about the model so far (syntax and interpretation).

Best,
John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
messages.body_plain:
Let me say my usual thing:  Are you sure you want hard constraints on theta_mu?  Hard constraints almost never make sense unless they are an automatic part of the model (e.g., probabilities have to be between 0 and 1).

> On Jul 1, 2015, at 2:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> This isn't a non-centered parameterization (aka Matt trick) issue.
> There's simply no way to constrain mu and sigma so that
> normal(mu, sigma) falls in (-5,5).  The best you can do is make it
> unlikely that you fall out by taking mu in (-5,5) and taking sigma
> small enough that it's unlikely to fall outside.
>
> If you really need a value in (-5,5), you can scale and translate.
>
>  theta <- 10 * inv_logit(alpha) - 5;
>
> This guarantees that theta is in (-5, 5) no matter what alpha is, so
> you can have
>
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    theta[n] <- 10 * inv_logit(mu_theta + theta_raw * sigma_theta) - 5;
>
> It's a different regression, though --- mu_thtea and sigma_theta now mean
> something different.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  I think you meant theta_raw ("raw" as in uncooked).
>
>
>> On Jul 1, 2015, at 2:17 PM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Stan,
>>

>> using Matt Trick may cause theta go beyond the range. Possible I need to constrain theta_row with some math?

>> parameter {
>>  real<lower=-5,upper=5> theta_mu;
>>  real<lower=0> theta_sd;
>>  real theta_row[N];
>> }
>>
>> transformed parameters {
>>   real<lower=-5,upper=5> theta[N];

>> }
>>
>> Thanks in advance,
>> Lei

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 1:09:20 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> I'm not familiar with scale indeterminacy. Is there a standard way to go about doing that?

If you were to multiply X by some a > 0, then X_unitTrace is unaffected. Thus, the likelihood has no information to distinguish between X and aX. So the prior has to distinguish between X and aX in order for the posterior to be proper. For example, independent normal priors with known standard deviation would do the trick but not if the standard deviation were unknown and had an improper uniform prior. A proper prior on the standard deviation would work, but you might not get very good sampling if it is weak.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Firstly when you divided by the trace of X you need to
take into account the Jacobian (d/dtheta 1 / Tr(X(theta)) )
— you should see a warning about this.

Scale indeterminacy is just as Ben said — many parameter
settings will give the same likelihood, so the posterior will
be non identified (it will stretch to infinity) causing poor fits.

In any case you might as well use the rank-2 tensor decomposition —

X = (Tr(X) / n) * I + S + A

where S and A are symmetric and antisymmetric matrices, respectively.

You’ll have to declare n(n-1)/2 parameters for the symmetric and
asymmetric parts and then build up the matrix in transformed parameters,
but you’ll be guaranteed to have a unit-trace matrix without any
worried about scale indeterminacy.

messages.subject_clean: Unit trace matrix
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 4:19:22 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> Do you have any sources that you can recommend I learn about this in more detail? I guess I know enough about Bayesian statistics to be dangerous. I chose Wisharts mostly because it returned a matrix I was looking for (ie. symmetric positive definite).

A lot of people are that way. It is true that the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions are for random variables that are symmetric and positive definite. However, that fact alone is insufficient to justify their use because for any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma there are an infinite number of matrix decompositions where Sigma = Z * Z'. So literally any prior distribution on the elements of Z implies a prior distribution over the symmetric and positive definite matrix Sigma.

If so, why are the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions essentially the only distributions for symmetric and positive definite matrices that you read about in the Bayesian literature? The sole reason is that they are conjugate with a multivariate normal distribution, so Gibbs samplers can do updates of the symmetric and positive definite matrix by drawing from a Wishart or inverse Wishart full-conditional distribution. That raises the fundamental point that Stan does not do Gibbs sampling because Gibbs sampling can easily be antithetical to the goal of getting an adequate number of effective samples from a posterior distribution. Also, 25 years of Gibbs sampling has conditioned people into asking "What prior distribution is conjugate?" instead of "What prior distribution reflects my beliefs about a parameter?"

So, what are your beliefs about this symmetric positive definite matrix? If you are like 99% of people, you don't really have any. Presuming so, what would be an uninformative prior for a symmetric positive definite matrix? We can't really answer that question for an arbitrary symmetric positive definite matrix, but we can answer it for a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix. (What we at Stan call) The LKJ distribution with shape parameter eta = 1 is jointly uniform among among all correlation matrices of dimension K. You could read the paper 2009 by Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe referenced in the Stan manual but it is as frustrating as it is fundamental to multivariate probability. The main implication is that it allows you to put a uniform prior on a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix.

A correlation matrix has a trace of K, whereas you need a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1 for some reason. That is no problem because any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma can be decomposed as Sigma = Delta * Lambda * Delta where Delta is a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and Lambda is a correlation matrix. The i-th diagonal element of Sigma is the i-th variance, namely Delta[i,i]^2, and you need the variances to sum to 1. A simplex is a random vector that is constrained to be positive and sums to 1, which is perfect for your situation. So, what are your prior beliefs about this simplex? If you are like 90% of people, you don't really have any, in which case a Dirichlet prior distribution with all concentration parameters (contained in the fixed vector alpha) equal to 1 reflects your prior belief that all simplexes are equally probable a priori, i.e. it is a uniform distribution over a simplex. The other 10% set all the elements of alpha equal to some other positive constant besides 1 to reflect non-uniform but symmetric beliefs about the simplex.

In summary, it is quite possible to utilize a uniform prior distribution over a correlation matrix and a uniform prior distribution over a simplex, and multiply some stuff together to obtain a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1. To do that, in my previous post, I set sds[i] = sqrt(pi[i]) where pi is a simplex and implicitly set Lambda = L * L' where L is a Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix Lambda. Then the line

X_unitTrace <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose( diag_pre_multiply(sds, L) );

efficiently does what in R code would be

diag(sqrt(pi)) %*% L %*% t(L) %*% diag(sqrt(pi))

The remaining wrinkle is that we want a uniform distribution on the correlation matrix Lambda, but Lambda is not actually a parameter of the model. Rather its Cholesky factor, L, is. By applying a multivariate change-of-variables, it is possible to work out what the prior distribution of L is if you have an LKJ prior on Lambda = L * L' . We call this log-prior the lkj_corr_cholesky distribution, but it needs to be called explicitly in the model block (presumably with eta = 1).

It so happens that --- under these priors --- simplexes and Cholesky factors of correlation matrices tend to be pretty easy for Stan to efficiently draw samples of, although, to repeat my fundamental point, not via Gibbs sampling. That is really just icing on the cake but in part follows from the process of thinking carefully about what probability distributions reflect your (lack of) beliefs and people like us thinking carefully about what multivariate transformations do to the geometry of the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from. It also happens to be the case that Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions often do unspeakable acts to the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from, so there is not only essentially no reason to use them in Stan (because Stan does not do Gibbs sampling) but also a strong reason to not use them in Stan (because Stan often can't sample them very effectively).

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Parameterizing the negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
Neg_binomial_2 scale parameter . . . hmmm . . . Let me just clarify that we’re talking about the same thing.  neg_binomial has two parameters, alpha and beta, where alpha is the shape parameter and 1/beta is the scale parameter.

neg_binomial_2 has 2 parameters, mu and phi.  mu = alpha/beta and phi = alpha.  At least, I think I’m getting the algebra right.  I suppose we could call mu a scale parameter here.  But I think section 39.2 of the manual is wrong:  there it says that phi is a precision parameters and 1/phi is represents overdispersion, and I think neither of these statements are correct.  I think (if I’m not getting confused) that phi in the neg_binomial_2 distribution is simply alpha, the shape parameter.

The overdispersion (as usually defined) is 1 + 1/beta, hence is always at least 1.

I think this all might be explaining some of the confusion we’ve been having lately, also suggests we should have negative_binomial_3 that is given in terms of mu and the overdispersion.

A

messages.body_plain:
I always thought that the first parameter of neg_binomial_2 represents mean.  Since mean in GLM context is exp(beta'x) where beta is a parameter and x is independent variable, I never intended to put a prior on mu.  However I wanted to put a hierarchical prior on the second parameter, phi.  My expectation was that variance is expressed as mu+mu^2/phi so by giving a hierarchical prior on phi I implicitly attributed different variability to each sample (in my case particle count).  So what is correct?

Anyway, what hierarchical prior (lognormal/gamma/etc) should phi have (i.e. phi~lognormal(loc,scale) as well as what hyper priors (i.e. loc~normal(0,5) and scale~half-cauchy(0,2)) should be used?

Linas

I’m not exactly sure what you are expecting — 4 minutes per iteration for
a big model like this is pretty fast.  Especially when you consider that
with that much data your posterior is likely concentrating on some very
small neighborhood, and if you have any non-identifiabilities that
neighborhood will be a thin, warped surface that requires a very small
step size to explore adequately.  The I/O overhead can be substantial,
especially if you’re using RStan or PyStan, and you might want to
run from CmdStan to focus computational resources on sampling alone.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Custom Distribution with double indexing
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Custom Distribution with double indexing
messages.body_plain:
1.  You need to provide your whole model --- there weren't
any sampling statements in what you sent, so no way to diagnose
the warning.

2.  There's not a whole lot more opportunity for
vectorization given our available operations.  You've already
properly converted to log-scale multiplies and used the
vectorization built into log_sum_exp.

With things like this:

> log( p[cust_id[t]]) + x[t] * log1m(c[cust_id[t]] ) + log(c[cust_id[t]] ) );
> }

You might try precomputing three vectors:

log_p_cust_id[t]

log1m_c_cust_id[t]

log_c_cust_id[t]

if they get reused.  You can even combine the first and last, for

 log_p_cust_id_plus_log_c_cust_id[t]

Removing duplicated subexpressions is a huge savings for autodiff.

3. You just need to define x as the first argument to a function
ending in _log, as indicated in the manual.  Then all the increments
go on the inside of the function.

4.  Prediction works exactly the same way with custom-defined
functions --- you'll just need to write what you need for prediction.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Just think about the variance — the over dispersion is
significant when mu^{2} / phi is on the same order of mu,
so

mu^{2} / phi ~ mu
mu / phi ~ 1
mu ~ phi

Consequently the absolute amount of over dispersion
depends on the mean so you have to think about your prior
in terms of relatively over dispersion.

generated quantities {
vector[N] log_lik;
for (n in 1:N){

}
}

I don't know what you mean by "chain temperature" so I can't

I'm not the best person to talk to about WAIC --- you want
Andrew or Aki, and hence really want to write to our users list."

you, what I found online is: "Temp -- The temperature parameter for
heating the chains. The higher the temperature, the more likely the heated
chains are to move between isolated peaks in the posterior
distribution..." cf. http://mrbayes.sourceforge.net/Help/mcmc.html

Does anyone know about "chain temperatures"?

Many thanks!

David

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Model Selection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Model Selection
messages.body_plain:
I would highly recommend that you don’t attempt these algorithms without
at least a basic understanding of what’s going on — they’re notoriously
difficult to implement with any reasonable quantification of error.

Firstly, the evidence/marginal likelihood is fundamentally different from
WAIC as they consider two completely different criteria for comparing
models.  See, for example, http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02273.

On to thermodynamic algorithms.  The essential idea behind all of these
algorithms (see, for example, https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ss/1028905934)
is to interpolate between a simple base distribution (typically the prior) and a
more complicated distribution (typically the posterior).  If we use the prior as
our base distribution then we can write the interpolation as

pi(theta, beta) = (likelihood(theta) )^{beta} prior(theta),

where beta is an “inverse temperature”.  For beta = 0 we recover the prior
while beta = 1 yields the posterior.

Thermodynamic integration defines a partition of beta \in [0, 1] and then
computes the averages

L(beta) = E_{pi_{beta}} [ likelihood ] = \int dtheta pi(theta, beta) likelihood(theta)

If you wanted to use Stan to compute these intermediate averages then
you need to define a model for each pi(theta, beta), compute the likelihood
in generated quantities, and _then_ average the likelihood at each iteration
over the entire Markov chain.  You could throw these ( L(beta), beta) pairs
into some code such as the one you mentioned, but unless you choose
the partition of beta very carefully then you’re likely to get a biased answer.

Again, it’s technically feasible to compute these intermediate averages in
Stan but that that will require implementing pi(beta, theta) for each beta
and not just a single model, and doesn’t even get you halfway because
you still have to worry about how accurate the thermodynamic integration is.

That's not enough context to debug.  It helps us immensely
to be able to see your whole program and exactly what you
typed to R and exactly what R gets back.

When you call inits(), do you get a value?  These
functions that depend on global variables can go wrong
if the globals aren't defined.  It's much safer and
easier for others to read if you make your functions
self contained.

And how did you call Stan?  If you provide the wrong argument,
you'll get the same problem.

I think this is largely our fault for not making our
error messages more informative --- did it find a list and
just not find that value?  Did it find a list with that key that
had an NA?

- Bob

> On Jul 6, 2015, at 1:40 AM, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
>
>
> If z is a K-dimensional parameter vector constrained so that
>
>   sum(z) = 0,
>
> then you can code up z as follows:
>
> Is that simplex-based thing somehow preferable to
>
> parameters {
>   vector[K-1] z_free;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[K] z;
>   for(k in 1:(K-1) z[k] <- z_free[k];
>   z[K] <- -sum(z_free);
> }

This is how we recommend doing this.  Except that
you need a further paren after (K - 1) or it won't parse.

>
> In this case z[K] could get far off from z[1..k-1], whereas in simplex based z[K] "behave" like the others.
>   However, the one additional parameters in the simplex adds additional noise and the solution is less optimal.

It's a different parameterization and the parameterization
of a model matters to Stan (and most samplers including Gibbs
and Metropolis) because it affects the posterior geometry.

This is still a wide-open area of research if anyone with
a theory of applied computational stats bent wants to delve
deeper.  The Betancourt and Girolami paper on hierarchical priors
is a good role model for what such papers will look like.  For
example, we've been playing around with IRT model identification
and that's ripe for a writeup.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Aside from the modeling issue, that statement will, perhaps
surprisingly, have absolutely no effect on sampling.

The problem is that it's branching on the value of a parameter,
then adding a constant to the log density.  Constants added to
the log density never do anything to sampling.  The log
density is either lp or lp + 1e-10, neither of which is an expression
involving theta.  It got there via examining theta, but it has no way
of exploiting that discontinuity at theta = 5 or theta = -5.

- Bob

> On Jul 5, 2015, at 7:54 AM, Philipp Upravitelev <uprav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> Unfortunately I can't understand the logic of vector arithmetics. Well, I can understand it in simple cases like an exponential function (pdf, of course).

> But it is difficult to me to write this (lognormal pdf):

>   for (n in 1:N)
>     increment_log_prob(-log(y[n] * sigma * ml) - pow((log(y[n]) - mu), 2)/(2 * pow(sigma, 2)));
>
>  in vectorized form. Could you help me with it? Where I should use "sum" and multiplication by N, and why?

What exactly are you trying to do?    If you have a lognormal PDF, you can
just write

  y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);

And the sampling statement will drop any constant terms not needed to
define the density up to a proportion.

I don't know what the term ml is.

You just want to do the algebra.  You have a sum of N terms.
Some of them will be repeated, so you can pull them out of the
lop and multiply by N, for instance a -log(sigma) term.

- Bob

quantities constraints get violated, the whole sampler stops because
we have no way to recover at that point.

> of the Stagnant model, for a simple case of an intercept and one covariate (data are 17 countries observed over ~50 years, N=854). It runs fine and converges quickly but I'm not confident that it's doing what I expect it to do. Here is the STAN code:
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;
>     real time[N];                    // time variable
>     real<lower=0> lincr[N];     // y variable
>     real sud[N];                     // x variable
> }
> parameters {
>     real <lower=0> alpha;
>     real beta[2];
>     real gamma[2];
>     real <lower=0> sigma;
>     real<lower=5, upper=45> cp;      // change point
> }
> model {
>     real mu[N];
>     alpha ~ normal(0,5);
>     beta ~ normal(0,5);
>     gamma ~ normal(0,5);
>     sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
>     for (i in 1:N)
>         mu[i] <- alpha +
>           if_else(time[i]<cp, beta[1] + gamma[1] * sud[i],
>           beta[2] + gamma[2] * sud[i]) * (time[i] - cp);
>     lincr ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
>

This isn't going to work well for sampling because you're
conditioning on a parameter and creating a discontinuous
desnity.  It might work, but it won't be able to leverage gradients
for efficient MCMC.

> And the results:
>
> Inference for Stan model: pris_cp_nox.
> 3 chains, each with iter=1000; warmup=500; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=500, total post-warmup draws=1500.
>

> beta[2]    0.012   0.000 0.002   0.008   0.015   611 1.005
> gamma[1]   0.010   0.001 0.015  -0.010   0.037   424 1.012
> gamma[2]  -0.015   0.000 0.002  -0.019  -0.012   387 1.009
> sigma      0.477   0.000 0.012   0.457   0.497   659 1.004
> cp        13.036   0.174 2.928   7.985  17.687   282 1.014
> lp__     209.159   0.116 2.147 205.152 211.945   345 1.015
>

Did you simulate the data and know this is recovering the right value?

Of course, values of cp between time[i] points have no meaning here --- there's
nothing to control them other than th eprior.

> My understanding is that alpha is the adjusted mean of Y, the betas are estimated differences in the mean before/after the change point, and gammas are before/after estimates of the effects of sud (a standardized measure). This could be wildly wrong since I don't really get the original Stagnant example.

Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters.  I
work through a simple example there.

> I want to extend this further into a multilevel model (random intercepts with country-level predictors), and would welcome any feedback and suggestions about the model so far (syntax and interpretation).

I'd try to keep the model continuously differentiable for the best
sampling, but I don't know how to do that with a continuous change point.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
A related issue here is how to apply soft constraints. I've previously imposed soft constraints in Stan by assigning a prior to the transformed parameter. For example, we often know a priori that log-odds of some event are not much below -5 and not much above +5. Applying regularization to the whole linear predictor seems a lot more natural at times than applying it to individual coefficients in the linear model.

If Andrew or anyone else has done some work on this issue, would be curious to read it.

On Sunday, July 5, 2015 at 3:45:51 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I repeat that you should avoid hard constraints unless they are physically part of the problem.
>
> > On Jul 5, 2015, at 6:22 AM, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
> >
> > How about?
> >
> > if(theta < -5 || theta > 5)
> >    increment_log_prob(-1.0e10);
> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how to use Matt Trick for constrained variables?
messages.body_plain:
If you apply a prior to a transformed parameter, be sure to
include the Jacobian.

Constraining the linear predictor can be viewed as a data-dependent
constraint on the coefficients.   But I don't see how to make sense of
it from a modeling point of view.

If you really need to constrain the linear predictor to fall
in (-5, 5), then the scaled and shifted logit (or tanh) is one
way to do it.

Andrew at one point suggested using an IRT 3PL-like trick to
tame logistic regression in BUGS/JAGS, taking:

  Pr[y[n] = 1] = 0.01 + 0.98 * inv_logit(alpha[n]);

where alpha[n] is the linear predictor for boolean observation y[n].
That guarantees the estimated probability stays in (0.01, 0.99).   I
have no idea where to find that among Andrew's gazillion published
and unpublished papers, or even if I'm remembering entirely correctly.

- Bob

messages.subject: Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

I am trying to fit a vector autoregressive model in Stan. For those not familiar with kind of model and to render the post a bit self-contained, let me sketch what I'm trying to estimate.

Model.
Let time be indexed by t=1, ..., T. For every time period t I have a (Mx1) vector of variables y_t. In matrix notation my model reads

> Y = X * A + U

where

> Y = [y_{p+1}', ..., y_T']'

is the (T-p x M) matrix of contemporaneous observations, and

> X = [x_{p+1},..., x_T ]' with x_t = [1, y_{t-1}', ..., y_{t-p}']

is the ((T-p) x (1+ M*p)) matrix of lagged observations (incl. an intercept). The matrix of coefficients A is therefore ((1+ M*p) x M) with the first row carrying the intercepts and all remaining rows the slopes.

I assume that U ~ Normal(0, Sigma) and for the moment an idependent N(0,1) prior for the coefficients in A. The prior for Sigma is inverse-Wishart with scale matrix S and DF nu.

> S = (Y - X*Â)'(Y-XÂ)

where Â = (X'X)^{-1} X'Y is the OLS estimate for A and nu = T-p-M-K-1 .

Implementation in Stan (also see VAR.stan attached).
I run the model from R, using RStan. I ran the model on an artificial dataset which I generate using the attached R script (see below). Since the model code in Stan is quite short, let me streamline it here:

> Data block & transformed data block
> I prepare the data mostly in R. In particular, I construct the matrix X in R and hand it over to Stan.
> data {
>     int<lower=0> T;         // No. of time periods observed
>     int<lower=0> M;         // No. of variables in y_t
>     int<lower=1> p;         // Lag order
>     matrix[T, M] y;         // Matrix of time series
>     matrix[T-p, M] Y;       // Matrix of time series for LHS
>     matrix[T-p, 1+M*p] X;   // Matrix of lags of LHS variables
> }
> transformed data {
>     int<lower=1> K;         // No. of parameters per equation
>     int<lower=1> K_slope;   // No. of slope parameters per equation
>     int<lower=0> T_eff;     // The effective number of obs. we can use, see below
>     matrix[M, M] S;         // Scale matrix for inv. Wishart prior on Sigma
>     int nu;                 // DF for Wishart prior on Sigma
>
>     S <- crossprod(Y - X * (crossprod(X)\X'*Y));
>     K <- 1 + M * p;
>     K_slope <- M * p;
>     T_eff <- T - p;
>     nu <- T_eff - K - M - 1;
> }
>
> Parameters & transformed parameters block.
> Parameters are A and Sigma, but for readability I like to separate them into slopes and intercepts.
> parameters {
>     matrix[K, M] A;         // Matrix of AR coefficients incl. intercept
>     cov_matrix[M] Sigma;    // Covariance of the error terms
> }
> transformed parameters {
>     row_vector[M] intercepts;
>     matrix[K_slope, M] slopes;
>
>     intercepts <- row(A, 1);
>     slopes <- block(A, 2, 1, K_slope, M);
> }
>
> Model block.
> Given the matrix X and A, I can write the mean for Y as a function of its own lags as the matrix product X * A. For
> model {
>     matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
>
>     // A toy prior on the slopes
>     for(i in 1:K)
>         A[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     // Inv-Wishart for covariance matrix
>     Sigma ~ inv_wishart(nu, S);
>
>     // Likelihood
>     mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>     for(n in 1:T_eff)
>         Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mus[n], Sigma);
> }
>

The file VAR_data.R generates an artificial dataset for this model with T=300, M=3, p=2 and then compiles the model from R and runs two chains. The file VAR.RData contains the artificial dataset and model results in the object 'fitted.model'.

My sessionInfo()

> R version 3.1.3 (2015-03-09)
> Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
> Running under: Windows 7 x64 (build 7601) Service Pack 1
>
>
> locale:
> [1] LC_COLLATE=...  LC_CTYPE=...    LC_MONETARY=... LC_NUMERIC=C                    LC_TIME=...
>
>
> attached base packages:
> [1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base
>
>
> other attached packages:
> [1] rstan_2.6.0      inline_0.3.13    Rcpp_0.11.5      MHadaptive_1.1-8 MASS_7.3-39      mnormt_1.5-1
>
>
> loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
> [1] stats4_3.1.3 tools_3.1.3
>

What comes out is not very encouraging. Since sampling here on my computer takes very long (unlike for other models with more parameters), I only ran two chains with 500 iterations each. Both the effective sample size and the Rhat statistic for the parameters are horrible and I am wondering why. The posterior means of the elements of the covariance are ok, but their Rhat still terrible. For parameters in A everything is just terrible. Do I simply need to run things longer?

I would expect a VAR to behave weird with really large dimensions, but this toy model is very small and should converge quickly, no? I would be grateful for any hints at the glaring mistakes or inefficiencies in my code - I'm still learning.

Many thanks in advance and cheers,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 7, 2015, at 10:08 AM, Shravan Vasishth <vasishth...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> I saw your HMC demo in your Australia talk. Is it possible to get the code for that, or is it too cumbersome to share? I guess it must be quite involved since you showed gifs.

I just responded to the list on this one:

  https://www.dropbox.com/sh/vobwxzt256l53jl/AAC6-ho_ESw37aNESkQlKvZHa?dl=0

> Very nice talk by the way.

Thanks.  It went awfully fast!

I just ran into Kyle Mahowald, a student of Ted Gibson at MIT, who was
telling me how much he liked your tutorial on Stan for psycholinguistics!
He was interested in getting involved, but thought you'd pretty much
covered all the bases that a psycholinguist would need.

>  I still can't understand where the Jacobian is in the LJK Cholesky factorization;
> is there an introductory book or article I can read that explains this to non-mathematicians like me?

It was Greek to me, too, when Ben first wrote it down.  But
once you get your head around the fact that determinants are
calculate volume, the rest is easy.  Think about an axis-aligned hyperrectangle,
represented as a diagonal matrix --- its volume is the
product of the diagonal entries, and the volume's invariant to
rotation off axis alignment.

> I know what a Jacobian is and what it's for, I just don't see where it comes in here. I understand that the Cholesky factorization takes a sort of square root, so that's a kind of transformation like
>
> Y = \sqrt{X}
>
> So, this is the classic situation where a change of variables will need a Jacobian term. I can write all that down analytically for the textbook examples. But I don't know how to proceed with the Jacobian involved in the Cholesky factor.

The Jacobian is calculated for the inverse function from unconstrained
to constrained.  It first creates a lower-triangular L and then
maps to L * L'.

There's a chapter near the end of the manual that goes over all the
Jacobians in gory detail, starting with the general definitions
of Jacobians.

The tricky bit of the Cholesky is generating an appropriate
L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix --- each row
of L is of Euclidean length 1 and must have a positive diagonal entry.
Then there's the algebra to reduce the Jacobian.

I still find the LKJ paper hard going, but that goes over several
alternative ways to do it --- the decomposition to unconstrained
parameters we use isn't the only one possible.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.body_plain:
We have advice on how to set up effective priors for sampling in
the manual.  We recommend (a) working with Cholesky factors, and
(b) using a scaled correlation matrix with LKJ priors.  Stan does
not use any conjugacy information, so using inv_wishart isn't going
to be any faster.   There are links to a paper by Ben on why we like
the LKJ.

There's also no efficient inverse Wishart on the Cholesky factor
scale.  It's on our to-do list, but given that we don't use or
recommend (inverse) Wishart priors, it's not a high priority.

You also want to vectorize, so this bit of the model

    matrix[T_eff, M] mus;

    // A toy prior on the slopes
    for(i in 1:K)
        A[i] ~ normal(0, 1);

    // Likelihood
    mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
    for(n in 1:T_eff)
        Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mus[n], Sigma);

becomes this:

  A ~ normal(0, 1);
  Y ~ multi_normal(X * A, Sigma);

But you really want to replace that Sigma with a Cholesky factor,
and use:

  Y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(X * A, L_Sigma);

I couldn't follow all your linear algebra in the transformed data, so
have no idea what it's doing or whether there might be a problem.  Hopefully
you would've tested it all somehow (like with print() statements) to make sure
it's doing what you want.

- Bob

> On Jul 7, 2015, at 7:02 AM, Paul Viefers <paulv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan users,
>
> I am trying to fit a vector autoregressive model in Stan. For those not familiar with kind of model and to render the post a bit self-contained, let me sketch what I'm trying to estimate.
>
> Model.
> Let time be indexed by t=1, ..., T. For every time period t I have a (Mx1) vector of variables y_t. In matrix notation my model reads
>
> Y = X * A + U
>
> where
>
> Y = [y_{p+1}', ..., y_T']'
>
> is the (T-p x M) matrix of contemporaneous observations, and
>
> X = [x_{p+1},..., x_T ]' with x_t = [1, y_{t-1}', ..., y_{t-p}']
>
> is the ((T-p) x (1+ M*p)) matrix of lagged observations (incl. an intercept). The matrix of coefficients A is therefore ((1+ M*p) x M) with the first row carrying the intercepts and all remaining rows the slopes.
>
> I assume that U ~ Normal(0, Sigma) and for the moment an idependent N(0,1) prior for the coefficients in A. The prior for Sigma is inverse-Wishart with scale matrix S and DF nu.
>
> S = (Y - X*Â)'(Y-XÂ)
>
> where Â = (X'X)^{-1} X'Y is the OLS estimate for A and nu = T-p-M-K-1 .
>
>
> Implementation in Stan (also see VAR.stan attached).
> I run the model from R, using RStan. I ran the model on an artificial dataset which I generate using the attached R script (see below). Since the model code in Stan is quite short, let me streamline it here:
>
> Data block & transformed data block
> I prepare the data mostly in R. In particular, I construct the matrix X in R and hand it over to Stan.
> data {
>     int<lower=0> T;         // No. of time periods observed
>     int<lower=0> M;         // No. of variables in y_t
>     int<lower=1> p;         // Lag order
>     matrix[T, M] y;         // Matrix of time series
>     matrix[T-p, M] Y;       // Matrix of time series for LHS
>     matrix[T-p, 1+M*p] X;   // Matrix of lags of LHS variables
> }
> transformed data {
>     int<lower=1> K;         // No. of parameters per equation
>     int<lower=1> K_slope;   // No. of slope parameters per equation
>     int<lower=0> T_eff;     // The effective number of obs. we can use, see below
>     matrix[M, M] S;         // Scale matrix for inv. Wishart prior on Sigma
>     int nu;                 // DF for Wishart prior on Sigma
>
>     S <- crossprod(Y - X * (crossprod(X)\X'*Y));
>     K <- 1 + M * p;
>     K_slope <- M * p;
>     T_eff <- T - p;
>     nu <- T_eff - K - M - 1;
> }
>
> Parameters & transformed parameters block.
> Parameters are A and Sigma, but for readability I like to separate them into slopes and intercepts.
> parameters {
>     matrix[K, M] A;         // Matrix of AR coefficients incl. intercept
>     cov_matrix[M] Sigma;    // Covariance of the error terms
> }
> transformed parameters {
>     row_vector[M] intercepts;
>     matrix[K_slope, M] slopes;
>
>     intercepts <- row(A, 1);
>     slopes <- block(A, 2, 1, K_slope, M);
> }
>
> Model block.
> Given the matrix X and A, I can write the mean for Y as a function of its own lags as the matrix product X * A. For
> model {
>     matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
>
>     // A toy prior on the slopes
>     for(i in 1:K)
>         A[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     // Inv-Wishart for covariance matrix
>     Sigma ~ inv_wishart(nu, S);
>
>     // Likelihood
>     mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>     for(n in 1:T_eff)
>         Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mus[n], Sigma);
> }
>
>
> The file VAR_data.R generates an artificial dataset for this model with T=300, M=3, p=2 and then compiles the model from R and runs two chains. The file VAR.RData contains the artificial dataset and model results in the object 'fitted.model'.
>
> My sessionInfo()
>
> R version 3.1.3 (2015-03-09)
> Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
> Running under: Windows 7 x64 (build 7601) Service Pack 1

> other attached packages:
> [1] rstan_2.6.0      inline_0.3.13    Rcpp_0.11.5      MHadaptive_1.1-8 MASS_7.3-39      mnormt_1.5-1
>
>
> loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
> [1] stats4_3.1.3 tools_3.1.3
>
>
> What comes out is not very encouraging. Since sampling here on my computer takes very long (unlike for other models with more parameters), I only ran two chains with 500 iterations each. Both the effective sample size and the Rhat statistic for the parameters are horrible and I am wondering why. The posterior means of the elements of the covariance are ok, but their Rhat still terrible. For parameters in A everything is just terrible. Do I simply need to run things longer?
>
> I would expect a VAR to behave weird with really large dimensions, but this toy model is very small and should converge quickly, no? I would be grateful for any hints at the glaring mistakes or inefficiencies in my code - I'm still learning.

> Paul

messages.body_plain:
We don't have it built-in, but if you mean this:

http://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0606238.pdf

then you can just implement that pmf directly in Stan
as a function.  You can even write it so that it uses
sampling notation,

  real generalized_poisson_log(int y, int n, real theta, real lambda) {
    return log(theta)
           + (n - 1) * log(theta + n * lambda)
           - lgamma(n + 1)
           - n * lambda
           - theta;
  }

Then you could use it in the code as:

  y ~ generalized_poisson(n, theta, lambda);

If you want efficient vectorization, you have to implement the function
you need to do it.  But the above will work in a loop and you can
always optimize later.

It'd probably be worthwhile to add error checking on the inputs.

- Bob

On Tuesday, July 7, 2015 at 10:53:33 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >  I still can't understand where the Jacobian is in the LJK Cholesky factorization;
> > is there an introductory book or article I can read that explains this to non-mathematicians like me?

No, there isn't. Part of the problem is that there are actually 4 Jacobians. If Lambda is a correlation matrix of order K, the LKJ (2009) paper derives a PDF
f(Lambda | eta) \ propto det(Lambda)^(eta - 1)
It is more useful numerically to work with a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix L, such that Lambda = L * L'. In that case, you have the new PDF via the change-of-variables theorem
f(L | eta) \propto det(J) * det(L * L')^(eta - 1) = det(J) * det(L)^(2 * eta - 2)
The Jacobian matrix, J, for the transformation from L to Lambda is not so bad (it only involves the diagonal elements of L) and is described at the end of the Stan User Manual. Although this transformation is straightforward, the LKJ (2009) paper did not actually work this PDF out. To compound matters, the LKJ (2009) paper shows an equivalence in distribution to something an earlier paper called the "onion method" of generating a random correlation matrix that would have been much simpler if they had just derived f(L | eta).

What the LKJ (2009) paper did do is derive a transformation from K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations to K * (K - 1) / 2 Pearson correlations (that fill a triangle of Lambda). What Stan actually does is a transformation from the (K * (K - 1) / 2 lower-triangular elements of L to the K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations. This part is potentially confusing because there are actually many different ways of defining a set of  K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations, depending on what gets partialed out. However, from a numerical perspective, the choice is obvious because only one partialization scheme avoids having to invert submatrices, which is what LKJ calls "partial correlations on a C-vine" or what I call "canonical partial correlations". A canonical partial correlation between variables i and j is the correlation in the residuals of i and the residuals of j when i and j are each regressed on all variables (if any) before the i-th where i < j. So, Stan only utilizes canonical partial correlations, which are proportional to the lower-triangular elements of L, in which case the Jacobian matrix for this transformation is diagonal.

In any event, the LKJ (2009) paper works out the transformation from canonical partial correlations to the lower-triangular elements of Lambda without going through L. It turns out that if the canonical partial correlations have independent symmetric Beta priors on the (-1,1) interval, then the PDF for Lambda given above follows. Anyway, whether you go through L or not, you have these canonical partial correlations that are constrained to the (-1,1) interval but Stan needs parameters over the whole real number line. So, we do a Fisher (inverse) transformation of each canonical partial correlation to the real line, which is pretty simple and described in the Stan manual.

So there you have it. That said, none of these transformations give much statistical insight. I don't know why you would believe that the canonical partial correlations have these particular Beta prior distributions, except that they imply a simple form for f(Lambda | eta) \proto det(Lambda)^(eta - 1) which is easy to make uniform by setting eta = 1 and easy to make the identity matrix the mode by setting eta > 1. And the only reasons --- although they are substantial --- to work with L rather than Lambda is numeric stability and computational speed.

Ben

At a high level, here's the drill.

Suppose Sigma is a correlation matrix and nu > 0, with

  p(Sigma | nu) = LKJ(Sigma | nu);

Then the density of its Cholesky factor

  L = chol(Sigma)

is given by

  p(L | nu) = LKJ(L * L' | nu) * | det(J_f) |

where J_f is the Jacobian of the function

   f(L) = (L * L').

Note that f is the inverse of the Cholesky factorization.

Then it's just a matter of being a lot better than me
at turning the crank on the determinant and derivative
calcluations :-).

- Bob

To compound matters, the LKJ (2009) paper shows an equivalence in distribution to something an earlier paper called the "onion method" of generating a random correlation matrix that would have been much simpler if they had just derived f(L | eta).
>
> What the LKJ (2009) paper did do is derive a transformation from K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations to K * (K - 1) / 2 Pearson correlations (that fill a triangle of Lambda). What Stan actually does is a transformation from the (K * (K - 1) / 2 lower-triangular elements of L to the K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations. This part is potentially confusing because there are actually many different ways of defining a set of  K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations, depending on what gets partialed out. However, from a numerical perspective, the choice is obvious because only one partialization scheme avoids having to invert submatrices, which is what LKJ calls "partial correlations on a C-vine" or what I call "canonical partial correlations". A canonical partial correlation between variables i and j is the correlation in the residuals of i and the residuals of j when i and j are each regressed on all variables (if any) before the i-th where i < j. So, Stan only utilizes canonical partial correlations, which are proportional to the lower-triangular elements of L, in which case the Jacobian matrix for this transformation is diagonal.
>
> In any event, the LKJ (2009) paper works out the transformation from canonical partial correlations to the lower-triangular elements of Lambda without going through L. It turns out that if the canonical partial correlations have independent symmetric Beta priors on the (-1,1) interval, then the PDF for Lambda given above follows. Anyway, whether you go through L or not, you have these canonical partial correlations that are constrained to the (-1,1) interval but Stan needs parameters over the whole real number line. So, we do a Fisher (inverse) transformation of each canonical partial correlation to the real line, which is pretty simple and described in the Stan manual.
>
> So there you have it. That said, none of these transformations give much statistical insight. I don't know why you would believe that the canonical partial correlations have these particular Beta prior distributions, except that they imply a simple form for f(Lambda | eta) \proto det(Lambda)^(eta - 1) which is easy to make uniform by setting eta = 1 and easy to make the identity matrix the mode by setting eta > 1. And the only reasons --- although they are substantial --- to work with L rather than Lambda is numeric stability and computational speed.
>
> Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Many thanks for the swift response. It's really awesome you guys provide support here for people to learn.

I spent the afternoon going over the code in an attempt to fix things.

A. Summary
Before going into details, I have implemented your suggestions as far as possible and it works much better now, but still not good I'd say. For a 2-dimensional vector process y_t (M=2), the model works somehow, but that's just a toy linear model with 10 parameters in A and 3 parameters in Sigma and no hierarchical structure. Intercepts are recovered much better than slopes, variances and covariances are awful. This gives me an indication that the code is not terribly off base - its' just not very good and I'd like to know why.
Setting M=3 and (i) the sampler slows down dramatically - both in terms of wall time and effective sample size, (ii) Rhat explodes and (iii) posteriors means nowhere close to the actual value. Increasing the number of observed time periods (T) does not help dramatically.

I have attached the newest version of my code and the R file that creates the artificial data (for M=2 and M=3) and runs the model.

B. Details.
Concerning your comments and suggestions:
Prior on the covariance matrix: Inverse-Wishart -> LKJ + Cholesky

> > We have advice on how to set up effective priors for sampling in
> > the manual.  We recommend (a) working with Cholesky factors, and
> > (b) using a scaled correlation matrix with LKJ priors.  Stan does
> > not use any conjugacy information, so using inv_wishart isn't going
> > to be any faster.   There are links to a paper by Ben on why we like
> > the LKJ.
> > There's also no efficient inverse Wishart on the Cholesky factor
> > scale.  It's on our to-do list, but given that we don't use or
> > recommend (inverse) Wishart priors, it's not a high priority.

I suspected nobody here will like to see (inverse-)Wishart priors on covariances, but it served as a first brush and was meant to make thing comparable to other implementations, e.g in R with the Gibbs. I saw you suggest these priors for the covariance matrix of regression coefficients in a hierarchical model, but note that I am applying it to the sampling covariance matrix, so it didn't come to my mind immediately to use it for that purpose. But I implemented it the way it is suggested in the manual (an LKJ cholesky prior and a separate half-cauchy prior on the vector of variances) and I think it is a major improvement. Previously, the chain wasn't exploring at all and got stuck at the starting values, because all proposals were rejected. Now the chain isn't stuck anymore - so it's much more well-behaved. However, the scale matrix of the inverse-Wishart (S in my notation, see transformed parameter block in previous post) in my earlier code really helped to recover the parameters in the covariance matrix. The LKJ prior is worse in that respect - assuming I did not commit a mistake.

Vectorization

> > You also want to vectorize, so this bit of the model
> >
> >     matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
> >
> >     // A toy prior on the slopes
> >     for(i in 1:K)
> >         A[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
> >
> >     // Likelihood
> >     mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
> >     for(n in 1:T_eff)
> >         Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mus[n], Sigma);
> >
> >
> > becomes this:
> >
> >   A ~ normal(0, 1);
> >   Y ~ multi_normal(X * A, Sigma);
> >
> > But you really want to replace that Sigma with a Cholesky factor,
> > and use:
> >
> >   Y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(X * A, L_Sigma);

> I tried this, but I think this is not possible here, because both A and Y are matrices. So I get a syntax error when trying to hand a matrix over to 'normal' or 'multi_normal'. What I do is to continue to resort to the standard workaround and constuct a temporary matrix of linear predictors and loop over its rows. I.e. writing Y[n] returns the n-th row of the matrix Y and the likelihood part of my code

> // Likelihood
>         matrix[T_eff, M] mus;

>
>         mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>         for(n in 1:T_eff)

>
>             Y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mus[n], L_Omega);
> >
> loops over all T_eff rows of Y and mus. What I can vectorize is the prior on A by using the 'to_vector' function (see below) - thanks for that hint!

C. Updated model code.
Following your advice and changing the priors on the covariance and writing it terms of the Cholesky leads to the following updated code

> Data & Transformed data block.
> Note that I have added prior hyperparameters to the data, so I do not have to recompile the code every time I play with the prior.

> data {
>     int<lower=0> T;         // No. of time periods observed
>     int<lower=0> M;         // No. of variables in y_t
>     int<lower=1> p;         // Lag order

>
>     matrix[T-p, M] Y;       // Matrix of time series for LHS
>     matrix[T-p, 1+M*p] X;   // Matrix of lags of LHS variables

>
>
>     // Prior hyperparameters
>     real<lower=0> s_A;      // SD of the normal prior on elements of A
>     real<lower=0> cauchy_scale;
>     real<lower=0> lkj_shape;

>
> }
> transformed data {
>     int<lower=1> K;         // No. of parameters per equation
>     int<lower=1> K_slope;   // No. of slope parameters per equation
>     int<lower=0> T_eff;     // The effective number of obs. we can use, see below

>
>     K <- 1 + M * p;
>     K_slope <- M * p;
>     T_eff <- T - p;
> }

>
> Parameters & Transformed parameters.

> parameters {
>     matrix[K, M] A;         // Matrix of AR coefficients incl. intercept

>
>     cholesky_factor_corr[M] L_Omega;
>     vector<lower=0>[M] tau; // Vector of error variances
> }
> transformed parameters {
>     matrix[M,M] Sigma;

messages.subject: Re: performance cost of extra transformed parameters?
messages.subject_clean: performance cost of extra transformed parameters?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, July 8, 2015 at 4:28:57 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> So, is it worth the effort to calculate stuff twice (local block in tranformed parameters & generated quantities to output it)? Or would you advise to place the eta stuff in the model block which anyway does not store declared variables. I am asking because I wonder what is best performance wise, i.e. what reduces the burden for the autodiff stack of Stan during sampling?

Whether you put something in transformed parameters or the model block has the same implication for autodiff (and autodiff is not used in generated quantities). So, really the only way that there could be a noticeable performance implication is if the validation check --- which is performed for transformed parameters but not in the model or generated quantities blocks --- is expensive. But the only expensive one is the positive definiteness check, and that can be avoided if you know a matrix is positive definite by construction by declaring it as a plain square matrix rather than a covariance matrix.

The diag_pre_multiply() function, on the other hand, is designed to avoid putting unnecessary stuff onto the autodiff stack. It just scales each row of the right-most matrix by the corresponding element of the diagonal vector, rather than multiplying columns by the off-diagonal zeros and summing. So, there isn't a way to do it faster unless the right-most matrix is also structured.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Sorry I haven't gotten back to you on this.  We've been
swamped preparing a course and getting Stan 2.7 out.

The R-hat measure isn't whether the 10 different chains together
explored the space, but rather whether they each explored the space.
So we're measuring within-chain means and variances and comparing to
the result of pooling across chains, under the assumption the answer
should be the same.  We use that to compute n_eff as well as R-hat.

Strong correlations can certainly break sampling efficiency.  Sometimes
reparameterizing the model with the same posterior but a different
sampling basis can help.

- Bob

> On Jun 28, 2015, at 9:54 AM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>
> Given what Bob said, now I wonder if the issue is just an instance of extremely poor mixing, though I am a bit surprised that 12,000 samples from 10 different chains are not enough for NUTS to explore the space fully.
>
> I ran Stan with the same model three times and the smallest Rhat ranged 1.03 - 1.15. I have 750 latent parameters in addition to 3 hyper parameters and the latent parameters seem to be strongly correlated with one of the hyper parameter.

>
> There's a chapter in the manual that goes over the transforms
> and the Jacobians.  For upper and lower bounds we use a scaled
> and translated inverse-logit transform, which produces a logistic
> distribution once the Jacobian's applied.  (Basically, the logistic
> is the CDF.)
>
> > Given that the log transform does not result in a heavy tailed distribution, I am not too sure why Stan is not sampling near scale = 0 at all in my example.
> >
> > I think there are miscommunication (mode, mean, MSE, Bayesian & MLE, and etc), so I will just send the example as soon as I get a permission from the company.
>
> OK --- these terms all have pretty clear definitions, so I hope
> we're not miscommunicating about them.
>
> This is helpful for my understanding, too.  Here's what Stan does
> with a very simple model:
>
>   data { int<lower=0> N; vector[N] y; }
>   parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
>   model { y ~ normal(mu, sigma); }
>
> given data y that is 10 copies of the value 1 (equivalent to
> y being a random effect with complete pooling [variance=0]):
>
>             mean  se_mean        sd        2.5%       97.5% n_eff      Rhat
> mu      1.0000000 0.000000 0.0000001   0.9999998   1.0000002  3087 0.9995303
> sigma   0.0000002 0.000000 0.0000001   0.0000001   0.0000005     3 2.8025187
> lp__  137.4845920 1.918341 3.0348166 130.8990197 142.8267866     3 2.8581082
>
> And that's using an improper prior, which is fatter tailed
> than any proper density.  So you can see that Stan can get very
> close to 0.  But the problem is that it's not converging well
> by the R-hat values.  A better math stats person than me can
> probably work out the posterior.
>
> You get roughly the same result with a Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 9:05:39 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >> On Jun 25, 2015, at 9:41 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> I am not looking at the posterior mean of the hyper parameters, but the posterior distributions.
> >
> > But those aren't points.  How do you estimate square error with
> > a distribution?  In expectation?
> >
> >> The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.
> >
> > But Bayesian inference doesn't care about the mode.  But it
> > will correspond to the mean in a symmetric distribution, but
> > your posterior for a scale parameter can't be symmetric, because
> > it's bounded below at 0 and has support on (0, inf).  (Actually,
> > I'm just guessing here.)
> >
> >> To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.
> >>
> >> I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right?
> >
> > Right --- if you supply <lower=0>, we log transform
> > the parameter for sampling, and apply the appropriate Jacobian
> > adjustment.  And you only need to get to -700 or so to
> > underflow to 0 using the inverse transform, exp().
> >
> >> If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity.
> >
> > Not quite.  There's a positive *density* at the boundary, but
> > that doesn't translate into heavy mass near infinity because things
> > get very stretched out under the log transform.
> >
> > And then there's the Jacobian.
> >
> > Of course, it depends where you start, because log transforming
> > an improper uniform on (0, inf) to (-inf, inf) produces an improper
> > result.
> >
> > Here's a histogram of the log transformed half Cauchy(0, 2.5),

> >
> >

Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.
> >
> > You're right that if the distribution's heavy tailed enough (as in
> > a Cauchy) or light tailed enough (in an untransformed triangle distribution,
> > say), then you can run into problems.
