messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I had a similar issues and I think rstan should improve here. For the moment I do the following:

1. I assume that you do compute in Stan the mean prediction for your model, i.e. commonly called mu or ypred (for the example model, the x*beta would need to be saved somewhere)
2. I wrote myself a function which takes as input the data I want to simulate and in addition those parameter values I want to simulate
3. This data I pass into a function together with the posterior
4. I then iterate over each draw from the posterior and combine the data + parameters to simulate with the posterior draw and pass this into Stan, calling the "Fixed_Param" algorithm
5. You end up with a prediction of the mean for each posterior draw and all you need to do is add your error term (if needed)

This procedure works nice and reliable, but is terribly slow if large amounts of data are generated as the communication between rstan and Stan itself is for reasons yet unknown (most likely Rcpp related) terribly slow. But, it is a nice method to simulate off a posterior after the fit has been done.

@ Ben: A function like this would be wonderful to have in rstan :)

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
I guess some are willing to try the ADVI algorithm, http://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03431.pdf, currently available in Github in some developer branches for the cmdStan interface. Below is what I did to get it apparently working:

1. git clone https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan.git -b feature/advi-command

2. In the cmdstan directory, "make stan-revert". (With "make stan-update/develop" I ended up having no math library.)

3. "make manual", then read the short chapter on variational estimation.

4. "make examples/bernoulli/bernoulli"

5. Within the bernoulli directory, first " ./bernoulli sample data file=bernoulli.data.R" to make sure Stan is working in general, then "./bernoulli variational data file=bernoulli.data.R"

I understand ADVI is experimental and any kind of support is limited, etc. I'm just eager to try it with some models that are slow with NUTS.

Thanks for making it available.

>

>
> 1. I assume that you do compute in Stan the mean prediction for your model, i.e. commonly called mu or ypred (for the example model, the x*beta would need to be saved somewhere)

> 3. This data I pass into a function together with the posterior
> 4. I then iterate over each draw from the posterior and combine the data + parameters to simulate with the posterior draw and pass this into Stan, calling the "Fixed_Param" algorithm

>

Yep, right. I also think that using some array structure would have been a much better choice. Generally, I was surprised to learn that rstan uses internally many nested lists to handle stan output. R is orders of magnitude faster if such things are handled with multi-dimensional arrays. They are a pain to program (index war), but are worth the effort. Maybe worth while for rstan3...

For efficiency, I'd first suggest a weakly informative prior on sigma.

Rewriting this:

> for (n in 1:N) {'
> '        xtemp <- col(x,n);'
> '        xttemp <- col(xt,n);'
> '        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[1,n],A[1]*xtemp,sigma));'

> '        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[4,n],A[4]*xttemp,sigma));'

using vectorization as

  increment_log_prob(beta * (normal_log(y[1], A[1] * x, sigma)
                             + normal_log(y[2], A[2] * x, sigma)
                             + normal_log(y[3], A[3] * xt, sigma)
                             + normal_log(y[4], A[4] * xt, sigma)));

should be much more efficient.

I couldn't follow what was going on with this:

> for (i in 1:4) {'
> '        for (j in 1:4) {'
> '            A[i,j] ~ normal(p[1,(i-1)*4+j], p[2,(i-1)*4+j]);'
> '        }'

but I'm guessing it could also be vectorized by rearranging that
p matrix, though it looks like a different mean and sd for each A[i,j],
so there might not be much to gain there.

I'm afraid there's no way to speed up the generated quantities calc, but

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, July 11, 2015 at 1:21:59 AM UTC-4, Sean Raleigh wrote:
> In Gelman and Hill, one finds the functions se.fixef() and se.ranef() for pulling standard errors out of a model fit by lmer(). Is there some way to get these standard errors from Stan (or, for that matter, any MCMC sample)?

The se.fixef() and se.ranef() functions are part of the arm package, which supports a closed set of models. Stan allows you to do pretty much any model, but as a consequence, rstan has no way of recognizing which parameters are constant across groups and which parameters are group-specific. Moreover, MCMC output does not produce frequentist standard errors (the se_mean column refers to the estimated standard deviation of that mean across many chains) but rather posterior standard deviations. So, nothing is stopping you from looking at the sd column of the output for posterior margins that you know to be constant across groups vs. margins that are group-specific. If you need to access that programatically, do

s <- summary(posterior)$summary
s[,"sd"]

Ben

> It seems that Stan is giving me consistently larger standard deviations than lmer. The bigger deviations are in groups like 4 and 12 in which--not coincidentally, I imagine--the sample sizes are quite small (7 and 4 respectively, where several other groups are well over 100).
>
> Not sure what to make of that.

The best way to look at is to say that lmer is an asymptotic approximation to a full-Bayesian approach like Stan. Thus, if you don't utilize (much) prior information in your Stan program and lmer() understates some of uncertainty, then it is not surprising that the posterior standard deviations produced by Stan are larger than the standard errors produced by lmer, particularly in small groups.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
That indeed looks stuck.  Have you tried fitting simulated data
from the model?

In terms of the code, we'd strongly recommend parameterizing
multivariate priors directly in terms of correlation matrix
Cholesky factors.   There's a discussion in the regression chapter of
the manual.

You can also vectorize the multi_normal and compute Y using
matrix operations, which would make things much faster.  YOu want
to declare

  vector[n_site] y[n_time];

and same for Y, then define Y[t] for t in 1:n_time and then
use a vectorized form of multi_normal,

  y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(Y, L_Sigma);

where L_Sigma is the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix.

- Bob

messages.subject: WAIC and hierarchies
messages.subject_clean: WAIC and hierarchies
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Apologies if this has been raised already, but search did not find it: WAIC approximates leave-one-out cross-validation. To be more specific it approximates leave one observation out. However, now assume we have some grouped data, i.e.

y_jk ~ Normal(a_k + b * x_j, sigma)

a_k ~ Normal(mu_a, sigma_a)

Here a_k is a group specific intercept, b a slope and x_j a continuous co-variate. Now, WAIC (as implemented in the R package loo) would compare models by leaving out individual y_jk. But what can be done to compare models on the basis of leave-one-group out? That is, I would like to assess if the model can predict groups well (and not just single observations). The problem is that groups can be unbalanced, i.e. some groups may have in realty more observations than others.

So what to do in this situation or is this question not meaningful in a WAIC type approach?

Bonus question: In the linear case the likelihood for a group is analytically tractable (albeit I am not sure about what to do about the scaling of the log-lik with the number of data items), but how about cases where this is lost like logistic regression?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: WAIC and hierarchies
messages.subject_clean: WAIC and hierarchies
messages.body_plain:
WAIC and importance-sampling LOO work well if the full posterior and leave-one-out posterior are close together, or in other words if a single observation is not highly influential. It's possible to use LOO and WAIC for groups, but it's likely that the group of observations is highly influential and the full posterior and leave-one-group-out posterior are too different, and the distribution of the importance ratios has too high variance to get useful results. Figure 11 in Vehtari & Lampinen (2002) http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/VehtariLampinen_NC2002_preprint.pdf shows an example where the performance of the importance sampling approximation is bad for leave-one-group-out. Although computation in WAIC is different than in importance sampling, it has similar behavior to IS-LOO (expect with lower variance and higher bias due to the truncation in the Taylor series approximation). We'll post soon more results on IS-LOO and WAIC.

I would recommend computing the leave-one-group-out in brute-force way, or if there are too many groups then in k-fold-CV way. You could also test importance-sampling leave-one-group-out using very good importance sampling <http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646>, which would also warn you if it's not going to work.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Intialization with the current ADVI (develop branch) seems to be difficult at times. I have a model with a Cholesky-factor correlation matrix, and while NUTS sometimes complains at the beginning, it samples eventually fine. The LBFGS optimiser similarly reports a few non-finite gradient at first, then starts to iterate.

With this model, the mean field ADVI seems to evaluate ELBO to nan quite often, then eventually crashes with

"Exception: stan::variational::normal_meanfield::set_mu: Input vector[1] is nan, but must not be nan!"

This is with init=0, which works better than random initialisation. Playing with ADVI parameters (number of gradient samples, eta) does not help much. More diagonal LKJ prior maybe helps a bit.

Gradient seems to be fine when I look at it with "diagnose init=0". At least there are no infinities or eye-popping differences between the gradient and the finite approximation. Some gradient components are zero, for missing value "parameters" of the model. (They are not zero with init=1.)

With init=2, ADVI constantly fails without reporting any iteration steps (even when eval_elbo=1).

I don't know what happens at the initialisation phase in general, but ADVI code does not seem to have any retries or checks for failed gradients? (I only took a quick look at the advi.hpp file, so could be wrong.)

(This is not critical for me in any way, just wanted to share the observation in case it helps with development.)

Shamil.

messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
messages.subject_clean: Unit trace matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

I believe my code is now working and producing the results I wanted. I have yet to run a few tests but I'm very excited. In your post you mentioned that a Dirichlet prior distribution with all concentration parameters (contained in the fixed vector alpha) equal to 1 reflects your prior belief that all simplexes are equally probable a priori, i.e. it is a uniform distribution over a simplex. Do you have a source for this?

On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 6:16:17 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 4:19:22 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> > Do you have any sources that you can recommend I learn about this in more detail? I guess I know enough about Bayesian statistics to be dangerous. I chose Wisharts mostly because it returned a matrix I was looking for (ie. symmetric positive definite).
>
> A lot of people are that way. It is true that the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions are for random variables that are symmetric and positive definite. However, that fact alone is insufficient to justify their use because for any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma there are an infinite number of matrix decompositions where Sigma = Z * Z'. So literally any prior distribution on the elements of Z implies a prior distribution over the symmetric and positive definite matrix Sigma.
>
> If so, why are the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions essentially the only distributions for symmetric and positive definite matrices that you read about in the Bayesian literature? The sole reason is that they are conjugate with a multivariate normal distribution, so Gibbs samplers can do updates of the symmetric and positive definite matrix by drawing from a Wishart or inverse Wishart full-conditional distribution. That raises the fundamental point that Stan does not do Gibbs sampling because Gibbs sampling can easily be antithetical to the goal of getting an adequate number of effective samples from a posterior distribution. Also, 25 years of Gibbs sampling has conditioned people into asking "What prior distribution is conjugate?" instead of "What prior distribution reflects my beliefs about a parameter?"
>
> So, what are your beliefs about this symmetric positive definite matrix? If you are like 99% of people, you don't really have any. Presuming so, what would be an uninformative prior for a symmetric positive definite matrix? We can't really answer that question for an arbitrary symmetric positive definite matrix, but we can answer it for a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix. (What we at Stan call) The LKJ distribution with shape parameter eta = 1 is jointly uniform among among all correlation matrices of dimension K. You could read the paper 2009 by Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe referenced in the Stan manual but it is as frustrating as it is fundamental to multivariate probability. The main implication is that it allows you to put a uniform prior on a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix.
>
> A correlation matrix has a trace of K, whereas you need a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1 for some reason. That is no problem because any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma can be decomposed as Sigma = Delta * Lambda * Delta where Delta is a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and Lambda is a correlation matrix. The i-th diagonal element of Sigma is the i-th variance, namely Delta[i,i]^2, and you need the variances to sum to 1. A simplex is a random vector that is constrained to be positive and sums to 1, which is perfect for your situation. So, what are your prior beliefs about this simplex? If you are like 90% of people, you don't really have any, in which case a Dirichlet prior distribution with all concentration parameters (contained in the fixed vector alpha) equal to 1 reflects your prior belief that all simplexes are equally probable a priori, i.e. it is a uniform distribution over a simplex. The other 10% set all the elements of alpha equal to some other positive constant besides 1 to reflect non-uniform but symmetric beliefs about the simplex.
>
> In summary, it is quite possible to utilize a uniform prior distribution over a correlation matrix and a uniform prior distribution over a simplex, and multiply some stuff together to obtain a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1. To do that, in my previous post, I set sds[i] = sqrt(pi[i]) where pi is a simplex and implicitly set Lambda = L * L' where L is a Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix Lambda. Then the line
>
> X_unitTrace <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose( diag_pre_multiply(sds, L) );
>
> efficiently does what in R code would be
>
> diag(sqrt(pi)) %*% L %*% t(L) %*% diag(sqrt(pi))
>
> The remaining wrinkle is that we want a uniform distribution on the correlation matrix Lambda, but Lambda is not actually a parameter of the model. Rather its Cholesky factor, L, is. By applying a multivariate change-of-variables, it is possible to work out what the prior distribution of L is if you have an LKJ prior on Lambda = L * L' . We call this log-prior the lkj_corr_cholesky distribution, but it needs to be called explicitly in the model block (presumably with eta = 1).
>
> It so happens that --- under these priors --- simplexes and Cholesky factors of correlation matrices tend to be pretty easy for Stan to efficiently draw samples of, although, to repeat my fundamental point, not via Gibbs sampling. That is really just icing on the cake but in part follows from the process of thinking carefully about what probability distributions reflect your (lack of) beliefs and people like us thinking carefully about what multivariate transformations do to the geometry of the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from. It also happens to be the case that Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions often do unspeakable acts to the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from, so there is not only essentially no reason to use them in Stan (because Stan does not do Gibbs sampling) but also a strong reason to not use them in Stan (because Stan often can't sample them very effectively).
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: Simple ODE code for multiple dosing setting
messages.subject_clean: Simple ODE code for multiple dosing setting
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Things are quit tedious under Stan at the moment concerning multiple dosing: You have to stop the ODE inegrator each time you want to inject a new dose. The Stan ODE integrator cannot handle events which is why you have to manually stop the ODE at each dosing time-point (then add the dose and restart). It works, but is tedious; hopefully we get this event handling at some point in Stan directly.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] 15 hours processing time for 10k rows of data??
messages.body_plain:
Great advice from James Camac.

A remaining drag in your code is this:

  model {
    matrix[M,M] Sigma_beta;
    Sigma_beta <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(100.0, M));

    ...

    for (j in 1:J)
      beta[j] ~ multi_normal((u[j] * gamma)', Sigma_beta);

Two key pieces of advice:

1.  Always vectorize for speed.

2.  Never use a diagonal covariance matrix.

You should replace all of the above with:

  for (j in 1:J)
    beta[j] ~ normal(u[j] * gamma, 100);

You can make that even more efficient by following the advice in the
arrays and vectors chapter of the manual --- Here making u an array
of row vectors is ideal --- it avoids the copy and memory non-locality
problems of pulling out a row of a vector.

And two more as an added bonus:

3.  Never use exp() if you can avoid it.

4.  Never recompute subexpressions.

So your

   mu[i]  <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
                  + a[i]
                  + theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
                  + psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));

  ...
  y ~ poisson(mu);

should define log_mu instead of mu and then use the Poisson taking
a log-scale parameter:

  ...
    log_mu[i]  <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
                  + a[i]
                  + theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
                  + psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));
  ..
  y ~ poisson_log(log_mu);

Also, you want to assign the value of (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
to a local variable and reuse it in both places.

That should speed things up a lot, but won't help with statistical
efficiency.  For that, you're going to need better priors or look
for places log_mu might be non-identified and causing problems,
as in adding b0 and a[i].

- Bob

  *** variational inference is experimental ***

was prominent enough!

That's because we haven't run it on very many models yet.
This would be a great project if someone wants to help out.
It should lead to at least some kind of paper and hopefully
more robust algorithms for Stan's variational inference.

Until then, we really appreciate feedback on what works and what
doesn't.  So thanks very much.  And thanks for running with diagnose,
HMC and L-BFGS, because that would've been my first comment!

messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 13, 2015, at 2:03 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> I learned your words, Bob, by heart "you should be scared about exp" and it gave me good guidance so far. But, I wonder in this context:
>
> - what makes exp so terrible?

Underflows to 0 below about -700, overflows to +inf above 700 or
so and huge derivatives for values much greater than 0.

And it's expensive to compute.

But it's mainly that you don't want to have round trips of log
and exp, as you just lose arithmetic accuracy.  If you do
everything on the log scale, which is where we need to wind up
eventually, it's much more robust.

For instance, check out

  y ~ poisson_log(alpha)

vs.

  y ~ poisson(exp(alpha))

The latter evaluates to

  y * log(exp(alpha)) - lgamma(y + 1) - exp(alpha)

If we use a log-scale, we can avoid the round trip of log(exp(...)),
which accounts for about half of the computation (because the lgamma(y + 1) just
drops out because y is an integer and the (multiply and subtract are nearly free
relative to log and exp).

  y ~ poisson_log(alpha)

just having to do

  increment_log_prob(Y * alpha - exp(alpha));

So you still are going to have problems with overflow and underflow if
alpha is too far away from 0.  But then that implies a Poisson with a mean
above 2 billion :-)

> - does it make a difference if I calculate in log space or on the natural space?

Algebraically, no.  Arithmetically, yes.  Log scale won't underflow or overflow.

> I mean I can define stuff to be log-normally distributed and then compute my means on the natural scale or I can use normals, but then do the computation in log-space.

Yes, but you have to consider the entire round trip out to unconstrained
parameters and back.  If you have a parameter with lower=0, then it's
log transformed, with an explicit exp() on the way back from unconstrained
to constrained.  There's no way to completely get rid of it if you need
a positive-constrained variable.

> Does the choice of what is better depend on what error model I use (proportional for log-space or additive for natural space).

Yes, as far as regression is concerned.

But all I was talking about was keeping the same model, but staying
on the log scale as much as possible.

- Bob

Stan is strict on types.  It's telling you that you're
trying to add a row vector and a vector, which isn't possible.

So you can transpose the row vector, beta0[id[n]], which is a row
vector because it pulls out row id[n] from beta0.  You're
better off declaring beta0 an array of vectors as I suggested
in my last e-mail.  It's substantially more efficient, especially
if the matrix is large.

The next version of Stan, if we can ever get it out the door,
has much cleaner error messages for this kind of thing.

Would there by a a more principled way to specify them to better reflect my prior beliefs so that I can avoid having to make some claim about the upper limit of the hyperparameters?

> transformed parameters {

> real<lower = 0, upper = 1> q[O_1];
> real<lower = 0> epsilon_p1[O_1];
>
>   for (oo1 in 1:O_1) {
>
>     q[oo1] <- (H_1[FI30ss[oo1]]/(H_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1));
>     epsilon_p1[oo1] <- (epsilon_1[FI30ss[oo1]] + 1);

> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(q[oo1]) + gamma_log(FI30y[oo1], epsilon_p1[oo1], c_1[FI30ss[oo1]]),
>                             log(1-q[oo1]) + exponential_log(FI30y[oo1], K_1[FI30ss[oo1]])));
>
> Will this improve stability or would it still be better to do the algebra on the log scale?

It's always safer to do the algebra on the log scale for both log(q)
and log(1-q).  For instance, define new variables

  log_q[oo1] <- log(H_1[...]) - log1p(H_1[...]);

  log1m_q[oo1] <- -log1p(H_1[...]))

You need to do some algebra on the latter to see that

  1 - u/(u + 1) = 1 / (u + 1)

and work from there.

But if you're not having problems with the other alternative, then I
wouldn't worry about it.

But if you do stick with your version, use log1m(u) instead of log(1 - u)
and log1p(u) in place of log(1 + u), or even swap out all of that for
our newish binary mixture function

  increment_log_prob(log_mix(q[oo1], gamma_log(...), exponential_log(...)).

But that assumes q is on the linear scale, not on the log scale.

- Bob

>

The problem is that groups can be unbalanced, i.e. some groups may have in realty more observations than others.

> So what to do in this situation or is this question not meaningful in a WAIC type approach?

> Bonus question: In the linear case the likelihood for a group is analytically tractable (albeit I am not sure about what to do about the scaling of the log-lik with the number of data items), but how about cases where this is lost like logistic regression?

messages.subject: Tree depth and Leapfrog
messages.subject_clean: Tree depth and Leapfrog
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fitting a model that seems to have an ok Rhat for all parameters. I have recently moved to a more natural parameterisation which has resulted in very few n_divergent iterations, but at the expense of tree depth being greater than 10; almost always 11 in fact. Correspondingly, n_leapfrog is now often much greater than 1000.

My questions here are threefold:

1. What are the problems with treedepth being greater than 10 here? Does this mean that NUTS is terminating prematurely? What are the consequences of this for my posterior densities? I am trying to get to grips with the terminology here, and the concrete effects on my inferences of failing the specific diagnostics.

2. How should I deal with this? I assume that increasing max_treedepth will do the job, but is there anything else I need to do?

3. There is a trade off between parameterisations that have no divergent iterations, with large tree sizes, and those with many divergent iterations, but small tree sizes. I can understand why this trade off would come about when I vary the parameter adapt_delta, or stepsize, but am less sure why changing parameterisations would have this effect. In my case, I am moving from:

neg_binomial_2(mu,kappa) to neg_binomial_2(mu,1\phi)

To me, the second case is somewhat easier to cope with using priors for my data, since the bulk is not over-dispersed; meaning that kappa = 1\phi -> infinity, or alternatively phi = 0. In the first case, I am using a lognormal density for kappa. For the second, I am using a gamma density for phi.

Do you know why I may be seeing this trade off, and am I likely going about this the correct way?

My apologies for the verbosity of this message!

Best,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 13, 2015, at 9:35 PM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am fitting a model that seems to have an ok Rhat for all parameters. I have recently moved to a more natural parameterisation which has resulted in very few n_divergent iterations, but at the expense of tree depth being greater than 10; almost always 11 in fact. Correspondingly, n_leapfrog is now often much greater than 1000.
>
> My questions here are threefold:
>
> 1. What are the problems with treedepth being greater than 10 here? Does this mean that NUTS is terminating prematurely?

Yes, if it bumps up against the limit, NUTS is stopping before
it hits a U-turn.

> What are the consequences of this for my posterior densities?

HMC becomes more of a random walk.

> I am trying to get to grips with the terminology here, and the concrete effects on my inferences of failing the specific diagnostics.
>
> 2. How should I deal with this? I assume that increasing max_treedepth will do the job, but is there anything else I need to do?

You should increase tree depth until you don't butt up against
the max.

It may also help to rescale parameters (usually by rescaling
predictors) and/or try to change parameterizations so there's not
so much posterior curvature (which is what causes the need for small
step sizes for a first-order approximation with gradients).

>
> 3. There is a trade off between parameterisations that have no divergent iterations, with large tree sizes, and those with many divergent iterations, but small tree sizes.

The problem with the divergent iterations is that they can bias the sampler;
rather than reducing to a random walk, which at least has the right stationary
properties, the divergences are due to arithmetic failures near boundaries that
might be important for estimates.

It's not such a big deal during warmup, though often reducing initial stepsize.

> I can understand why this trade off would come about when I vary the parameter adapt_delta, or stepsize, but am less sure why changing parameterisations would have this effect. In my case, I am moving from:
>
> neg_binomial_2(mu,kappa) to neg_binomial_2(mu,1\phi)
>
> To me, the second case is somewhat easier to cope with using priors for my data, since the bulk is not over-dispersed; meaning that kappa = 1\phi -> infinity, or alternatively phi = 0. In the first case, I am using a lognormal density for kappa. For the second, I am using a gamma density for phi.

What do the posteriors for phi (or 1 / phi) look like?  Is it trying to get
close to 0?

How much do you care about getting really close to zero?  Because
otherwise the direct kappa parameterization seems easier --- once it
gets fairly large, it'll be almost zero and in those cases you probably
don't care exactly what it is.

> Do you know why I may be seeing this trade off, and am I likely going about this the correct way?

It would help to see the actual model to debug the parameterization.

> My apologies for the verbosity of this message!

Mine too for the answer :-)

- Bob

On Tuesday, July 14, 2015 at 1:18:59 AM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Great advice from James Camac.
>
> A remaining drag in your code is this:
>
>   model {
>     matrix[M,M] Sigma_beta;
>     Sigma_beta <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(100.0, M));
>
>     ...
>
>     for (j in 1:J)
>       beta[j] ~ multi_normal((u[j] * gamma)', Sigma_beta);
>
> Two key pieces of advice:
>
> 1.  Always vectorize for speed.
>
> 2.  Never use a diagonal covariance matrix.
>
> You should replace all of the above with:
>
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     beta[j] ~ normal(u[j] * gamma, 100);
>
> You can make that even more efficient by following the advice in the
> arrays and vectors chapter of the manual --- Here making u an array
> of row vectors is ideal --- it avoids the copy and memory non-locality
> problems of pulling out a row of a vector.
>
> And two more as an added bonus:
>
> 3.  Never use exp() if you can avoid it.
>
> 4.  Never recompute subexpressions.
>
> So your
>
>    mu[i]  <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
>                   + a[i]
>                   + theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
>                   + psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));
>
>   ...
>   y ~ poisson(mu);
>
> should define log_mu instead of mu and then use the Poisson taking
> a log-scale parameter:
>
>   ...
>     log_mu[i]  <- exp(b0 + log(i) * b
>                   + a[i]
>                   + theta * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
>                   + psi * a[i - 1] * (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1]));
>   ..
>   y ~ poisson_log(log_mu);
>
> Also, you want to assign the value of (y[i - 1] - mu[i - 1]) / sqrt(mu[i - 1])
> to a local variable and reuse it in both places.
>
> That should speed things up a lot, but won't help with statistical
> efficiency.  For that, you're going to need better priors or look
> for places log_mu might be non-identified and causing problems,
> as in adding b0 and a[i].
>

messages.body_plain:
[a bit of x-over with stan-dev]

R-hat's possible to calculate as you go using sufficient
stat accumulators, but split R-hat's trickier unless you know
the chain length ahead of time because otherwise you need
a lot of buffering to anticipate the split.

n_eff isn't possible because it requires the whole chain
for autocorrelations (some approximation would probalby
be possible, with same split-chain issues as R-hat).

The quantiles are also tough --- you need q% of the samples to
properly compute a q% quantile at each end.

We'd probably want to generalize to the ragged version,
which we haven't decided how to do yet (weight by chain, weight
by draw, or somewhere in between), but either way will
reduce to the usual method in the non-ragged case.

-Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thank you for the suggestion.

I implemented your suggestion for multple discrete dosing, the model compiles, but sampling is not done. Attached is my model code and the R code with input data. Somehow Stan thinks I have two variables y[1] and y[2], but I only have one dependent variable (concentration). I think the code has problems with dimensions of the variable y_hat returned by the integrate_ode()

The error I get during sampling is:

"SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'ode_stan2' NOW (CHAIN 1).
Error : assign(y): size of y1 (19) and size of y2 (6) must match in size
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"

I only have one variable and one equation , but Stan thinks I have a system of two equations. Would you please point out what the correct dimensions for y_hat should be?

On Monday, July 13, 2015 at 6:57:16 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you have initial state y(t = 0), observation times t[1] through t[10]
> with a dose delta_y at t[5], then you run the integrator with initial
> state y(t=0) for times t[1] through t[5], get the value for y out of the
> result for t[5], add the dose delta_y, then integrate with that as the initial
> condition for times t[6] through t[10].
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jul 13, 2015, at 11:51 AM, Shamil Sadigov <sha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Hello!
> >
> > Thank you for the hint. It makes sense. However, I am not proficient in Stan ODE syntax (Stan manual is terse on ODE solvers). Would you kindly provide a toy example code on how to stop the ODE integrator and add a new dose in Stan?
> >
> > Best,
> > Shamil.
> >
> > On Monday, July 13, 2015 at 5:42:38 PM UTC+2, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > Hi!
> >
> > Things are quit tedious under Stan at the moment concerning multiple dosing: You have to stop the ODE inegrator each time you want to inject a new dose. The Stan ODE integrator cannot handle events which is why you have to manually stop the ODE at each dosing time-point (then add the dose and restart). It works, but is tedious; hopefully we get this event handling at some point in Stan directly.
> >
> > Best,
> > Sebastian
> >
> > On Monday, July 13, 2015 at 3:37:04 PM UTC+2, Shamil Sadigov wrote:
> > Dear Stan Developers,
> >
> > I am experimenting with the ODE solvers in Stan. I managed to simulate data governed by a simple first order ODE with a goal to extend the stan code to real PK and Toxicology problems. Currently I am able to simulate data with a single initial dose. However, I would like to implement multiple dosing regimen, as described here (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-Support)
> >
> > "Dosing: discontinous inputs to the differential equation in the form of "dosing". For example, a drug is injected into a tissue, and complete diffusion is assumed, so it looks like a discontinuous jump."
> >
> > I include the stan code and the R code to run it. I also included the plot of the results from R 'deSolve' package. These are what I would like to reproduce in Stan.
> >
> > Many thanks in advance,
> > Shamil.

Hello again,

I am working with Heather and have read the section in the manual as well looked at a few examples declaring data using matrices, but I am (with apologies) still stuck at declaring the data including a matrix without Stan complaining:

SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:

expression denoting integer required; found type=int[1]

ERROR at line 4

  2:        int M;

  3:        int N[M];

  4:        matrix[M,N] y;

                     ^

  5:      }

Here's the current Stan code:

data {

    int M;

    int N[M];

    matrix[M,N] y;

  }

  parameters {

    real mu[M];

  }

  model {

    for (m in 1:M)

      y[m] ~ normal(mu[m], 1);

  }

And just for clarity's sake the R code leading up to my error (as part of me wonders if I eventually will need the data in R as a matrix…):

# Simulate fake data

M <- 5 # number of datasets

n_data_per_M <- round(runif(M, 5, 40)) # how many datapoints per M?

N <- rep(1:M, n_data_per_M)

y <- rnorm(length(N), 5, 2)

# fit the model

fit_simple <- stan("stan/lmfit_arghh.stan", data=c("N","M", "y"), iter=2000, chains=4)

Sorry for the super basic query. Many thanks for any help,

Lizzie

messages.subject: R-hat
messages.subject_clean: R-hat
messages.body_plain:
I have an intuition that some sort of super-split R-hat exists, following a FFT principle.  But I’ve not been able to come up with anything.
A

> On Jul 14, 2015, at 1:19 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> [a bit of x-over with stan-dev]
>
> R-hat's possible to calculate as you go using sufficient
> stat accumulators, but split R-hat's trickier unless you know
> the chain length ahead of time because otherwise you need
> a lot of buffering to anticipate the split.
>
> n_eff isn't possible because it requires the whole chain
> for autocorrelations (some approximation would probalby
> be possible, with same split-chain issues as R-hat).
>
> The quantiles are also tough --- you need q% of the samples to
> properly compute a q% quantile at each end.
>
> We'd probably want to generalize to the ragged version,
> which we haven't decided how to do yet (weight by chain, weight
> by draw, or somewhere in between), but either way will
> reduce to the usual method in the non-ragged case.
>
> -Bob
>

> On Jul 14, 2015, at 8:35 AM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Thanks Bob and Ben for your answers; those are helpful for my understanding. If I understand it correctly, does NUTS terminating early just mean HMC is like bog standard Metropolis;

More like Langevin, but yes, more like a random walk.
The big advantage of HMC is that it can follow the Hamiltonian
across the posterior.

> meaning that the posteriors should be ok, but the model will take a long time to run?
>
> Ok - it actually seems that on reflection, the dispersion parameter of the negative binomial is not the part that is causing the problem. If I move to a hierarchical poisson regression model of the form below, I still run into issues of a large tree depth. Below K=106, and is the total number of individual time series. nSpecies=21, and shows the total number of distinct species across all the studies.
>
> I have tried moving to a non-centered parameterisation, do you think this could help?

Maybe --- depends on how much data you have.  Read Michael's paper for
more details.

> If so, is there any way you could hint how I can do this, as the centered models I have tried are not working?

What are you trying to center?

> Are there any other ideas for how to make the below less likely to run into the issues of large tree sizes?
>

Well, you don't need locals for integer indexing --- they won't
hurt, but they won't help with time as they're not involved in
autodiff.  You can just use Cauchy instead of a Student-t with 1 degree
of freedom.  Those aren't very tight priors, which can be problematic
in some cases.  I have no idea what the effect of the logit transform
is going to be on phi and eta.  I take it that's what the Jacobian's for.
Is that really

 log |d/du log(u / (1 - u))|

Rather than logit transforming a constrained variable between (0,1),
it might be better to do it the other way around --- just delcare the
variables you care about to be unconstrained.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model consultation: Vector Autoregression (VAR) in Stan
messages.body_plain:
I have some comments inline, but I'll put the comments on the model code
here.

If you need to compute Sigma, it's more efficient to do that in the
generated quantities block --- that way it doesn't throw a ton of
complicated functions and expressions at autodiff.

Also, you don't ever want to do a complicated computation twice (like diag_pre_multiply),
so this:

 Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega)';

is better off written as this:

  Sigma <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));

I think the example using post_multiply in the manual is wrong and
this is right.

You want to scale L_Omega with a vector of positive-constrained
standard deviations --- as is, you're constraining the diagonal of
the covariance matrix to be zero.  There are instructions in the
regression chapter of the manual.

> On Jul 8, 2015, at 11:41 AM, Paul Viefers <paulv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob,
>
> Many thanks for the swift response. It's really awesome you guys provide support here for people to learn.
>
> I spent the afternoon going over the code in an attempt to fix things.
>
> A. Summary
> Before going into details, I have implemented your suggestions as far as possible and it works much better now, but still not good I'd say. For a 2-dimensional vector process y_t (M=2), the model works somehow, but that's just a toy linear model with 10 parameters in A and 3 parameters in Sigma and no hierarchical structure.

Often the hierarchical models will fit much better for
something like this by getting the prior standard deviation
right.

> Intercepts are recovered much better than slopes, variances and covariances are awful.

But how is the interval coverage?  If you don't have much data, there
will be a lot of posterior uncertainty in a model like this.

> This gives me an indication that the code is not terribly off base - its' just not very good and I'd like to know why.

What do you think is not very good?  Speed, or you think you're
getting the wrong answer?  Did all the parameters have R-hat values
near 1?

> Setting M=3 and (i) the sampler slows down dramatically - both in terms of wall time and effective sample size, (ii) Rhat explodes and (iii) posteriors means nowhere close to the actual value. Increasing the number of observed time periods (T) does not help dramatically.
>
> I have attached the newest version of my code and the R file that creates the artificial data (for M=2 and M=3) and runs the model.
>
> B. Details.
> Concerning your comments and suggestions:
> 	• Prior on the covariance matrix: Inverse-Wishart -> LKJ + Cholesky
>
> We have advice on how to set up effective priors for sampling in
> the manual.  We recommend (a) working with Cholesky factors, and
> (b) using a scaled correlation matrix with LKJ priors.  Stan does
> not use any conjugacy information, so using inv_wishart isn't going
> to be any faster.   There are links to a paper by Ben on why we like
> the LKJ.
> There's also no efficient inverse Wishart on the Cholesky factor
> scale.  It's on our to-do list, but given that we don't use or
> recommend (inverse) Wishart priors, it's not a high priority.
>
> I suspected nobody here will like to see (inverse-)Wishart priors on covariances, but it served as a first brush and was meant to make thing comparable to other implementations, e.g in R with the Gibbs.

You and a bunch of other people.  It's amazing to me how
ingrained standard practices become.  It does make sense to
make sure Stan's doing the "right thing", though it's surprisingly
subtle to measure what the right thing is.

> I saw you suggest these priors for the covariance matrix of regression coefficients in a hierarchical model, but note that I am applying it to the sampling covariance matrix, so it didn't come to my mind immediately to use it for that purpose. But I implemented it the way it is suggested in the manual (an LKJ cholesky prior and a separate half-cauchy prior on the vector of variances) and I think it is a major improvement. Previously, the chain wasn't exploring at all and got stuck at the starting values, because all proposals were rejected. Now the chain isn't stuck anymore - so it's much more well-behaved.

Part of that's just the Cholesky factor implementation.  If we
did the same thing for Wisharts they'd be more robust.  It's on
our to-do list.

> However, the scale matrix of the inverse-Wishart (S in my notation, see transformed parameter block in previous post) in my earlier code really helped to recover the parameters in the covariance matrix. The LKJ prior is worse in that respect - assuming I did not commit a mistake.

It shouldn't be, assuming you were using equally "informative"
version sof the priors.  In fact, you can drive the LKJ prior down
to uniform if you want, but we recommend some regularization for
all the usual reasons (here, mainly avoiding degenerate boundary
cases).

>
> 	• Vectorization

> You also want to vectorize, so this bit of the model
>
>     matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
>
>     // A toy prior on the slopes
>     for(i in 1:K)
>         A[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
>
>     // Likelihood
>     mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>     for(n in 1:T_eff)
>         Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mus[n], Sigma);
>
>
> becomes this:
>
>   A ~ normal(0, 1);
>   Y ~ multi_normal(X * A, Sigma);
>
> But you really want to replace that Sigma with a Cholesky factor,
> and use:
>
>   Y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(X * A, L_Sigma);
>
> I tried this, but I think this is not possible here, because both A and Y are matrices.

You need to make Y an array of vectors, and same with X * A.  It's
totally worth what looks to an R user like it's going to be slower.
Write the loop, create the array of vectors for X * A, and try it
yourself.

> So I get a syntax error when trying to hand a matrix over to 'normal' or 'multi_normal'. What I do is to continue to resort to the standard workaround and constuct a temporary matrix of linear predictors and loop over its rows. I.e. writing Y[n] returns the n-th row of the matrix Y and the likelihood part of my code
>
> // Likelihood
>         matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
>         mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>         for(n in 1:T_eff)
>             Y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mus[n], L_Omega);
>
> loops over all T_eff rows of Y and mus. What I can vectorize is the prior on A by using the 'to_vector' function (see below) - thanks for that hint!

At this point, all you need to do is this:

  vector[M] mus[T_eff];
  for (t in 1:T_eff)
    mus[t] <- X[t] * A;
  Y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mus, L_Omega);

You need to make sure Y is also an array of vectors.

>
> C. Updated model code.
> Following your advice and changing the priors on the covariance and writing it terms of the Cholesky leads to the following updated code
>
> Data & Transformed data block.
> Note that I have added prior hyperparameters to the data, so I do not have to recompile the code every time I play with the prior.
> data {
>     int<lower=0> T;         // No. of time periods observed
>     int<lower=0> M;         // No. of variables in y_t
>     int<lower=1> p;         // Lag order
>     matrix[T-p, M] Y;       // Matrix of time series for LHS
>     matrix[T-p, 1+M*p] X;   // Matrix of lags of LHS variables
>
>     // Prior hyperparameters
>     real<lower=0> s_A;      // SD of the normal prior on elements of A
>     real<lower=0> cauchy_scale;
>     real<lower=0> lkj_shape;
> }
> transformed data {
>     int<lower=1> K;         // No. of parameters per equation
>     int<lower=1> K_slope;   // No. of slope parameters per equation
>     int<lower=0> T_eff;     // The effective number of obs. we can use, see below
>     K <- 1 + M * p;
>     K_slope <- M * p;
>     T_eff <- T - p;
> }
>
> Parameters & Transformed parameters.
> parameters {
>     matrix[K, M] A;         // Matrix of AR coefficients incl. intercept
>     cholesky_factor_corr[M] L_Omega;
>     vector<lower=0>[M] tau; // Vector of error variances
> }
> transformed parameters {
>     matrix[M,M] Sigma;
>     Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega)';
> }
>
> Model block.
> model {
>     // Likelihood
>         matrix[T_eff, M] mus;
>         mus <- X * A;           // ((T-P) x M) matrix of conditional means
>         for(n in 1:T_eff)
>             Y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mus[n], L_Omega);
>
>     // Priors:
>         // A toy prior on A
>         to_vector(A) ~ normal(0, s_A);
>
>         // Prior on the error variances
>         tau ~ cauchy(0, cauchy_scale);
>
>         // LKJ prior for cholesky factor of correlation matrix
>         L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(lkj_shape);
> }
>
> D. Bottomline
> This is not a complicated model. As far as I can see it's a simple linear model - no complicated hierarchical structures. Admittedly, VARs are very parameter-rich, but (a) that's what Stan is supposedly good at and (b) my code isn't even good for low dimensions. I still don't understand why the model is not converging very quickly and fails to recover the parameters :-/

How much data do you have?  Are the parameters getting recovered
in their intervals and just the point estimates are bad?  Estimating
covariance matrices is hard with not much data.  But I'm assuming
you've already fit it with Gibbs code from somewhere and that worked (you
have to be careful that the Gibbs answers are right --- it can have a hard
time with multivariate structures, which as you note, is one of the reasons
we wrote Stan).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To me, with the experience of a single model :), this seems similar kind of initialisation issue that sometimes happens with optimisation and NUTS, and is cured by restarts. It has two parts.

One is failed elbo evaluation: it reports a NaN, maybe because one or more elbo samples return nan. The iteration still continues. Would it make sense to reject the nan samples, and maybe continue sampling until the configured number of (elbo) samples succeeds? This would introduce a bias, but that's ok if the problem disappears when the iteration continues.

The other issue that crashes the iteration with the set_mu exception looks like a gradient failure. That would be a place for a restart.

Ordinary non-convergence is usually a reason to tune eta or other parameters.

Hi leeang,

There's an 'ordered' type just for that. If you were to instead declare your parameters as:

  parameters {
    ordered[3] P;
  }

Then P[1] < P[2] < P[3].

You can also constrain 2 parameters as you've described.

Daniel

ode_stan2 <- '
functions {
   real[] ode1( real t
               , real[] y
               , real[] ke
               , real[] x_r

   y_ini[1] <- y0[1] + vdose[1];       // initial concentration + first dose at time = 0, if any

    }

I have used RStan's optimize function several times before without problems. However, I recently tried it on a new model and the optimizer is behaving strangely; it is giving me positive log probabilities. The log probability must be at most 0, as log(1)=0. The starting log probability is negative, but it increases beyond zero rather quickly. The algorithm still converges to a maximum, but I don't know whether it should be trusted. I can post the specific model if anyone wants to replicate the error, but I was just wondering whether this had happened to anyone before, or if anyone knows what the cause for this behavior could be.

Luis

messages.subject: Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
messages.subject_clean: Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

We just used stan in a Monte Carlo simulation study to look at the effects of sample size, number of items, prior (mis)specification, and data (non)normality, in recovering the intraclass correlation parameter. I'm attaching a sample stan script in case it helps clarify my question. Now, one of my colleagues asked if we could use stan to "quantify the effective amount of data imposed by the prior" in some of the conditions, and whether this was something stan could do automatically. I frankly have no idea what this means, and upon clarification he wrote "if the sample size is 100, approximately how many additional pseudo-observations does a prior include?".

So my question is how can I use stan to get this information? Is this something I can extract from the fitted model object using R? (I used rstan.) And... I dread this part, but I only saved the results of one replication per unique combination of experimental conditions (sample size, number of items, data distribution, etc.) for the sake of saving space. Am I going to have to refit all replications to get this information from every replication? Or is this something that will be constant across all replications of a given set of conditions (i.e., only affected by the experimental conditions, not by the randomness in the data)?

Sorry for how basic these questions are, but I am very much a Bayes novice and just happen to be the only person on this project who even knows how to start up stan in R!!

- Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
messages.body_plain:
The exponential family priors can all be viewed as prior data.
You can just inspect them to see how much prior data they represent.
For instance, a Beta(alpha,beta) density has (alpha + beta - 2) prior
observations.  If you have a uniform prior for a bernoulli observation
and have N successes and M failures, the posterior is Beta(1 + N, 1 + M).

I'm not sure how to calculate for other exponential family priors or for
non-exponential family densities (or even if the latter makes sense).

See:  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior#Pseudo-observations

Apparently the Wikipedia author knew about as much as me, but not more!

- Bob

The problem is that you are using a top-level ' to quote the Stan
program, so the transpose ' gets interpreted as a close string in
R.  Your model's fine, at least as far as compilation goes.

reject() or print() statements, or you can put the Stan program in
its own file, which is what we recommend (in person, if not yet on
our getting-started page).

messages.subject_clean: New papers on LOO/WAIC and Stan
messages.body_plain:
Aki, Jonah, and I have released the much-discussed paper on LOO and WAIC in Stan:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/loo_stan.pdf
We (that is, Aki) now recommend LOO rather than WAIC, especially now that we have an R function to quickly compute LOO using Pareto smoothed importance sampling.

Also 2 new tutorial articles on Stan will be appearing:
in JEBS:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/stan_jebs_2.pdf
in JSS:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/stan-paper-revision-feb2015.pdf
The 2 articles have very similar titles but surprisingly little overlap.

I guess I should blog this…

See you
A

messages.body_plain:
For reasons discussed in our paper with Hwang, we prefer LOO or WAIC to DIC.

> On Jul 16, 2015, at 1:46 AM, Fabricio Vasselai <fabricio...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear all,
>
> In all my models fitted with Stan, I include a generated quantities block in order to get what is needed to later calculate DIC and WAIC. Hoever, in my current model, I am trying a slight modification since the matrix with the predicted values is consuming too much memory due to the data and model having respectively N~200k and iter~100k. Therefore, I want to get the predicted values to at least calculate DIC and them discard them (I don't know if WAIC will be possible to get).
>
> Let me explain it better. Suppose I have something like, for instance, the following:
>
> generated quantities{
>   vector[N] p;
>   real log_lik;
>   log_lik <- 0;
>   for ( i in 1:N ) {
>     p[i] <- b_0 + X[i]*b_1;
>   }
>   log_lik <- bernoulli_logit_log( win , p );
>   dev <- dev + (-2)*log_lik
> }
>
> In my situation, just saving the sampling of vector 'p' results in a 200k x 100k matrix, what is of course draining the RAM memory, the hardware memory and even delaying the processing of the model run. Therefore, what I would like to know first is:
>
> 1)  whether there is an efficient way for me to retrieve only 'log_lik' and 'dev' (in the example above, not saving 'p'). If my model had few parameters, I though that one solution for RStan users like myself could be to pass the name of all parameters but 'p' in the "pars" option of the "stan" function. But my model is a multilevel model, in which I end up having more than two hundred parameters. It doesn't seem to make sense to inform all the hundreds of parameters names, just leaving 'p' out. I hope there is a better way of achieving that. Maybe a direct way within the Stan model itself?
>
> Second thing is:
>
> 2) by the code above, what I've called log_lik is not exactly the same as in the discussion of the BDA3 and in Gelman and Vehtari, 2015, since I am saving only one value of log_lik per iteration, not the full log_lik matrix of dimensions n x iter. Would it be still reasonable to calculate WAIC with he resultant log_lik, even if less ideal?
>
> Thanks for your time!
>
> Fabricio Vasselai
> Polisci Dep. - USP
>
>
>
> PS: maybe a future feature for the "stan" function in RStan would be to have "pars_keep" and "pars_drop" options, instead of only "pars".  Then, one could both specify parameters to be kept but also parameters to be dropped.
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
The original question was on modelling real-valued data on sphere, or actually on sphere and over time. It was not about modelling complex or spherical-valued data.

So I don't understand what the problem is if one defines a metric on the sphere, something like rho1*arccos(x \dot y) + rho2*(t_x-t_y)^2, a bit like in the beginning of https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~gentz/pages/WS13/RDS13/slides/A_Lang_RDS13.pdf, and then spans a real-valued gaussian process on that metric.

What will go wrong? (Except that it will probably be too slow to compute with Stan for realistic EEG data.)

Spatial statistics use the von-Mises-Fisher distribution as an analogue of gaussian on the sphere, and the above (probably, haven't checked) leads to such a kernel for the GP if marginalised over time.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Failure with transpose matrix when defining model
messages.body_plain:
Nothing jumped out at me from looking at that model, but it may also
depend on the data.  Have you tried simulating data from the model and
fitting that?  If a model's very missspecified, it can get stuck.

Are you getting rejection warnings during the iterations?

I'd suggest reparameterizing covariance matrices in terms of Cholesky factors.
Some of the covariance matrix transforms will be problematic in more than a
few dimensions.  We should have stronger warnings in the manual about this.

The other issue to worry about is whether one parameter constrains another
parameter exactly --- that won't fly because we can't sample when there are
deterministic relations among parameters (technically the problem is that we're
sampling in K dimensions and randomizing each dimension independently, whereas
pinning one param in terms of others produces a submanifold of less than K
dimensions that we can't satisfy the constraints for with K independent jumps).

What you want to be careful of is pinning some parameter value as a function
of another variable --- that won't work in Stan and it'll cause parameters
to get stuck.

- Bob

matrices (otherwise we have issues with possibly complex results).

messages.subject: ADVI for beginner questions
messages.subject_clean: ADVI for beginner questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I have started to play with ADVI and I must say I am impressed by the speed, but I still need to check if I get garbage (on a first look everything looks ok). Now, a couple of questions (and if you answer with RT(F)M that's fine - justlet me know which document to read):

- A run with the default settings took 3h, a run with eta_agrad=0.05 (half of the default) took only 20 minutes. Is this normal? On what scale should I vary eta_agrad? I.e. try multiples or offsets (so 1/2^n or eta_agrad= 0.1, 0.09, 0.08 ...)

- ADVI complained about diverging ELBO during the first 1000 iterations and the delta_ELBO_mean was in the thousands whereas the delta_ELBO_median was around or below 1. Do I need to worry now?

- For which type of problems does ADVI work well and which ones not?

- Is the resulting CSV a dump of MCMC-like samples? So can I use it in the usual way?

- Does Rhat mean anything? What else do I need to check for non-convergence?

- Can read_stan_csv from rstan read in these csv files or should I read these in with R and skip over the first 1000 warmups?

I am still evaluating, but just let me say that ADVI crunched an ODE problem which takes almost 3 days per chain in just 20-30 minutes !!! If the result is any usable then this is just awesome!

Best,
Sebastian

On Jul 16, 2015, at 11:52 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> I have started to play with ADVI and I must say I am impressed by the speed, but I still need to check if I get garbage (on a first look everything looks ok). Now, a couple of questions (and if you answer with RT(F)M that's fine - justlet me know which document to read):

Other than the doc in the Stan manual and CmdStan manual (2.7.0 versions
of both of which are now available), you'll want to read Alp's
arXive paper for a deeper description of how it works:

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03431

> - A run with the default settings took 3h, a run with eta_agrad=0.05 (half of the default) took only 20 minutes. Is this normal? On what scale should I vary eta_agrad? I.e. try multiples or offsets (so 1/2^n or eta_agrad= 0.1, 0.09, 0.08 ...)
>
> - ADVI complained about diverging ELBO during the first 1000 iterations and the delta_ELBO_mean was in the thousands whereas the delta_ELBO_median was around or below 1. Do I need to worry now?

These first two, Dustin or Alp are going to have to tackle.

> - For which type of problems does ADVI work well and which ones not?

It's labeled "experimental" exactly because we don't know
under what conditions it'll work well or how best to tune it.
So all these data points are super helpful.

> - Is the resulting CSV a dump of MCMC-like samples? So can I use it in the usual way?

As to the draws, those are from the variational approximation,
as explained in the paper.  But they're meant to be usable in
the same way as the MCMC output.  So if everything's done right,
you should be able to read them in just like MCMC output.

I think the plan is to perhaps do some importance weighting
in the future to make expectation calculations closer to the
true posterior, but I'm not 100% sure.

> - Does Rhat mean anything? What else do I need to check for non-convergence?

The Rhat won't mean anything --- it should have n_eff close to the
number of iterations because it's using pure Monte Carlo (not Markov chain)
draws.

> - Can read_stan_csv from rstan read in these csv files or should I read these in with R and skip over the first 1000 warmups?

If everything's coded correctly, it should be.  I haven't tried it.

> I am still evaluating, but just let me say that ADVI crunched an ODE problem which takes almost 3 days per chain in just 20-30 minutes !!! If the result is any usable then this is just awesome!

This is really exciting news.  Thanks again for trying this out.  I
can see a whole stream of PK/PD publications coming out of this if
it really is that great.  Do you have an estimate of how long NONMEM
would take to fit a similar problem?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To answer what Bob hasn’t:

> - A run with the default settings took 3h, a run with eta_agrad=0.05 (half of the default) took only 20 minutes. Is this normal?  On what scale should I vary eta_agrad? I.e. try multiples or offsets (so 1/2^n or eta_agrad= 0.1, 0.09, 0.08 …)

We’re looking into autotuning the hyper parameter for the learning rate. At the moment, the general idea is to increase the hyper parameter if it looks like it is converging slowly at the beginning, and to decrease the hyper parameter if it looks like it goes down fast at the beginning but takes too long during the middle/end.

> - ADVI complained about diverging ELBO during the first 1000 iterations and the delta_ELBO_mean was in the thousands whereas the delta_ELBO_median was around or below 1. Do I need to worry now?

We've seen it complain about diverging ELBO at the beginning on many models. In general, convergence diagnostics are very rough in the works; it's not uncommon to see what you are experiencing so I wouldn't worry about it.

> - For which type of problems does ADVI work well and which ones not?

For now, it will work well for any posterior which can be reasonably approximated by independent normal distributions (on the unconstrained parameter space). We're looking into using better variational families in a fully generic way, c.f., http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03159

Thank you for trying this out! Your results are very promising, and hopefully we can motivate more to consider the feasibility of approximate Bayesian inference. :-)

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
I have to warn you: I have had a quick look at the mean estimates and they looked similar to what I am used to see from MCMC results. However, I have to check more closely. I am happy to report back success or failure. Right now I need to understand what to look at to make sure ADVI works for my case.

@ Dustin: I am not sure if I understood your comment about changing eta_agrad. I just followed the advice in the manual which says "if you see ELBO diverging, then decrease eta_agrad". Other than that I have no clue on this and I was surprised to see that changing from 0.1 to 0.05 made such a difference in computing time. If I remember right, then the result for the larger eta_agrad=0.1 (default) was indeed garbage to me. So I am a bit worried about this at the moment - I mean if I try this on a problem where I don't know the MCMC result, then how do I know that ADVI worked? Given the speed, I would just try out different eta_agrad values... so some guidance here would be very helpful. I am happy to throw this thing on our cluster - trying out these eta_agrad in parallel is not a problem here (500 cores are waiting to be feed).

@ Bob: No idea how fast Nonmem is on this problem, I haven't run it in ages with Nonmem with this parametrization. However, for this problem size anything below 30minutes for a fully Bayesian solution is just amazing. And yes, if this turns out to work so well, we have to print a lot of papers (but before the main-stream can use this we have to get the generic dosing thing into Stan, really).

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
The hyperparameter eta in AdaGrad only affects the convergence rate, and, theoretically, should not affect the results you get. If you did get different results, then it likely comes from one of two possibilities: the algorithm hasn’t fully converged, or the algorithm converged at a different local optima. Checking for convergence is easy based on looking at the differences in the ELBO from iterations, and I imagine this is most likely the case because we have a cap on the maximum number of iterations ADVI can run for.

At the moment, the best thing is to run ADVI on a subset of the data for different values of the hyper parameter, e.g., eta={0.01, 0.5, 0.1, 0.5, 1}; then run ADVI on the full data using the hyperparamter which performed best. This is what we aim to implement within Stan itself.

Dustin

Eigenvectors are overkill. For a given matrix P,

p P = p
p 1 = 1

is a linear problem (the 1 on the LHS is a vector, on the RHS a

messages.body_plain:
I'm getting the following error when I add parameter initialization to a pystan.stan call:

terminate called after throwing an instance of 'boost::exception_detail::clone_impl<boost::exception_detail::error_info_injector<boost::bad_lexical_cast> >'

This happens after compilation is complete and it's trying to run the model, so I think it has to do with how pystan is packaging up the initialization dict and shipping it off to the compiled model (utility functions in stanfit4model.pyx ?).

The details...

pystan.__version__
'2.6.3.0'

% python --version
Python 2.7.9 :: Anaconda 2.0.1 (x86_64)

% cc --version
Apple LLVM version 6.1.0 (clang-602.0.53) (based on LLVM 3.6.0svn)
Target: x86_64-apple-darwin14.4.0
Thread model: posix

And here's a minimal example that works fine before you add initialization:

import pystan

model_code = '''
data { }
parameters { real mu; }
model { mu ~ normal(0, 1); }
'''

fit = pystan.stan(
    data = {},
    model_code = model_code,
    iter = 2000,
    warmup = 1000,
    chains = 1,
    n_jobs = 1
)

If I then add this initialization function:

def init_params(chain_id=1):
    return {'mu' : 0.1}

and change the stan call to this:

fit = pystan.stan(
    data = {},
    model_code = model_code,
    iter = 2000,
    warmup = 1000,
    chains = 1,
    n_jobs = 1,
    init = init_params
)

then I get the error. I get the same result if I remove the chain_id kwarg from the function.

Any ideas?

And one other related issue: the PyStan documentation implies that you should instead be able to write a function that returns a list of dicts, e.g. for one chain, something like this:

def init_params():
    return [{'mu' : 0.1}]

but you get an exception:

ValueError: The function specifying initial values must return a dictionary.

This list-of-dicts option seems like an unnecessary feature anyway--might as well just take it out of the docs.

Ed

My experience with a big hierarchical model (not the same one that had problems to init):

- Mean field ADVI was very fast, something like 10–30 minutes compared to 4–7 days of HMC. Means were on the right ballpark, variances not always so, generalisation over hierarchy was not so good (I got a geographic map out of it).

- Full rank ADVI seems to take about the same CPU time as a single HMC chain. I did not run it to the end, so can't be sure. ADVI can't be really blamed here, for the model has over 7000 parameters.

With a smaller regression/AR/t-residuals model both converged fast.

My current impression was that it is often necessary to use a smaller eta than the default 0.01, and more advi samples. Otherwise the final converge does not happen.

messages.subject: Re: Calculating WAIC from "dev", or: going from DIC's dev to WAIC's log_lik
messages.subject_clean: Calculating WAIC from "dev", or: going from DIC's dev to WAIC's log_lik
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately, what you really need is the pointwise log-likelihood. You need to save the log-likelihood evaluated at every data point (for each posterior simulation) instead of adding them up. For Stan this means defining log_lik to be a vector of length N (number of data points). When you extract the draws you'll have an S by N matrix, where S is the number of saved posterior draws.

The good news is that if you can write the log-likelihood function in R then you can evaluate it yourself using the posterior draws of the parameters from your model. Then you could use the loo R package.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
I think that's just a typo--there's only two parameters in the
distribution and the observation is denoted n (but don't be
confused--later it's in a variable y).

real generalized_poisson_log(int n, real theta, real lambda) {

    return log(theta)
           + (n - 1) * log(theta + n * lambda)
           - lgamma(n + 1)
           - n * lambda
           - theta;
  }

And then later:

y[j] ~ generalized_poisson(mu[j]*(1-lambda), lambda);

Recall that this is equivalent to:

increment_log_prob(generalized_poisson_log(y[j], mu[j]*(1-lambda), lambda));

So for consistency you may want to relabel either n or y...
Seth

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ed,

The function one passes as the `init` argument needs to accept a chain
id argument and return a dictionary of parameters. So the following will
work

def init_params(chain_id):
    return {'mu': 0.1}

Alternatively you can explicitly provide the initial parameters for each
chain:

In [12]: init_list = [{'mu': 0.1}] * 4

In [13]: init_list
Out[13]: [{'mu': 0.1}, {'mu': 0.1}, {'mu': 0.1}, {'mu': 0.1}]

In [14]: fit = sm.sampling(data={}, iter=200, chains=4, n_jobs=1, init=init_list)

I hope this helps!

Best wishes,

Allen

> def init_params():
>     return [{'mu' : 0.1}]
>
> but you get an exception:
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi All

I'm modeling a housing sales dataset with 3 grouped predictors and 3 individual predictors. One of the indivdual predictors is the 'last sales average value of this group' to capture the time trend in the series (there could be more than one transactions on a given date hence the average) The data is sparse as far as the time series is concerned- i.e. sales  may occur months or even years apart. I'm using the fixed parameter mode and generated quantities module to generate esimations for new data, but can't figure out how to predict ahead in time since the periods aren't fixed for every group. For example, group A might have had the last transactions in January 15; predicting one period ahead by taking the last period sales would generate an estimate for February, not one period ahead of current date i.e. August. Can anyone suggest how to handle this ?

On a separate note, I am trying to use the estimates to be exposed via a Shiny App. The Stan code (in fixed param mode and without a model) takes about 30 seconds to generate the estimates which is quite fast but not fast for a user-facing application.  I suppose the latency is due to the connection between R and STAN as discussed in some threads i read in this forum, but is there any way I could improve the performance?

Any help will be appreciated

Thanks and Regards

Jonah

> On Jul 18, 2015, at 2:58 PM, UD1989 <upasa...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi All
>
> I'm modeling a housing sales dataset with 3 grouped predictors and 3 individual predictors. One of the indivdual predictors is the 'last sales average value of this group' to capture the time trend in the series (there could be more than one transactions on a given date hence the average) The data is sparse as far as the time series is concerned- i.e. sales  may occur months or even years apart. I'm using the fixed parameter mode and generated quantities module to generate esimations for new data, but can't figure out how to predict ahead in time since the periods aren't fixed for every group. For example, group A might have had the last transactions in January 15; predicting one period ahead by taking the last period sales would generate an estimate for February, not one period ahead of current date i.e. August. Can anyone suggest how to handle this ?

You can just keep predicting ahead from wherever your last observation
is.   Presumably the latent parameters in the time series are something
like baseline prices or something.

Or you could generalize and use something like a Gaussian process, where
you don't necessarily need exact spacing.

> On a separate note, I am trying to use the estimates to be exposed via a Shiny App. The Stan code (in fixed param mode and without a model) takes about 30 seconds to generate the estimates which is quite fast but not fast for a user-facing application.  I suppose the latency is due to the connection between R and STAN as discussed in some threads i read in this forum, but is there any way I could improve the performance?

It would help to see how you're running it.  If you precompile the
model first and it still takes 30 seconds and you're just using RNGs,
you're probably generating too many samples.  How high an n_eff do you need?

There's no latency in the connection between R and Stan per se,
just that it can take a long time to load big list data structures
into R no matter where they come from.

It always helps to send us more rather than less as it's hard to guess
what people might be doing.

- Bob

I'm using the fixed parameter mode and generated quantities module to generate esimations for new data, but can't figure out how to predict ahead in time since the periods aren't fixed for every group. For example, group A might have had the last transactions in January 15; predicting one period ahead by taking the last period sales would generate an estimate for February, not one period ahead of current date i.e. August. Can anyone suggest how to handle this ?
>
> You can just keep predicting ahead from wherever your last observation
> is.   Presumably the latent parameters in the time series are something
> like baseline prices or something.
>
> Or you could generalize and use something like a Gaussian process, where
> you don't necessarily need exact spacing.
>

>

> you're probably generating too many samples.  How high an n_eff do you need?
>

> just that it can take a long time to load big list data structures
> into R no matter where they come from.
>
> It always helps to send us more rather than less as it's hard to guess
> what people might be doing.
>
> - Bob

stan_glm(y ~ X1 + X2, family = binomial)

messages.subject: slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.subject_clean: slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to use STAN to model the high-dimensional output of a detailed, deterministic, black-box computer simulation L(x). I model L(x) as the linear combination of a set of basis functions (principal components), where the number of basis functions in the model is much less than dims(L(x)). For a given x, each basis function has a weight that is modeled as a gaussian process. The GP covariance matrices depend on x, the point at which the surrogate model is to be evaluated, and x_T, the points for which the full simulation has already been evaluated, and the realizations from the GP posteriors depend on coeffs_T, the principal component coefficients derived from the evaluations of x_T. This may be familiar to some as “gaussian process emulation,” following the work of Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001), and others.

For some observed L* I would like to use this model to infer the corresponding x*, via

L(x*) ~ normal(L*, L*_err);

where L*_err is observational error on L*.

A simplified version of my implementation of this model in STAN is attached. It compiles and runs, but the iteration completion time increases dramatically with increasing iteration number, while the time to execute the “model” block remains constant throughout. I can clock the time it takes the code to hit the end of the model block with a print statement. During execution, the final line of the model block is reached an average of 2 or 3 times a second per chain. For iterations < ~30 during the warmup phase, the frequency at which a chain completes an iteration is also about 2 or 3 per second. However, for iterations > ~30, tens of seconds, then minutes, then hours go by without an advance in the iteration number. As a consequence of this, I have never been able to get my model past the warmup phase (the highest iteration I ever let it hit was ~150 out of 2000, which took several hours). Results from the print statement at the end of the model block, however, continue to go by at 2 or 3 times a second, independent of iteration number.

Can anyone offer some advice on this issue? I also wonder if I have implemented my model, specifically the GP realizations, as efficiently as possible.

Thanks in advance for your help,

Danny

Just to be the pedant — R-hat is a diagnostic of distributional behavior,
whereas the variational optimization of ADVI is a point behavior.  An
R-hat-like diagnostic can diagnose the lack of convergence to a unique
optimum, but there is no theory arguing that there _should_ be a unique
optimum.  We’re flying on heuristics here!
