messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.body_plain:
When you put together “high-dimesional output” and “gaussian process emulation”
you should get very, very scared.

The problem is that in high-dimensions Gaussian process emulation does not
work particularly well unless you have _lots_ of points.  And by lots I mean
a number that grows exponentially with the size of dimension.  When you
don’t have enough points then you run into the problem that the GP isn’t
sufficiently regularized — there are an exponentially growing number of
functions that interpolate between the given points equally well.

The consequence for doing full Bayes is that the posterior in this case is
_nasty_.  Just crazy nasty.  What’s likely happening is that the adaptation
quickly moves towards a really small step size and NUTS then moves
towards a huge number of leapfrog steps to maintain a reasonable
exploration and drives up the computation time accordingly (note that
print statements are evaluated at each leapfrog step, so if you have
a huge number of steps you’ll still see lots of print statements without
necessarily any advance to the next iteration).

Others might suggest otherwise, but I’ll firmly say to not try to use
GP emulation (or really any emulation) in high dimensions!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

Thanks for your feedback.

Although the output of the computer simulation is high-dimensional (len(L) ~ 120, len(x) = 5), the dimensionality of the space in which realizations are drawn from the emulator is smaller by ~an order of magnitude or more due to the use of basis functions to represent L. In this particular problem, the reduced order model for L is just a sum over a truncated PCA basis, where the PCs are derived from evaluations of the full simulation at many x, designed to fill parameter space, and each coefficient is associated with an independent GP:

L_emulated(x) = \Sum_i^N pc_coeffs[i] * pc_component[i]
pc_coeffs[i] ~ GP(0, Sigma[i]);

The dimensionality of pc_component[i] is equal to the dimensionality of L. Using N=3, we only have to train 3 GPs, to predict coefficients for 3 PCs, but we can capture ~95% of the variance in the 700 instance training sample.

Originally I was using N=15, which is still quite a few GPs to train and may lend itself to the nasty posteriors you mentioned. However, for the sake of example, if I reduce the size of my PCA basis to only N=2 components with 200 training examples (a low-dimensional, well-conditioned space in my particular problem), I experience similar sampling times and a similar slowdown of the advancement of the iterations as I did when making realizations in the 15 dimensional space. I find this to be pretty confusing as the emulator is just realizing scalars from the posterior predictive distributions of 2 GPs and fitting a number of nuisance hyperparameters.

I’ll note that gaussian process reduced order models have been applied successfully as emulators for the high-dimensional outputs of computer simulations over the years, in several different fields. Many of these applications include the implementation of fully bayesian inference for x* using MCMC.

http://amstat.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000888
http://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.5177v1.pdf

Danny

On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 4:53:48 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
When you put together “high-dimesional output” and “gaussian process emulation”
you should get very, very scared.

The problem is that in high-dimensions Gaussian process emulation does not
work particularly well unless you have _lots_ of points. And by lots I mean
a number that grows exponentially with the size of dimension. When you
don’t have enough points then you run into the problem that the GP isn’t
sufficiently regularized — there are an exponentially growing number of
functions that interpolate between the given points equally well.

The consequence for doing full Bayes is that the posterior in this case is
_nasty_. Just crazy nasty. What’s likely happening is that the adaptation
quickly moves towards a really small step size and NUTS then moves
towards a huge number of leapfrog steps to maintain a reasonable
exploration and drives up the computation time accordingly (note that
print statements are evaluated at each leapfrog step, so if you have
a huge number of steps you’ll still see lots of print statements without
necessarily any advance to the next iteration).

Others might suggest otherwise, but I’ll firmly say to not try to use
GP emulation (or really any emulation) in high dimensions!

On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 2:36:31 PM UTC-7, Daniel Goldstein wrote:

I am attempting to use STAN to model the high-dimensional output of a detailed, deterministic, black-box computer simulation L(x). I model L(x) as the linear combination of a set of basis functions (principal components), where the number of basis functions in the model is much less than dims(L(x)). For a given x, each basis function has a weight that is modeled as a gaussian process. The GP covariance matrices depend on x, the point at which the surrogate model is to be evaluated, and x_T, the points for which the full simulation has already been evaluated, and the realizations from the GP posteriors depend on coeffs_T, the principal component coefficients derived from the evaluations of x_T. This may be familiar to some as “gaussian process emulation,” following the work of Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001), and others.

For some observed L* I would like to use this model to infer the corresponding x*, via

L(x) ~ normal(L*, L*_err);

where L*_err is observational error on L*.

A simplified version of my implementation of this model in STAN is attached. It compiles and runs, but the iteration completion time increases dramatically with increasing iteration number, while the time to execute the “model” block remains constant throughout. I can clock the time it takes the code to hit the end of the model block with a print statement. During execution, the final line of the model block is reached an average of 2 or 3 times a second per chain. For iterations < ~30 during the warmup phase, the frequency at which a chain completes an iteration is also about 2 or 3 per second. However, for iterations > ~30, tens of seconds, then minutes, then hours go by without an advance in the iteration number. As a consequence of this, I have never been able to get my model past the warmup phase (the highest iteration I ever let it hit was ~150 out of 2000, which took several hours). Results from the print statement at the end of the model block, however, continue to go by at 2 or 3 times a second, independent of iteration number.

Can anyone offer some advice on this issue? I also wonder if I have implemented my model, specifically the GP realizations, as efficiently as possible.

Thanks in advance for your help,

Danny

import pickle, pystan

and bad multi modality .

> On Jul 19, 2015, at 4:58 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> There’s a big difference between converging “in distribution”
> and converging “to a distribution” and my point stands.  My
> feeling is that most ADVI problems will be multimodal so we
> need to figure out the difference between good multi modality
> and bad multi modality before we assume that the users can.
>
> On Jul 19, 2015, at 3:25 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
>> Ahhh, excellent.  It’s so much more satisfying to disagree with Michael!
>>

>>>> Bob:
>>>>
>>>> No, ADVI converges to a distribution, it’s just an approximate distribution that’s part of a parametric family.  If different chains converge to different distributions, that doesn’t mean there’s anything wrong with the algorithm—but the user should still know it.
>>>>
>>>> A
>>>>
>>>>> On Jul 18, 2015, at 7:42 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Just to be the pedant — R-hat is a diagnostic of distributional behavior,
>>>>> whereas the variational optimization of ADVI is a point behavior.  An
>>>>> R-hat-like diagnostic can diagnose the lack of convergence to a unique

How come you think that ADVI problems are multi-modal? Also: Why not simply run an anova on the results from on the unconstrained parameter space; should this be sufficient. I don't see the point for running Rhat stuff which is geared towards chains, but ADVI is a parametric approximation, so what would an anova miss?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advi multiple chains
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] advi multiple chains
messages.body_plain:
Problems in ADVI on the optimization level share all problems with nonconvex optimization, and a big one is the multi-modality of most interesting models, where one would like to use variational inference in the first place.

Another is that even many convex optimization problems are hard, and while the “chains” may be converging to the same solution eventually, we’d like to assess the quality of its convergence at finite runtime. This latter note is more analogous to the setting of R-hat for MCMC, where the chains are somewhere inbetween the starting distribution and the target distribution. If I recall correctly, the original paper also references that the problem applies more generally to “iterative maximization” and not just “iterative simulation”.

Dustin

Ah, I see. And yes, now that you say it: I work with non-linear models and most of my time I spent with figuring out appropriate parametrizations coupled with clever priors to rule out the multi-modality. Does this approach make sense or should I live with the possibility that depending on my starting point I end up in a different local extremum? I never trust these multi-modal solutions or should I? To  my understanding algorithms are not built to deal with this which is why I prefer to rule them out.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: rstan 2.7.0 is on CRAN !!!
messages.subject_clean: rstan 2.7.0 is on CRAN !!!
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 3:54:26 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>
> Most of you know the good news already: rstan 2.7.0-1 is on CRAN servers! This will make installation of Stan so much easier.

It also makes crashing your R session so much easier, which is why we hadn't announced it previously. But it is being used in the Stan short course going on yesterday, today, and tomorrow. You still have to install a C++ compiler to actually estimate the parameters of a Stan program, but having the ability to do binary installs (particularly on Windows) is helpful if your computer / toolchain could not previously compile the Stan parser.

There are a lot of changes on the Stan side since 2.6.0, but Daniel will probably mention some of those sometime today. On the R side, the main two things are that it incorporates the ability to automatically save a bare version of a compiled model and to execute chains in parallel. Thus, you should not use the stan.R function from http://mc-stan.org.R anymore. When you do

library(rstan)

you will see the startup message

rstan (Version 2.7.0-1, packaged: , GitRev: 05c3d0058b6a)
For execution on a local, multicore CPU with excess RAM we recommend calling
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

Doing

rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

means that a small foo.rda file will be saved in the same directory as foo.stan (or in tempdir() if that is not writable or you pass a Stan program in the form of a character string to stan()) when foo.stan is parsed into foo.cpp and compiled. Then, in the future, stan() will search the calling environment for the same stanmodel and if it doesn't find that will search for foo.rda on the hard disk or in tempdir(). If it finds such a foo.rda and some checks are passed (such as foo.stan has not been modified more recently or was parsed with an older version of rstan), then it will be loaded rather than recompiling foo.cpp. This approach was originally suggested by Sebastian.

However, it is easy to crash R this way and we have not been entirely successful at preventing all crashes. In particular, with that option enabled, if you pass non-existent data to stan(), it will compile then throw an error but not create an empty stanfit object. Then, when you fix the error, it won't find the non-existent stanfit object but will find foo.rda which will create two instances of the same DSO object in R's memory and crash R. Ironically, it is safer to not pass a list or environment of data to stan() because another feature is that stan() will automatically search the calling environment for objects whose names are the same as the objects in the data block of foo.stan and use those if it finds them. Thus, you can do something like

J <- 8
y <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12)
sigma <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)
fit <- stan(file="8schools.stan")

and it will find matching objects named J, y, and sigma in both the data block of 8schools.stan and R's global environment.

If you have previously called

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

it will execute the chains in parallel (using the parLapply() function), utilizing (if necessary) as many cores as your computer has. This is only a problem if your computer does not have enough RAM to hold several copies of the data and the MCMC output simultaneously. You can also pass a cores argument to stan() or sampling() to override the mc.cores option. By default, cores is 1 and if you encounter a runtime error, you should call stan() again with cores = 1 to possibly see a better version of the error message before posting on stan-users.

If you are not using RStudio but instead using the R GUI for Windows or Mac (there is something seriously wrong with you but whatever) calling stan() in parallel will by default open a web browser on a temporary file that you can refresh to see the progress of the chains. This can be annoying for chains that execute very quickly and can be prevented by specifying open_progress = FALSE in the call to stan() or sampling(). This should not be an issue if you are using RStudio or a terminal, in which case the output will be piped to the console. Users of knitr will like this better because it the progress is not captured in the processed file. The most recent version of RStudio also has basic support for .stan files and a "Check" button you can press to see if the active .stan file parses. If anyone knows how to make RStudio do code completion on .stan files in the future, let us know.

There is no set_cppo() function anymore (or rather there is but it doesn't do anything but throw a warning), which I have seen a lot of people using in .R scripts (which was inappropriate even when the function did stuff). If you need to change the optimization level or other settings, you have to edit your personal .Makevars file yourself, see

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#configuration

Basically, it should be fine with -O2 but executes slightly faster with -O3.

If you are installing rstan from source using g++ version 4.9.x or later, definitely specify a CXXFLAGS that does not include the -g flag or does include -flto -ffat-lto-objects; otherwise, the Stan parser will take up 250+ Mb of space on your disk. This shouldn't be a problem if you install the binary version of the rstan package from CRAN (which is typical for Windows and recent Macs).

The expose_stan_functions() R function --- which was formerly referred to as testify() --- allows you to test that your user-defined Stan functions are working correctly by calling them in R and comparing them to the results of other R functions that are known to be correct. This is, e.g. how I figured out Phillip's problem described here

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/ErUE-Z25sec/ScHiTmtI_GYJ

So, if you are not utilizing user-defined Stan functions for all non-trivial operations in your .stan file and / or not validating those user-defined Stan functions in R before you call stan(), you are doing it wrong. User-defined Stan functions can also do random number generation, and thus can be used to draw from a posterior predictive distribution after stan() is done or to even do simulations that are not connected to any Stan program.

We see a lot of posts on stan-users about Stan programs that do not sample well, but we do not see a lot of corresponding pairs() plots. You should have been using the pairs() function already, but its defaults have been improved for rstan 2.7.0. Now, it splits the lower and upper triangles at the median accept_stat__ and overplots points if the Markov Chain diverges on that iteration (in red) or exceeds the maximum treedepth (in yellow). This gives you a sense of what parameter interaction causes these sampling difficulties and whether it is a problem of the Markov Chain(s) getting stuck in the tail or being unable to navigate around the mode. The pairs() function takes a pars argument that you should use to specify which parameters to plot. By default, it does all the parameters which is often unreadable (and slow). You should definitely be looking at lp__ and things like variance parameters and other hyperparameters.

Any function that takes a pars argument (like stan, plot, traceplot, and print.stanfit) now has an include argument that defaults to TRUE. This means that any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are included by that function. If include = FALSE, then any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are excluded by that function. So, if you have a lot of named parameters but only a small number that you want to omit, then you can name them with the pars argument and specify include = FALSE. This is particularly useful for stan() if you have latent variables that you do not want to store MCMC samples of (because there are so many of them) but you still want to see the posterior means of those latent variables by subsequently calling get_posterior_mean(). See

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/t2B2W_AjlDc/GvwlKi3fk1QJ

There is also a new lookup() function in RStan that inputs an R function or a name of an R function and returns the corresponding Stan function (if it finds one). For example,

> lookup(chol)
         StanFunction  Arguments ReturnType Page
72 cholesky_decompose (matrix A)     matrix  331

Page refers to the page of the current Stan User's Manual where the cholesky_decompose function is defined. If you pass it "~", it returns all sampling statements defined in the Stan language. Otherwise, if it fails to find a Stan function, it interprets the input as a regexp and returns matching Stan functions.

There is probably a bunch more stuff that I don't remember now since I haven't been using rstan 2.6.0 personally or for my class. You should definitely upgrade to 2.7.0-1 but be very careful about passing the correct data to Stan until we can upload a 2.7.0-2. If you are maintaining a non-CRAN R package that relies on rstan or a CRAN package that unofficially relies on rstan, let us know by posting on stan-users or emailing. Otherwise, we won't know whether changes to rstan breaks something.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
This is a big release.  We've been saving the official announcement until
PyStan is ready.  Here are the release notes (and we've added another
developer, Dustin Tran, since then).

Below are the release notes for Stan C++.  CmdStan has variational
inference, but I don't think there's an R interface for variational
inference in 2.7.0.  We should have that interface worked out very soon
and will be releasing a 2.7.0.2 version of RStan or a 2.7.1 version
of Stan and RStan.

- Bob

v2.7.0 (9 July 2015)
======================================================================

New Team Members
--------------------------------------------------
* Alp Kucukelbir, who brings you variational inference
* Robert L. Grant, who brings you the StataStan interface

Major New Feature
--------------------------------------------------
* Black-box variational inference, mean field and full
  rank (#1505)

New Features
--------------------------------------------------
* Line numbers reported for runtime errors (#1195)
* Wiener first passage time density (#765) (thanks to
  Michael Schvartsman)
* Partial initialization (#1069)
* NegBinomial2 RNG (#1471) and PoissonLog RNG (#1458) and extended
  range for Dirichlet RNG (#1474) and fixed Poisson RNG for older
  Mac compilers (#1472)
* Error messages now use operator notation (#1401)
* More specific error messages for illegal assignments (#1100)
* More specific error messages for illegal sampling statement
  signatures (#1425)
* Extended range on ibeta derivatives with wide impact on CDFs (#1426)
* Display initialization error messages (#1403)
* Works with Intel compilers and GCC 4.4 (#1506, #1514, #1519)

Bug Fixes
--------------------------------------------------
* Allow functions ending in _lp to call functions ending in _lp (#1500)
* Update warnings to catch uses of illegal sampling functions like
  CDFs and updated declared signatures (#1152)
* Disallow constraints on local variables (#1295)
* Allow min() and max() in variable declaration bounds and remove
  unnecessary use of math.h and top-level :: namespace (#1436)
* Updated exponential lower bound check (#1179)
* Extended sum to work with zero size arrays (#1443)
* Positive definiteness checks fixed (were > 1e-8, now > 0) (#1386)

Code Reorganization and Back End Upgrades
--------------------------------------------------
* New static constants (#469, #765)
* Added major/minor/patch versions as properties (#1383)
* Pulled all math-like functionality into stan::math namespace
* Pulled the Stan Math Library out into its own repository (#1520)
* Included in Stan C++ repository as submodule
* Removed final usage of std::cout and std::cerr (#699) and
  updated tests for null streams (#1239)
* Removed over 1000 CppLint warnings
* Remove model write CSV methods (#445)
* Reduced generality of operators in fvar (#1198)
* Removed folder-level includes due to order issues (part of Math
  reorg) and include math.hpp include (#1438)
* Updated to Boost 1.58 (#1457)
* Travis continuous integration for Linux (#607)
* Add grad() method to math::var for autodiff to encapsulate math::vari
* Added finite diff functionals for testing (#1271)
* More configurable distribution unit tests (#1268)
* Clean up directory-level includes (#1511)
* Removed all lint from new math lib and add cpplint to build lib
  (#1412)
* Split out derivative functionals (#1389)

Manual and Dcoumentation
--------------------------------------------------
* New Logo in Manual; remove old logos (#1023)
* Corrected all known bug reports and typos; details in
  issues #1420, #1508, #1496
* Thanks to Sunil Nandihalli, Andy Choi, Sebastian Weber,
  Heraa Hu, @jonathan-g (GitHub handle), M. B. Joseph, Damjan
  Vukcevic, @tosh1ki (GitHub handle), Juan S. Casallas
* Fix some parsing issues for index (#1498)
* Added chapter on variational inference
* Added strangely unrelated regressions and multivariate probit
  examples
* Discussion from Ben Goodrich about reject() and sampling
* Start to reorganize code with fast examples first, then
  explanations
* Added CONTRIBUTING.md file (#1408)

On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 6:04:39 PM UTC-4, Charles Driver wrote:
> Thanks for this, I didn't realise transformed parameters all had to be specified - I'm getting sensible results now.

The transformed parameters block is for conditionally deterministic functions of the things in the parameters block. I'm not sure what you were expecting to happen if one were undefined.

>  Regarding the jacobian warnings though - do I really need to worry about them if I am just taking single parameters or data values and placing them in a matrix?

For identity "transformtions", the Jacobian determinant is just 1, so excluding it would not affect the posterior kernel.

Ben

It's pretty tough to say what is right. Saying what is wrong is easier and lognormal would be wrong for mu and nu because they are defined over the entire real line. messages.subject: Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.subject_clean: Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.body_plain:
Hi -- I'm fitting a model with 10 parallel chains (each with 2,000 iterations). It typically takes a couple of hours for the first chain to finish, and then another 2-3 hours for all of them to complete. When I intermittently inspect the fitted parameters, R_hat and N_Eff on the first several chains to complete, everything looks great; but if I include the last 2-3 chains to finish, the results don't look good anymore (and the average number of leap frog steps goes way up, to about 1,000).

Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains? I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.

Nice. I've found the forward-backwards type algorithms marginalizing over latent states work pretty well with Stan, although I've found it challenging to extend to greater than 2 discrete states. You can also use the backwards sampling algorithm in the generated quantities block to sample the discrete states. messages.body_plain:
Thanks for rstan 2.7.0-1. Great work.

You encouraged use of pairs() following stanfit. The following suggestion might make pairs.stanfit more useable.

I tried requesting a log scale for the 8schools.stan example for the tau parameter. Tau is bunched up right next to 0, and a log(tau) plot would spread it out better. The base "pairs" function has an example specifying the log scale for the first four variables in the iris data set with pairs(iris, log=1:4), but pairs(fit, log=2, pars=c("mu","tau","lp__")) doesn't work with fit from the 8schools.stan example. I've searched "pairs" and "log scale" on stan-user google groups to no avail. While it's simple to create a transformed xx = log(tau) variable and have graphical plots of xx, often the interpretation or familiarity is on the original tau scale. And the log scale plots are usually closer to symmetrical than the original scale.

More generally, I would like to request a log scale option for traceplot, pairs, and other stan graphics. And would it be possible to have the log scale as the default for scale parameters (sigma's), since they naturally have a log scale (e.g. distance scale - mm, cm, m, km etc)? I'm not sure how feasible it is for stan to recognize automatically a scale parameter though. Finally, back to the pairs(fit) example, having a -2 Log Likelihood variable = -2 * (L - L_max) in addition to lp__ would be helpful.

Thank you!

On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 10:17:53 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 3:54:26 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> >
> > Most of you know the good news already: rstan 2.7.0-1 is on CRAN servers! This will make installation of Stan so much easier.
>
> It also makes crashing your R session so much easier, which is why we hadn't announced it previously. But it is being used in the Stan short course going on yesterday, today, and tomorrow. You still have to install a C++ compiler to actually estimate the parameters of a Stan program, but having the ability to do binary installs (particularly on Windows) is helpful if your computer / toolchain could not previously compile the Stan parser.
>
> There are a lot of changes on the Stan side since 2.6.0, but Daniel will probably mention some of those sometime today. On the R side, the main two things are that it incorporates the ability to automatically save a bare version of a compiled model and to execute chains in parallel. Thus, you should not use the stan.R function from http://mc-stan.org.R anymore. When you do
>
> library(rstan)
>
> you will see the startup message
>
> rstan (Version 2.7.0-1, packaged: , GitRev: 05c3d0058b6a)
> For execution on a local, multicore CPU with excess RAM we recommend calling
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
> options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
>
> Doing
>
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
>
> means that a small foo.rda file will be saved in the same directory as foo.stan (or in tempdir() if that is not writable or you pass a Stan program in the form of a character string to stan()) when foo.stan is parsed into foo.cpp and compiled. Then, in the future, stan() will search the calling environment for the same stanmodel and if it doesn't find that will search for foo.rda on the hard disk or in tempdir(). If it finds such a foo.rda and some checks are passed (such as foo.stan has not been modified more recently or was parsed with an older version of rstan), then it will be loaded rather than recompiling foo.cpp. This approach was originally suggested by Sebastian.
>
> However, it is easy to crash R this way and we have not been entirely successful at preventing all crashes. In particular, with that option enabled, if you pass non-existent data to stan(), it will compile then throw an error but not create an empty stanfit object. Then, when you fix the error, it won't find the non-existent stanfit object but will find foo.rda which will create two instances of the same DSO object in R's memory and crash R. Ironically, it is safer to not pass a list or environment of data to stan() because another feature is that stan() will automatically search the calling environment for objects whose names are the same as the objects in the data block of foo.stan and use those if it finds them. Thus, you can do something like
>
> J <- 8
> y <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12)
> sigma <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)
> fit <- stan(file="8schools.stan")
>
> and it will find matching objects named J, y, and sigma in both the data block of 8schools.stan and R's global environment.
>
> If you have previously called
>
> options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
>
> it will execute the chains in parallel (using the parLapply() function), utilizing (if necessary) as many cores as your computer has. This is only a problem if your computer does not have enough RAM to hold several copies of the data and the MCMC output simultaneously. You can also pass a cores argument to stan() or sampling() to override the mc.cores option. By default, cores is 1 and if you encounter a runtime error, you should call stan() again with cores = 1 to possibly see a better version of the error message before posting on stan-users.
>
> If you are not using RStudio but instead using the R GUI for Windows or Mac (there is something seriously wrong with you but whatever) calling stan() in parallel will by default open a web browser on a temporary file that you can refresh to see the progress of the chains. This can be annoying for chains that execute very quickly and can be prevented by specifying open_progress = FALSE in the call to stan() or sampling(). This should not be an issue if you are using RStudio or a terminal, in which case the output will be piped to the console. Users of knitr will like this better because it the progress is not captured in the processed file. The most recent version of RStudio also has basic support for .stan files and a "Check" button you can press to see if the active .stan file parses. If anyone knows how to make RStudio do code completion on .stan files in the future, let us know.
>
> There is no set_cppo() function anymore (or rather there is but it doesn't do anything but throw a warning), which I have seen a lot of people using in .R scripts (which was inappropriate even when the function did stuff). If you need to change the optimization level or other settings, you have to edit your personal .Makevars file yourself, see
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#configuration
>
> Basically, it should be fine with -O2 but executes slightly faster with -O3.
>
> If you are installing rstan from source using g++ version 4.9.x or later, definitely specify a CXXFLAGS that does not include the -g flag or does include -flto -ffat-lto-objects; otherwise, the Stan parser will take up 250+ Mb of space on your disk. This shouldn't be a problem if you install the binary version of the rstan package from CRAN (which is typical for Windows and recent Macs).
>
> The expose_stan_functions() R function --- which was formerly referred to as testify() --- allows you to test that your user-defined Stan functions are working correctly by calling them in R and comparing them to the results of other R functions that are known to be correct. This is, e.g. how I figured out Phillip's problem described here
>
> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/ErUE-Z25sec/ScHiTmtI_GYJ
>
> So, if you are not utilizing user-defined Stan functions for all non-trivial operations in your .stan file and / or not validating those user-defined Stan functions in R before you call stan(), you are doing it wrong. User-defined Stan functions can also do random number generation, and thus can be used to draw from a posterior predictive distribution after stan() is done or to even do simulations that are not connected to any Stan program.
>
> We see a lot of posts on stan-users about Stan programs that do not sample well, but we do not see a lot of corresponding pairs() plots. You should have been using the pairs() function already, but its defaults have been improved for rstan 2.7.0. Now, it splits the lower and upper triangles at the median accept_stat__ and overplots points if the Markov Chain diverges on that iteration (in red) or exceeds the maximum treedepth (in yellow). This gives you a sense of what parameter interaction causes these sampling difficulties and whether it is a problem of the Markov Chain(s) getting stuck in the tail or being unable to navigate around the mode. The pairs() function takes a pars argument that you should use to specify which parameters to plot. By default, it does all the parameters which is often unreadable (and slow). You should definitely be looking at lp__ and things like variance parameters and other hyperparameters.
>
> Any function that takes a pars argument (like stan, plot, traceplot, and print.stanfit) now has an include argument that defaults to TRUE. This means that any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are included by that function. If include = FALSE, then any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are excluded by that function. So, if you have a lot of named parameters but only a small number that you want to omit, then you can name them with the pars argument and specify include = FALSE. This is particularly useful for stan() if you have latent variables that you do not want to store MCMC samples of (because there are so many of them) but you still want to see the posterior means of those latent variables by subsequently calling get_posterior_mean(). See
>
> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/t2B2W_AjlDc/GvwlKi3fk1QJ
>
> There is also a new lookup() function in RStan that inputs an R function or a name of an R function and returns the corresponding Stan function (if it finds one). For example,
>
> > lookup(chol)
>          StanFunction  Arguments ReturnType Page
> 72 cholesky_decompose (matrix A)     matrix  331
>
> Page refers to the page of the current Stan User's Manual where the cholesky_decompose function is defined. If you pass it "~", it returns all sampling statements defined in the Stan language. Otherwise, if it fails to find a Stan function, it interprets the input as a regexp and returns matching Stan functions.
>
> There is probably a bunch more stuff that I don't remember now since I haven't been using rstan 2.6.0 personally or for my class. You should definitely upgrade to 2.7.0-1 but be very careful about passing the correct data to Stan until we can upload a 2.7.0-2. If you are maintaining a non-CRAN R package that relies on rstan or a CRAN package that unofficially relies on rstan, let us know by posting on stan-users or emailing. Otherwise, we won't know whether changes to rstan breaks something.
>
> Ben
>

Excellent use of pairs(). In this case, there is only 1 divergent transition when accept_stat__ is above is median but several (indicated by red points) when accept_stat__ is below its median. To me, this often suggests a (possibly numeric) problem with the model in the tails. (If the situation were reversed, I would just say keep making adapt_delta higher until the problem goes away). It seems that log_sigma_b0 has a bimodal posterior, which is not ideal for sampling, and some of the other log_sigma terms are bunched up against the lower bound of zero (For plotting purposes, it may be better to generate the logarithm of log_sigma_* in the generated quantities block and put these unbounded parameters into your pairs plot rather than their constrained counterparts). If it is not plausible to you that the log_sigma_* terms could be zero, then a different prior could help. Andrew is a great champion of these half-Cauchy priors but they do have a mode at zero.

The clog log is useful for survival analyses such as this and has a few advantages in terms of interpretation over the logit.

Hi Michael,
What I'm trying to do is have build a model with additive hazards (the negative exponential defined by alpha and beta) and the independent term gamma.

Originally I had the following form:
log(-log(1-p)) = log(census_length) + log(alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma)
where
p = 1- exp(-(census_length * alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma

But due to numerical instabilities and avoiding hard constraints I put this on the log scale.
In stan I implemented this like this

p[i] <- inv_cloglog(log(census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(b_log[i]) * growth_dt_s[i]) + exp(c_log[i]))));

However, this model was still full of numerical instabilities. The solution was to do some algebra to reduce the logging and exponentiating associated with the inv_cloglog function. (Hopefully I haven't stuffed the maths up).

Pr(y=1) = 1 - exp(-lambda x T)
where
lambda =exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_measure[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]))
and T = census_length[i]

Pr(y=0) = 1 - Pr(y=1) = 1 - (1- exp(-lambda x T) = exp(-lambda x T)

We then add a log to each (conforming with our original model form).
Pr(y=1) = log(1-exp(-lambda x T)

Pr(y=0) = log(exp(-lambda x T) = -lambda x T

I then use the increment_log_prob() and the log1m_exp() to calculate the likelihood.
cumulative_hazard[i] <- -census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_measure[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]));

      if (y[i] == 0) {
        increment_log_prob(cumulative_hazard[i]);
      } else {
        increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard[i]));
      }
    }
Hopefully I've explained this ok... (these models make me queasy too!)

In terms of the priors around the log_mu_a0 and log_mu_c0 these are informed by other datasets and on the survival scale they aren't really that tight.
For example
log_a0_mu ~ normal(-0.87,0.75)
means that 95% of the posterior encompasses the probability of dying from

1-exp(-exp(-0.87 + 1.5)) = p =0.84 chance of dying
whereas
1-exp(-exp(-0.87 - 1.5)) = p =0.09 chance of dying

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.body_plain:
> Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains?

No.
No no.
No no no no no.

> I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.

Yup!

The problem with MCMC is that it has to work from _any_ initial condition
(okay, almost any for the math pedants).  What’s happening here is that
the “good” chains are exploring only well-behaved regions of the posterior
and missing the more pathological regions.  So they’re not really good,
they’re just ignorant of the bad.  The “bad” chains are actually you’re
friend here — they find the pathological regions and let you know that
your model has some problems.

As Andrew noted you can often fix these pathological regions by
better parameterizations and other tricks.  Try looking at pairs()
or the trace plots to identify where the problems are arising.

messages.body_plain:
Your likelihood has _three_ nested exponentials which drastically
amplify any perturbation of the underlying parameters (I thought these
models usually only had two — ugh).  The gradients are going to be huge
and require really small step sizes, as you see.  And then you add a huge
number of parameters and make everything worse — even if the marginal
posterior for each parameters is reasonably well-behaved the probability
that at least one of them varies to an extreme in a sample grows with the
number of parameters.  It’s going to be really hard to avoid divergences and
explore everything.

I’m not sure what to tell you.  Maybe others have suggestions for
reparameterizations.

On Tue, Jul 21, 2015 at 9:09 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Sorry for the delay on this. Only progress to share so far is that I confirmed with Danny that the huge range of values he has in L_star (from 0 to 10^43) are intentional.
>

> On Sun, Jul 19, 2015 at 2:21 PM, Daniel Goldstein <da...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > Hi Seth,
> >
> > Yes, the original model I sent out should have f --> y. Attached is a model that implements this change as well as the new priors. I have also attached two data sets, one that uses a truncated PCA basis of size N=2 and another that uses a truncated PCA basis of size N=15. Running the model on both data sets should reveal similar slowdown behavior. The datasets are in the python format of a pickled dictionary of numpy arrays. To load a dataset and run it, you can use the following python code:
> >
> > import pickle, pystan
> > data = pickle.load(open('em_data.N2.pkl','rb'))
> > result = pystan.stan(file='emulator.stan', data=data, refresh=1)
> >
> >
> > Note the refresh=1 keyword argument in the call to pystan.stan -- this is crucial for seeing the slowdown.
> >
> > Danny
> >
> > On Sunday, July 19, 2015 at 4:41:31 AM UTC-7, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> > > Can you share some data so I can try running the model? Also, does
> > > what you sent compile? On lines 132-134 should y be f?
> > >
> > > Seth
> > >
> > > On Sat, Jul 18, 2015 at 10:03 PM, Daniel Goldstein <da...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > > Hi Michael,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for your feedback.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Although the output of the computer simulation is high-dimensional (len(L) ~
> > > > 120, len(x) = 5), the dimensionality of the space in which realizations are
> > > > drawn from the emulator is smaller by ~an order of magnitude or more due to
> > > > the use of basis functions to represent L. In this particular problem, the
> > > > reduced order model for L is just a sum over a truncated PCA basis, where
> > > > the PCs are derived from evaluations of the full simulation at many x,
> > > > designed to fill parameter space, and each coefficient is associated with an
> > > > independent GP:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > L_emulated(x) = \Sum_i^N pc_coeffs[i] * pc_component[i]
> > > >
> > > > pc_coeffs[i] ~ GP(0, Sigma[i]);
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > The dimensionality of pc_component[i] is equal to the dimensionality of L.
> > > > Using N=3, we only have to train 3 GPs, to predict coefficients for 3 PCs,
> > > > but we can capture ~95% of the variance in the 700 instance training sample.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Originally I was using N=15, which is still quite a few GPs to train and may
> > > > lend itself to the nasty posteriors you mentioned. However, for the sake of
> > > > example, if I reduce the size of my PCA basis to  only N=2 components with
> > > > 200 training examples (a low-dimensional, well-conditioned space in my
> > > > particular problem), I experience similar sampling times and a similar
> > > > slowdown of the advancement of the iterations as I did when making
> > > > realizations in the 15 dimensional space. I find this to be pretty confusing
> > > > as the emulator is just realizing scalars from the posterior predictive
> > > > distributions of 2 GPs and fitting a number of nuisance hyperparameters.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I’ll note that gaussian process reduced order models have been applied
> > > > successfully as emulators for the high-dimensional outputs of computer
> > > > simulations over the years, in several different fields. Many of these
> > > > applications include the implementation of fully bayesian inference for x*
> > > > using MCMC.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > http://amstat.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000888
> > > >
> > > > http://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.5177v1.pdf
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Danny
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 4:53:48 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > >>
> > > >> When you put together “high-dimesional output” and “gaussian process
> > > >> emulation”
> > > >> you should get very, very scared.
> > > >>
> > > >> The problem is that in high-dimensions Gaussian process emulation does not
> > > >> work particularly well unless you have _lots_ of points.  And by lots I
> > > >> mean
> > > >> a number that grows exponentially with the size of dimension.  When you
> > > >> don’t have enough points then you run into the problem that the GP isn’t
> > > >> sufficiently regularized — there are an exponentially growing number of
> > > >> functions that interpolate between the given points equally well.
> > > >>
> > > >> The consequence for doing full Bayes is that the posterior in this case is
> > > >> _nasty_.  Just crazy nasty.  What’s likely happening is that the
> > > >> adaptation
> > > >> quickly moves towards a really small step size and NUTS then moves
> > > >> towards a huge number of leapfrog steps to maintain a reasonable
> > > >> exploration and drives up the computation time accordingly (note that
> > > >> print statements are evaluated at each leapfrog step, so if you have
> > > >> a huge number of steps you’ll still see lots of print statements without
> > > >> necessarily any advance to the next iteration).
> > > >>
> > > >> Others might suggest otherwise, but I’ll firmly say to not try to use
> > > >> GP emulation (or really any emulation) in high dimensions!
> > > >>
> > > >> On Jul 18, 2015, at 11:10 PM, Daniel Goldstein <da...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > >>
> > > >> I should also note that memory usage is quite stable for the duration of
> > > >> the warmup phase, independent of iteration number. If one does a `top` on
> > > >> the machine where the code is running, the result is basically as follows,
> > > >> at any iteration:
> > > >>
> > > >>   PID USER      PR  NI  VIRT  RES  SHR S   %CPU %MEM    TIME+  COMMAND
> > > >> 26840 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R    100  0.0  11:58.17 python
> > > >> 26842 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R    100  0.0  11:58.82 python
> > > >> 26841 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R     99  0.0  11:57.99 python
> > > >> 26845 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R     99  0.0  11:57.95 python
> > > >>
> > > >> Danny
> > > >>
> > > >> On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 2:36:31 PM UTC-7, Daniel Goldstein wrote:
> > > >>>
> > > >>> I am attempting to use STAN to model the high-dimensional output of a
> > > >>> detailed, deterministic, black-box computer simulation L(x). I model L(x) as
> > > >>> the linear combination of a set of basis functions (principal components),
> > > >>> where the number of basis functions in the model is much less than
> > > >>> dims(L(x)). For a given x, each basis function has a weight that is modeled
> > > >>> as a gaussian process. The GP covariance matrices depend on x, the point at
> > > >>> which the surrogate model is to be evaluated, and x_T, the points for which
> > > >>> the full simulation has already been evaluated, and the realizations from
> > > >>> the GP posteriors depend on coeffs_T, the principal component coefficients
> > > >>> derived from the evaluations of x_T. This may be familiar to some as
> > > >>> “gaussian process emulation,” following the work of Kennedy and O’Hagan
> > > >>> (2001), and others.
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> For some observed L* I would like to use this model to infer the
> > > >>> corresponding x*, via
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> L(x) ~ normal(L*, L*_err);
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> where L*_err is observational error on L*.
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> A simplified version of my implementation of this model in STAN is
> > > >>> attached. It compiles and runs, but  the iteration completion time increases
> > > >>> dramatically with increasing iteration number, while the time to execute the
> > > >>> “model” block remains constant throughout. I can clock the time it takes the
> > > >>> code to hit the end of the model block with a print statement. During
> > > >>> execution, the final line of the model block is reached an average of 2 or 3
> > > >>> times a second per chain. For iterations < ~30 during the warmup phase, the
> > > >>> frequency at which  a chain completes an iteration is also about 2 or 3 per
> > > >>> second. However, for iterations > ~30, tens of seconds, then minutes, then
> > > >>> hours go by without an advance in the iteration number. As a consequence of
> > > >>> this, I have never been able to get my model past the warmup phase (the
> > > >>> highest iteration I ever let it hit was ~150 out of 2000, which took several
> > > >>> hours). Results from the print statement at the end of the model block,
> > > >>> however, continue to go by at 2 or 3 times a second, independent of
> > > >>> iteration number.
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> Can anyone offer some advice on this issue? I also wonder if I have
> > > >>> implemented my model, specifically the GP realizations, as efficiently as
> > > >>> possible.
> > > >>>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> Thanks in advance for your help,
> > > >>>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.body_plain:
Ok, thanks for the advice. Any tips on how to re-parameterize the attached model (or other tricks to fix things)?

If I initialize the chains at any reasonable point, the pathologies seem to disappear. Is that an ok solution, or is it really just the same thing as discarding the slow chains (since they were presumably slow because of their "bad" starting values).

Without initialization, the slow chains have step size an order of magnitude smaller than the fast ones and consistently run into the tree depth limit; if I increase max depth, it takes prohibitively long for the chains to complete.

On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 4:45:40 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains?
>
> No.
> No no.
> No no no no no.
>
> > I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.
>
> Yup!
>
> The problem with MCMC is that it has to work from _any_ initial condition
> (okay, almost any for the math pedants).  What’s happening here is that
> the “good” chains are exploring only well-behaved regions of the posterior
> and missing the more pathological regions.  So they’re not really good,
> they’re just ignorant of the bad.  The “bad” chains are actually you’re
> friend here — they find the pathological regions and let you know that
> your model has some problems.
>
> As Andrew noted you can often fix these pathological regions by
> better parameterizations and other tricks.  Try looking at pairs()
> or the trace plots to identify where the problems are arising.
>

messages.body_plain:
Does anyone on the Stan development team do consulting?

I'm likely to have some salary money left over on a grant, because my postdoc got a fellowship. To finish what we wanted to do, we need to fit a multivariate linear stochastic differential equation time series model with multinomial observation error in Stan. We're working with stochastic differential equations that have explicit solutions. I haven't yet written down exactly what the solutions are, but they will definitely involve matrix exponentials. If I've understood the current state of Stan correctly, matrix exponentials aren't yet implemented, but could be with a bit of work. We'd also need the models coded efficiently in Stan (I could only code them very inefficiently). Obviously, coauthorship on the resulting paper would be part of the deal.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 1:34:13 PM UTC-4, Matthew Spencer wrote:
> If I've understood the current state of Stan correctly, matrix exponentials aren't yet implemented, but could be with a bit of work.

A bit would be an understatement since
Eigen wouldn't take my patch to make the pseudo-eigendecomposition only use real operations internally ( http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/bz/show_bug.cgi?id=1029 )
And we're not particularly close to supporting complex numbers ( https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/123 )
And the unsupported matrix exponential function that is already in Eigen doesn't support custom scalar types ( http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/unsupported/group__MatrixFunctions__Module.html )
So you would have autodiff the matrix exponential function analytically ( https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=7538355619694802842&hl=en&as_sdt=1,33 ), which that paper claims "can be obtained by combining the earlier results for the matrix inverse product and polynomial (page 7)"
But we don't exactly understand that paper
And even if we did, the whole thing might well be numerically unstable.

Ben

messages.subject: pairs() reloaded
messages.subject_clean: pairs() reloaded
messages.body_plain:
I have now made it possible for the pairs() plot of a stanfit object to have logarithmic axes for (some) variables, the same way pairs() does for a regular matrix. It will be in the next version of rstan but you can use it now by executing

devtools::source_url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/R/pairs.R")

To illustrate this with a model that samples from a bivariate Wishart distribution, you can do

Wishart <- stan_demo("wishart2x2")
pairs(Wishart, pars = c("W", "lp__"), log = TRUE, las = 1)

The log = TRUE option implies that all strictly positive variables will have logarithmic axes, or you can pass an integer vector to log. You should get something like

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-kLXNoFjsYeE/Va7U9lI5ubI/AAAAAAAAAs0/ciLS-S_c1XM/s1600/wishart_pairs.png>
As you can see, there is a good deal of dependence between the covariance and each of the variances (in log units). In particular, these two planes have funnel-like shapes with larger variance at the top and lower variance at the bottom. Thus, it is difficult with a single stepsize and standard deviation of the momentum to navigate both parts of the bivariate distribution efficiently.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
There are a variety of ways to do it. The one that is closest to your current code is to pass integer arrays of length NT to the data block called country_id and year_id. Then if you loop over the data country_id[i] returns the country index for the i-th individual and year_id[i] returns the year index for the i-th individual. If you embed those as parameter indices, like alpha[country_id[i]] and gamma[year_id[i]], you can extract from vectors whose lengths are N and T respectively.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Attaching a didactic script I made for my lab. It first simulates data with varying intercepts and slopes and a specified correlation. Then the first Stan model is the "centered" parameterization. Then the second Stan model is the "non-centered" parameterization that uses the Cholesky factor.

I should have written it for general number of covariates and dimensions. But hopefully extrapolating to more than two dimensions is obvious.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
It looks like that it takes forever to compile this C++ code this your model using Clang on Mac, so for now I can only suggest simplifying the model.

I think it wasn’t a crash for you (I mean not crushing R).  It’s just the C++ compiler on Windows that cannot compiler the C++ and then it  stops.  The C++ compiler in Rtools on windows itself is a 32 bit program, so it can use at most 4G memory (in fact I guess it’s less than 4G) and it is easy to abort compiling.

Jiqiang

Possibly all the transformed parameters are just too much of an abuse, and I need to find another way to specify the models, I'm not sure... in any case I think you don't want such crashes.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.body_plain:
Hey Sharad, have you tried the pairs plot to look at the chains that don't sample well? (Ben just posted updated code and an example.)

Also, I think Stan's parameterization for pareto means pareto(0.1,1.5) is bounded below by 0.1. Does this make sense for your model? If so, I think you're thus supposed to have lower=0.1 for lambda and t_lambda to match. (Not sure this'll help but it's worth a try.)

Seth

On Tue, Jul 21, 2015 at 12:08 PM, Sharad Goel <5hara...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Ok, thanks, good to know. I created an issue but didn't know how to assign it to you:

>
>
> On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 8:51:32 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > I didn’t propagate the improved incomplete beta function derivatives
> > to the beta_cdf in any version of the code yet, so that won’t matter.
> > The current beta_cdf implementation is very numerically fragile and
> > may be contributing to the problem is the parameters are able to take
> > on large values.  You should create an issue about this fragility and
> > assign it to me.
> >
> > On Jul 21, 2015, at 4:46 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > What version of the code are you running?
> > >
> > > On Jul 21, 2015, at 3:13 PM, Sharad Goel <5hara...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Ok, thanks for the advice. Any tips on how to re-parameterize the attached model (or other tricks to fix things)?
> > > >
> > > > If I initialize the chains at any reasonable point, the pathologies seem to disappear. Is that an ok solution, or is it really just the same thing as discarding the slow chains (since they were presumably slow because of their "bad" starting values).
> > > >
> > > > Without initialization, the slow chains have step size an order of magnitude smaller than the fast ones and consistently run into the tree depth limit; if I increase max depth, it takes prohibitively long for the chains to complete.
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 4:45:40 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > > > Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains?
> > > > >
> > > > > No.
> > > > > No no.
> > > > > No no no no no.
> > > > >
> > > > > > I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.
> > > > >
> > > > > Yup!
> > > > >
> > > > > The problem with MCMC is that it has to work from _any_ initial condition
> > > > > (okay, almost any for the math pedants).  What’s happening here is that
> > > > > the “good” chains are exploring only well-behaved regions of the posterior
> > > > > and missing the more pathological regions.  So they’re not really good,
> > > > > they’re just ignorant of the bad.  The “bad” chains are actually you’re
> > > > > friend here — they find the pathological regions and let you know that
> > > > > your model has some problems.
> > > > >
> > > > > As Andrew noted you can often fix these pathological regions by
> > > > > better parameterizations and other tricks.  Try looking at pairs()
> > > > > or the trace plots to identify where the problems are arising.

messages.subject_clean: alt. to Pareto prior for (a + b) in Beta(a,b) rec. in BDA ch. 5?
messages.body_plain:
Andrew:

I recall you saying at one point that you would now use
something other than the following parameterization for
hierarchical priors a vector of binomial/bernoulli parameters
theta in (0, 1):

   phi ~ uniform(0,1)         [equivalently, beta(1,1)]

   kappa ~ Pareto(epsilon, 1.5)     [requires constant epsilon and kappa > epsilon]

   theta[k] ~ beta(phi * kappa, (1 - phi) * kappa)

I currently just copied that recommendation from BDA chapter 5
into the Stan manual, but now that we're thinking more about
weakly or even more strongly informative priors, it may be time
to update that advice.

And should we be more informative on phi?  Perhaps something
as simple as Beta(2,2) as the default on the grounds that we probably
don't want estimates for theta at the boundary?

- Bob

messages.subject: What are best practices for pairs() plots with big multilevel models?
messages.subject_clean: What are best practices for pairs() plots with big multilevel models?
messages.body_plain:
There have been some great discussions here about how important it is to use pairs() plots to check for sampling problems (bottlenecks, correlations, etc.), but I would love advice about how to work with big multilevel models where there are a small number of top-level hyperparameters characterizing hyperpriors, but at lower levels have one or more priors (each with one or more parameters) for each of a large number of groups, so pairs() plots of all combinations of parameters would require too many panes to be useful or practical.

Even for a small example, like 8 schools, plotting all possible pairs (2 hyperparameters and 16 school-level parameters) would require more than 300 panes, and with larger cases that are common in MLM, one can have thousands of group-level parameters, implying millions of panes in an exhaustive pairs() plot.

I've found it very useful when I'm working on models to do pairs() plots of all combinations of hyperparameters to check for bad parameterizations, but have ignored correlations among the site-level parameters because I don't know what to do with so many dimensions.

It would be very helpful to me to know how other people think about this kind of thing and what they do.

On Wednesday, July 22, 2015 at 12:26:45 PM UTC-4, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
> There have been some great discussions here about how important it is to use pairs() plots to check for sampling problems (bottlenecks, correlations, etc.), but I would love advice about how to work with big multilevel models where there are a small number of top-level hyperparameters characterizing hyperpriors, but at lower levels have one or more priors (each with one or more parameters) for each of a large number of groups, so pairs() plots of all combinations of parameters would require too many panes to be useful or practical.

I would say to always include lp__, top-level hyperparameters, and any variance / standard deviation that goes into the likelihood. If that does not point to the source of your problem, then maybe do additional pairs plots with lp__ and a batch of lower-level parameters. High correlations are not a big deal, per se, but can be problematic when combined with changing variances.

Ben

learning.  But if everyone in stats expects mu for a prior mean parameter,
I'm OK with that.

What do we call the prior count (- 2) parameter?

I added a rider to add symmetric forms of both densities.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, July 22, 2015 at 1:06:02 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, July 22, 2015 at 12:26:45 PM UTC-4, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
> > There have been some great discussions here about how important it is to use pairs() plots to check for sampling problems (bottlenecks, correlations, etc.), but I would love advice about how to work with big multilevel models where there are a small number of top-level hyperparameters characterizing hyperpriors, but at lower levels have one or more priors (each with one or more parameters) for each of a large number of groups, so pairs() plots of all combinations of parameters would require too many panes to be useful or practical.
>
> I would say to always include lp__, top-level hyperparameters, and any variance / standard deviation that goes into the likelihood. If that does not point to the source of your problem, then maybe do additional pairs plots with lp__ and a batch of lower-level parameters. High correlations are not a big deal, per se, but can be problematic when combined with changing variances.

When choosing which lower-level parameters to plot it helps to divide them into groups based on the amount of data available.

Krzysztof

>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for letting us know that worked.   It can be hard to
converge in difficult problems, even for Stan, because the
convergence and adaptaiton present the canonical chicken-and-egg
problem, where you need good adaptation to converge and vice-versa.

Andrew's been thinking about various kinds of cross-chain adaptation,
but we have be careful that we can figure out how to do it without
destroying desirable properties of the sampler (not that anything we
do in warmup will destroy the theoretical properties of the sampler,
it's just that they might fail practically speaking and make it hard
to diagnose convergence).

- Bob

As Michael suggested, numerical instability in beta_cdf is possibly the underlying culprit for poor performance when starting far from the typical set.

> hierarchical priors a vector of binomial/bernoulli parameters
> theta in (0, 1):

>   phi ~ uniform(0,1)         [equivalently, beta(1,1)]
>
>   kappa ~ Pareto(epsilon, 1.5)     [requires constant epsilon and kappa > epsilon]

> I currently just copied that recommendation from BDA chapter 5
> into the Stan manual, but now that we're thinking more about
> weakly or even more strongly informative priors, it may be time
> to update that advice.
>
> And should we be more informative on phi?  Perhaps something
> as simple as Beta(2,2) as the default on the grounds that we probably
> don't want estimates for theta at the boundary?

messages.body_plain:
Nooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo!
Those analyses are incredibly biased because
they optimize on the wrong parameters (step
size and number of leapfrog step instead of
step size and integration time) and their artificial
bounds on the number of leapfrog steps is
waaaaaaaaaay too small.

Anyways, NUTS (or its generalization!) is the right
answer to the optimal integration time (proof coming
soon!) and we know how to globally optimize
the step size.  Position dependent curvature is
best handled by RHMC or reparameterizations.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
messages.body_plain:
BDA3, Section 5.3, Page 110, equation (5.9):

 p(alpha, beta) propto (alpha + beta)^(-5/2)

If I'm doing my algebra right, that means

  p(alpha + beta) = Pareto(alpha + beta | 1.5)

alpha and beta are hyperprior parameters for a Beta
distribution over tumor risks in rats.  You reasoned
that making the following uniform would make sense

  alpha / (alpha + beta) and sqrt(alpha + beta)

The suggestion that I think people want to see in order to
think about informative priors, is similar to what you
do, namely to reparameterize beta for mu in (0, 1) and phi > 0 as

  Beta_mean(y | mu, phi) = Beta(y | mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi)

I suggested in the manual

  mu ~ uniform(0, 1);

and

  phi ~ Pareto(1.5)

in attempt to follow section 5.3 of BDA.

We could put informative priors on both mu and phi.  A beta's
a natural choice for mu, though you also consider logit transforming
it, and then we could use anything.   We could also log-transform
phi to an unconstrained space.

In fact, the more I think about Stan computation, the more sense
it makes to start reparameterizing everything on the unconstrained
scale so we don't have to transform and pay the Jacobian cost in
autodiff.  For example, the most natural seeming parameterization for
Beta would be this

  Beta_unc(y | logit_mu, log_phi)

    = Beta_mean(y | inv_logit(logit_mu), exp(log_phi)

    = Beta(y | inv_logit(logit_mu) * exp(log_phi),
               (1 - inv_logit(logit_mu)) * exp(log_phi))

but we could also just log transform the usual parameterization

  Beta_unc_2(y | log_alpha, log_beta)

    = Beta(y | exp(log_alpha), exp(log_beta))

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan 2.7 available (all interfaces)
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.7 available (all interfaces)
messages.body_plain:
Stan 2.7 is now available for all interfaces.

This is a fairly substantial release.  As usual, everything you
need can be found starting from the Stan home page:

  http://mc-stan.org/

Some highlights:

  RStan is on CRAN! (1)

  Variational Inference in CmdStan!! (2)

  Two new Stan developers!!!

  A whole new logo!!!!

  Math library with autodiff now available in its own repo!!!!!

-------------------

(1) Just doing install.packages("rstan") isn't going to work
because of dependencies;  please go to the RStan getting
started page for instructions of how to install from CRAN.  It's
much faster than building from source and you no longer need
a machine with a lot of RAM to install.

(2) Coming soon to an interface near you.

Here's the full set of release notes:

v2.7.0 (9 July 2015)
======================================================================

New Team Members
--------------------------------------------------
* Alp Kucukelbir, who brings you variational inference
* Robert L. Grant, who brings you the StataStan interface

Major New Feature
--------------------------------------------------
* Black-box variational inference, mean field and full
  rank (#1505)

New Features
--------------------------------------------------
* Line numbers reported for runtime errors (#1195)
* Wiener first passage time density (#765) (thanks to
  Michael Schvartsman)
* Partial initialization (#1069)
* NegBinomial2 RNG (#1471) and PoissonLog RNG (#1458) and extended
  range for Dirichlet RNG (#1474) and fixed Poisson RNG for older
  Mac compilers (#1472)
* Error messages now use operator notation (#1401)
* More specific error messages for illegal assignments (#1100)
* More specific error messages for illegal sampling statement
  signatures (#1425)
* Extended range on ibeta derivatives with wide impact on CDFs (#1426)
* Display initialization error messages (#1403)
* Works with Intel compilers and GCC 4.4 (#1506, #1514, #1519)

Bug Fixes
--------------------------------------------------
* Allow functions ending in _lp to call functions ending in _lp (#1500)
* Update warnings to catch uses of illegal sampling functions like
  CDFs and updated declared signatures (#1152)
* Disallow constraints on local variables (#1295)
* Allow min() and max() in variable declaration bounds and remove
  unnecessary use of math.h and top-level :: namespace (#1436)
* Updated exponential lower bound check (#1179)
* Extended sum to work with zero size arrays (#1443)
* Positive definiteness checks fixed (were > 1e-8, now > 0) (#1386)

Code Reorganization and Back End Upgrades
--------------------------------------------------
* New static constants (#469, #765)
* Added major/minor/patch versions as properties (#1383)
* Pulled all math-like functionality into stan::math namespace
* Pulled the Stan Math Library out into its own repository (#1520)
* Included in Stan C++ repository as submodule
* Removed final usage of std::cout and std::cerr (#699) and
  updated tests for null streams (#1239)
* Removed over 1000 CppLint warnings
* Remove model write CSV methods (#445)
* Reduced generality of operators in fvar (#1198)
* Removed folder-level includes due to order issues (part of Math
  reorg) and include math.hpp include (#1438)
* Updated to Boost 1.58 (#1457)
* Travis continuous integration for Linux (#607)
* Add grad() method to math::var for autodiff to encapsulate math::vari
* Added finite diff functionals for testing (#1271)
* More configurable distribution unit tests (#1268)
* Clean up directory-level includes (#1511)
* Removed all lint from new math lib and add cpplint to build lib
  (#1412)
* Split out derivative functionals (#1389)

Manual and Documentation
--------------------------------------------------
* New Logo in Manual; remove old logos (#1023)
* Corrected all known bug reports and typos; details in
  issues #1420, #1508, #1496
* Thanks to Sunil Nandihalli, Andy Choi, Sebastian Weber,
  Heraa Hu, @jonathan-g (GitHub handle), M. B. Joseph, Damjan
  Vukcevic, @tosh1ki (GitHub handle), Juan S. Casallas
* Fix some parsing issues for index (#1498)
* Added chapter on variational inference
* Added strangely unrelated regressions and multivariate probit
  examples
* Discussion from Ben Goodrich about reject() and sampling
* Start to reorganize code with fast examples first, then
  explanations
* Added CONTRIBUTING.md file (#1408)

messages.subject: weird segfault problem with rstan (only with parallel sampling, only on one computer)
messages.subject_clean: weird segfault problem with rstan (only with parallel sampling, only on one computer)
messages.body_plain:
I have a weird segfault problem with rstan. I see it with both version 2.6.0 and 2.7.0-1.

I have two machines running Debian 8.1 (jessie), both up to date via apt-get update, upgrade, and dist-upgrade, and both up to date with R 3.2.1 and update.packages()

One machine is a workstation and the other is a laptop (a Lenovo Thinkpad W541). I see segfaulting only on the laptop and never on the workstation.

rstan runs the 8schools model fine on both machines, running 10,000 iterations both with serial sampling and with parallel sampling (mclapply for rstan 2.6.0 and with setting cores > 1 on rstan 2.7.0-1).

However, I am working on a large multilevel mixture model. This model runs correctly when I sample the chains serially. But when I sample the chains in parallel it runs fine on the workstation whereas on the laptop it consistently (every time) segfaults on some (but not all) of the chains.  The segfaults don't happen right away. They typically run for tens to hundreds of iterations before one or more chains segfaults with "address (nil), cause 'unknown' " (always that exact message).

I do the stan run from the command line using Rscript and I monitor the run with htop, which shows that I always have at least 20 GB of RAM free. I also have plenty of free space on all my disk partitions, so it's not an issue of running out of room for temporary files.

After a chain segfaults, the R script continues to run and the other chains continue to sample.

I'm attaching my model and a driver script, the sessionInfo() output, the stderr output for the crash (but I edited down the printout of the function call arguments on lines 9 and 10 of the traceback, which printed out a data list with more than 20,000 elements)

The laptop is very new and I've seen some weirdness at boot time with the Linux drivers not quite being up to date for the chipset and sometimes failing to initialize the machine properly, so my problem might be an OS driver issue, not a stan issue. On the other hand, I have not had segfaulting problems with other software on this laptop after a successful boot, except for rstan when I'm doing parallel sampling. Also, I ran stress-ng for about 8 hours and didn't get any errors.

So I'm not at all sure that this is a stan issue but it might be, so I'm reporting it just in case other people see something similar.

I do almost all my nontrivial stan computing on my workstation, not my laptop, so the fact that a few large models are segfaulting on the laptop when I sample in parallel is not preventing me from getting my work done. Thus, unless other people are having similar problems, this is probably a low priority issue with respect to the stan team's valuable time and energy.

If there is other useful information that I can provide, I'd be happy to do that.

messages.body_plain:
However, if the OP is desperate enough, a fixed number of
optimization steps for eg Newton-Raphson could be implemented
explicitly in Stan. If the problem itself is known and
well-behaved, 4-8 steps could provide convergence that is
indistinguisable from an optimization routine (it would be a bit
slower because of not terminating early).

I did not do the analysis for this problem, but I guess it is
worth an experiment.

Stan can be coaxed to do a number of things that are not
explicitly available built-in. Eg currently I am using an
closed-form formula for a matrix exponential (matrix is small,
<7x7, and sparse). Suboptimal and tedious, yes, but doable.

Best,

Tamas
