messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I was thinking about the mathematical expression for the likelihood. In the one-temperatrure model it is a convolution of the real underlying distribution (log-normal) with the noise (normal)  i.e. the probability of observing x_obs is :

(1)   p (x_obs) = INTEGRAL dx p_lognormal (x ,LN_mu, LN_sigma) * p_normal (x_obs - x, FB_mu, scatter)

integrated over the support of X. For the two temperature model it should be:

p(x_obs) = proportion p_1(x_obs) + (1-proportion) p_2(x_obs)

where p_1/2 are the probabilities defined in (1) but with different parameters for LN_mu_1/2 and LN_sigma_1/2.
Cheers,
Lukas

Am Freitag, 24. Juli 2015 00:30:21 UTC+1 schrieb statno...@gmail.com:
> Hi Bob,
>
> thanks for the fast reply.
>
> > Your model's not identified, so there are going to be problems.
>
> > Usually a noisy measurement model is assuming that the "true" value
> > of something being measured is equal to the measurement plus some
> > noise (often just centered normal).
>
> What do you mean by the model is not identified? I tested it with synthetic data and it works fine (The R-code and the stan model below).
> About the noise/model:
> The model is for the luminosities emitted from a turbulent medium. These luminosities should follow a log-normal distribution with LN_mu and LN_sigma.
> Unfortunately, does the fore/background radiation shift my measurements systematically with mean_FB. Additionally I have a normal noise on my measurements with mean zero and a standard deviation called scatter in the model. Here is the code:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> NumData;
>   real InData[NumData];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real                   LN_mu;
>   real<lower=0>  LN_sigma;
>   real                   FB_mu;
>   real<lower=0>  scatter;
>   real<lower=0>  mydata_true[NumData];
> }
>
> model {
>   LN_mu      ~ cauchy (0, 1);
>   FB_mu      ~ cauchy (0, 1);
>   LN_sigma  ~ cauchy (0, 1);
>   scatter       ~ cauchy (0, 1);
>
> for (i in 1:NumData)
>   {
>     mydata_true[i] ~ lognormal(LN_mu, LN_sigma);
>     InData[i]          ~ normal(FB_mu + mydata_true[i], scatter);
>   }
> }
>
> and the R-code for creating synthetic data:
> Synthetic_data <- rlnorm(NumData, Syn_LN_mu, Syn_LN_sigma) + rnorm(NumData, Syn_FB_mu, Syn_noise_sigma)
>
> > We don't recommend using these priors, by the way.  See the
> > regression chapter of the manual for discussion.
> >
> > Then when that's fixed, try simulating data from the model
> > then fitting it.
>
> I use now cauchy distributions as priors as recommended and my model fits the synthetic data.
>
> > I don't quite understand here what you're trying to do, because
> > I didn't understand the intention of your first noisy measurement
> > model, if that's what it is.
>
> The second model now assumes that we observe a warm and a cold turbulent medium, both following log-normal distributions, but because of the different temperatures with different mu's and sigma's.
> The systematic shift caused by the fore/background and the noise stays the same for both, as they are observed together in one picture. As I do not know, which radiation comes form which medium  this is a mixture model of two media with log-normal distributions (ignoring the noise and the fore/background). But including the noise is exactly my problem.
>
> Maybe it helps asking the other way around.... That is the code what creates the synthetic data:
>
> Synthetic_data <-                              rlnorm(       proportion *NumData, Syn_mu1, Syn_sigma1)
> Synthetic_data <- c(Synthetic_data, rlnorm((1.0-proportion)*NumData, Syn_mu2, Syn_sigma2))
> Synthetic_data <- Synthetic_data  +  rnorm(NumData, Syn_FB_mu, Syn_noise_sigma)
>
> The second model stated above measures the parameters (proportion, Syn_mu1, Syn_sigma1, Syn_mu2, Syn_sigma2) but not Syn_FB_mu and Syn_noise_sigma. How can I measure these?
>
> Thank you a lot for your time and your help.
> Cheers,
> Lukas

rstan

The algorithm is indeed hairy, and coding it in Stan is really
stretching the limits of the language, but then one gets the
derivative automatically.

My understanding is that Stan can't just grab expm from an
existing library, because it also need the Jacobian --- is this
correct, or are there other obstacles/requirements (licensing
etc)?

I did a bit of reading about the Jacobian of the matrix
exponential. Higham's "Functions of Matrices" mentions the
derivative in Section 10.6, and suggests that there is a nice
duality between the matrix exponential and its Frechet derivative
(you can use expm on a special block matrix to get the derivative
at the same time). But this is inefficient and there are two
special algorithms.

So the question is this: would a C++ function which, for a given
matrix A, computes expm(A) and its Jacobian, be sufficient for
solving this problem?

Al-Mohy's thesis is about the derivative too, but I don't have
time to read it right now.

Best,

Tamas

I see what's going on.  Neat.  I'm not used to seeing that mean.

I have no idea how to answer your second question by the way --- maybe
someone else can go back and take a look.  We
have an ODE solver built in if that helps.  I flagged it with physics
problem so Michael might notice.  If not, I suggest writing again with
just that in the title or I can ping him directly.  We're getting so
much mail now that it's hard to keep track of it all!

The (weak) identification problem is in FB_mu + mydata_true[i].
You can subtract a number from FB_mu and add it to all the mydata_true and
get the same likelihood.   This is very typical in hierarchical models (which
have same structure as your model).

Your model also has LN_mu to take up the slack for FB_mu.  So the only thing
identifiying this is the priors.  But the Cauchy is a weak, fat-tailed prior by
construction so it can give you problems in practice when you try to use it to
control the location of a bunch of parameters.

If you can fit simulated data to it, then it may not be a big
deal in practice.  There's a discussion of identifiability issues and
what they do to sampling in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

- Bob

For example, nparams is data, hypermeans is declared as a transformed parameter "vector[nparams] hypermeans", but elements 1 -- 11 are assigned directly.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
This is really just a latent variable model — i.e. don’t
think about mydata_true as data but rather as some
latent state describing the underlying source of the radiation.

>From this perspective the mixture is no problem — you
just write the latent luminosity as coming from a mixture
of the high and low sources,

for (n in 1:n_data) {
  latent_luminosity[n] ~ increment_log_prob(
                                       log_mix(theta,
                                                     lognormal_log(low_mu, low_sigma),
                                                     lognormal_log(high_mu, high_sigma)));
  measured_luminosity[n] ~ normal(latent_luminosity[n] + offset, scatter);
}

Here theta is the creative proportion of the two components
in your medium.  If you really want to go crazy you could
make theta depend on other parameters, but you should
start simple.

Also be careful with that assumed normal on the data.  It
should probably be a log_normal given the positivity
constraint (here you’re hoping that the measurements
are large enough that the normal is an okay approximation).

messages.body_plain:
If you're using rstan and you're just asking about making frequency plots (not specifically about a layout that has frequency on the left and traceplots on the right), then I'd recommend looking at the R package ggmcmc, which generates a lot of nice plots.

You have to convert your stanfit object into a coda object, but rstan has functions for that. The old way (before rstan 2.7) was
coda_obj <- mcmc.list(lapply(1:ncol(stanfit_obj), function(x) mcmc(as.array(stanfit_obj)[,x,])))

But now you can use

coda_obj <- As.mcmc.list(stanfit_obj)

(Be careful about capitalizing the first "A" in "As.mcmc.list" because there's a coda function "as.mcmc.list" that doesn't know about stanfit objects)

Look at ggs_histogram and ggs_density in particular, and you may find ggs_caterpillar useful as well.

of the model, which can be related.  Scaling can even be sublinear

the additional data help constrain the posterior to something nicely
shaped for sampling (roughly normal).

That axis should be seconds/draw, not seconds/sample!  And it's
for a pretty simple problem.

Andrew's still training me to say that a sample is a sequence
of draws.  And that a sample has a size.

messages.body_plain:
Also, it's going to take at least as long to run 4 chains
in parallel as it takes to run one chain serially, and probably
longer, because it'll be the max time of running 4 individual chains with
different starting points.  And there will be memory contention with
four parallel processes, which may or may not cause a slowdown.

The parallelization doesn't make a single chain go any faster, it just
pushes different chains to different processes (or at least I believe
it's a process-based parallelism behind those R packages).

- Bob

messages.subject: GP modelling a 2nd derivative?
messages.subject_clean: GP modelling a 2nd derivative?
messages.body_plain:
In neuroscience, we often collect EEG data to measure the activity of the brain. However, EEG voltage is a relative measure, and the specific choice of reference point can change the observed voltage topology quite dramatically. Apparently ([1]) there is a known-but-rarely-applied "solution" to this issue whereby you compute the 2nd derivative of the voltage topology using an arbitrary reference, resulting in a current density topology that provides an absolute measure of brain activity, and one that will be the same regardless of the reference chosen to generate the original voltage topology.

Ignoring for the moment the issue of the topology being on the surface of a sphere (which is being discussed elsewhere, [2]), is there a recommended way to model this scenario in stan? I know that one method would be to simply model the voltage as a function of a spatiotemporal GP, then put computation of the 2nd derivative of the GP in the transformed parameters section, but possibly there's a more direct approach whereby the voltage is modelled as a transformation of a current density GP?

[1] https://books.google.ca/books?id=SzavAwAAQBAJ&lpg=PA165&ots=I9lMzlss5L&dq=Luck%20current%20density&pg=PA165#v=onepage&q&f=false

[2] https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/stan-users/z2hj0Zb1I6A

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: rstan with cores > 1 and non-standard package library location
messages.subject_clean: rstan with cores > 1 and non-standard package library location
messages.body_plain:
With rstan 2.7.0, stan() stops with errors with cores > 0 and R packages (Rcpp, inline and rstan in particular) in a user-specified location, It results in errors like "4 nodes produced errors; first error: there is no package called 'rstan'". This might be resolved by adding an optional argument to sampling(), say something like userLibs that a user could set to a character string vector containing the paths where they store the package libraries. Then add a statement like the following "if(!is.null(userLibs)) parallel:::clusterEvalQ(cl = cluster, .libPaths(userLibs))" before the statement "parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, expr = require(Rcpp, quietly = TRUE))". In the mean time I guess I'll have to continue using parLapply or mclapply as before.

Thanks,
Bill

On Friday, July 24, 2015 at 3:35:54 PM UTC+2, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> On Friday, July 24, 2015 at 2:48:29 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > I am planning to include stan models in R package and have a couple of questions:
> >
> > - How can I make sure that the binary versions of the package come along with a pre-compiled stan binary?
>
> You have to compile them
>
> > - Is there a recommended way to do this?
>
> Download the .zip file but put it under inst/include of a copy of an unzipped rstan_2.7.0-1.tar.gz (not under the include/ directory of your installed rstan)
>
> setwd("/path/to/inst/include/example-models")
> models <- dir(getwd(), pattern = "stan$", full.names=TRUE, recursive = TRUE)
> library(paralell)
> options(mc.cores = 8) # or however many cores you have available
> output <- mclapply(models, mc.silent = TRUE,
>                    FUN = function(m) try(rstan::stan_model(m, auto_write = TRUE)))
>
> Then rebuild the rstan package via R CMD build
>
> > - Should I use the command-line interface or the rstan interface?
>
> rstan
>
> > - And which options make 100% sure that stan does not output anything (the open_progress=FALSE does not seem to be sufficient)
>
> The open_progress to sampling() or stan() is only relevant if you are running the model. Ostensibly the mc.silent argument suppresses stdout, but it is not as if the "COMPILING MODEL X NOW" statements hurt anything. You could also background the R process doing this.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
messages.body_plain:
I need to fix my understanding here as I am new to stan.

In the 2.7 version manual on page 40, we are saying that:
row_vector[N] b[M];
is equivalent (though more efficient than) to:
matrix b[M,N];

Now are we saying (as below) that:
vector[N] b[M];
is the same as:
matrix[M,N] b;

Both give the same shape. Is that correct?

Raghu.

On Monday, May 4, 2015 at 12:54:45 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> What's going on with:
>
>  vector[Obs] Losses[N];
>
>
> is that it produces an array of size N whose entries
> are vectors of size Obs.  So it's (N x Obs).  Same shape
> as this:
>
>   matrix[N,Obs] Losses;
>
> There's a chapter in the manual that goes over differences
> between arrays and vectors/row-vectors.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Raghu,

The short answer is no, they are not the same shape. More details below.

On Tue, Jul 28, 2015 at 10:18 AM, Raghu Naik <naik....@gmail.com> wrote:
> I need to fix my understanding here as I am new to stan.
>
> In the 2.7 version manual on page 40, we are saying that:
> row_vector[N] b[M];
> is equivalent (though more efficient than) to:
> matrix b[M,N];
>

matrix b[M,N] is not well formed. The square brackets always describe the thing directly to the left of it. The matrix type requires a size.

This is well formed: matrix[M,N] b;

Here, b is a matrix that is M rows and N columns. These are different types in the underlying Stan C++ implementation. If you wanted to operate over rows, the first, row_vector[N] b[M], will be more efficient than slicing rows out of matrix[M,N] b.

> Now are we saying (as below) that:
> vector[N] b[M];
> is the same as:
> matrix[M,N] b;
>
> Both give the same shape. Is that correct?

This is incorrect.

vector[N] is an N-vector, or in matrix terms, N x 1. So vector[N] b[M] looks like a matrix[N,M], not matrix[M,N].

Hopefully that helps.

Daniel

N is the number of vectors (each of length Obs) in the array Losses. In your example

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on an array of vectors finding the wrong dimensions
messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 28, 2015, at 11:52 AM, Raghu Naik <naik....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Daniel / Jonah:
>
> Thanks for the quick replies. Very helpful.
>
> It seems that in these declarations the vector[N] / row_vector[N] component is guiding the output matrix shape and we are not making any shape assumption of the b[M] array. For that reason
>
> row_vector[N] b[M];
>
> is matrix[M,N]  and
>
> vector[N] b[M];
>
> is  matrix[N,M].

I can see how you could conclude that, but it's not at all how Stan
actually works.  Analogies from R will not work.  We coded Stan directly
in C++ so you need to develop your intuitions there.

There's a whole chapter in the manual to help you get started.
Here are the data types in Stan and what they are in C++:

  matrix[M,N] a;   // Eigen:Matrix<T, Dynamic, Dynamic>

is a matrix, with data stored contiguously in column-major order in
the underlying C++ app.  It's also what you need for any matrix op.

  real a[M,N];   // std::vector<std::vector<T> >

is a 2D array, with data stored non-contiguously in row-major order.

And finally

  row_vector[N] a[M];  // std::vector<Eigen::Matrix<T, Dynamic, 1> >

is a 1D array whose elements are rwo vectors.

> If that is the case we may be  better off reading these statements as
> 	• a N dimensional row vector with M-dimensional columns as elements for the first declaration and
> 	• a N-dimensional column vector with M-dimensional rows as elements for the second declaration.

> Instead, for example,  if I read the second declaration as a M dimensional array with N dimensional vectors as elements, I do not get a clue about the output structure ?

The I/O is all encapsulated w.r.t. R.   When you go to the dump
format, we use R's dump ordering.  For JSON in Python, it's done
differently.

> of this declaration. Is it a rbind or a cbind of the M vectors in b? That was my problem in the first place that got me looking up the group threads.

Stan's written in C++, not R, so there are no rbind or cbind things going on anywhere.

- Bob

> Hi Bob and Michael,
>
> first thanks for your answers. I was playing around with synthetic data, but I could not fix my problems by myself. I implemented it now like you suggested, but I have the problem that the model does not converge when I include the scatter term. Here is my model:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1>  NumData;
>   real                 Measured_Data[NumData];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0>                   Latent_Data[NumData];
>   real<lower=0, upper=1>    Mixing_proportions;
>   real                                    mu_low;
>   real                                    mu_high;
>   real<lower=0>                   sigma_low;
>   real<lower=0>                   sigma_high;
> //  real<lower=0>                 Scatter;
> //  real                                  Offset;
> }
>
> model {
>   ///----------------------------///
>   ///   PRIORS                   ///
>   ///----------------------------///
>     mu_low       ~ cauchy(-2, 0.5);
>     mu_high      ~ cauchy(+2, 0.5);
>     sigma_low   ~ cauchy( 0, 0.5);
>     sigma_high  ~ cauchy( 0, 0.5);
> //  Offset     ~ cauchy( 0, 1.0);
> //  Scatter    ~ cauchy( 0, 1.0);
> ///----------------------------///
>
>   for (n in 1:NumData)
>   {
>      increment_log_prob( log_mix( Mixing_proportions,
>      lognormal_log(Latent_Data[n], mu_low , sigma_low ),
>      lognormal_log(Latent_Data[n], mu_high, sigma_high) ));
>
> //     Measured_Data[n] ~ normal(Latent_Data[n] + Offset, Scatter);
>      Measured_Data[n] ~ normal(Latent_Data[n], 0.000001);
>   }
> }
>
> About the model:
> 1) Including the scatter makes the model really slow.

You mean including the commented-out lines?  In addition to or instead
of the one with the small constant scale?

The Cauchy priors may not be strong enough to deal with the
non-identifiability of Latent_Data[n] + Offset.

Sonetimes in small data settings, it helps to reparameterizing
using the non-centered parameterization.

For speed, you need to vectorize the measured_data and latent_data
statements.  Just pull them out of the loop, define them as vectors,
and use

  measured_data ~ normal(latent_data + offset, scatter);
  ...

See the manual chapter on vectorization (right before the list of
distributions).

There's nothing to identify the two mixture components, so you are
unlikely to get good convergence with 4 chains (1/8 they all wind
up in the same mode).

What's up with the scale on this?

>      Measured_Data[n] ~ normal(Latent_Data[n], 0.000001);

You do realize we work on the sd not the variance scale?

It's going to be hard to adapt if Measured_data is on the 1e-7 scale.
Can you standardize?  It's much easier than having to adapt, which is
hard when there are parameters of differenting scales (it's a conditioning
issue).

> Commenting the last line out and replacing Latent_Data with Measured_Data the model needs 2 minutes. With these lines the model needs few hours.
> Do I make here already my mistake? Is this normal? Do you expect this?
>
> 2) As you can see, I tried the model also with known Scatter and without the Offset.
> Even in this case it does not converge. Here are the parameter with, which I was testing it:
>

How are you measuring convergence?  You probably need more warmup
for this pathological a scale (you only get about 14 decimal places
accuracy max, and having things at multiple scales kills about half
that up front, so you'll probalby need lots of adaptation and need to
start at a very very small step size.  And also have the latent_data
initialized very close to the measured data, not on (-2, 2) uniform,
which makes no sense if the data's on the scale 1e-7.

> I have recently implemented an unsupervised HMM in Stan very successfully.  In the manual a fully unsupervised HMM is not discussed except to say that the posterior is typically very multi-modal.  Having read this I am surprised I got it to work so well.  I am writing this post for three reasons:
>
> 1) If anyone is interested in the model then an example is attached
> 2) To get feedback on whether other more experienced Stan users and better statisticians than myself are surprised I got it to work - is there something about my case that makes it work?
> 3) To get feedback on the model in general - is there anything I could do to make it more efficient
>
> I ran my model using rstan in R.  I attach the R script.  The script is completely self-contained.  The model is running on simulated data.
>
> My data is a large number (1000) of short timeseries (length=10).  I have two latent groups.  The data emitted at each timestep is normal with different parameters for the two groups.  I have specified time invariant transition probabilities.  I am interested in estimates of the model parameters (likelihood parameters, transition probabilities and prior for the first timestep) and group membership for each timestep of each timeseries.
>
> My strategy is to embed the forward-backward algorithm in the transformed parameters block.  From this block I keep the estimates of group membership (because I am interested in them) and the one-step prediction probabilities from the forward algorithm (which I need to increment the log_probability).
>
> Hopefully this is clear.  I suspect my coding of the forward-backward algorithm might be a bit non-standard.  It certainly could be made more general (e.g. I have hard-coded in two groups which is all I will ever need for this project).
>
> Thanks,
>
> Jon.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Successful unsupervised hidden Markov model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Successful unsupervised hidden Markov model
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, I've been meaning to write those up forever and haven't had time to write up clear examples.  Everything is in the repo: https://github.com/jrnold/ssmodels-in-stan/. It includes: forward-backward for HMMS, including a version specifically for change points, and Kalman filters and simulation smoothers calculated the usual way (with and without missing observations), and using sequential processing, (with and without missing values).  I wrote them before user-defined functions, so I may be able to simplify the code. I'll try to get them cleaned up and included in the examples, but it may not be in the immediate future.

On Tue, Jul 28, 2015 at 12:40 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Would you mind including that on our example-models repo?
>
> There's a "misc" directory now for things that aren't parts
> of books, or you could start something else.  I think you may
> have mentioned you had some Kalman filter examples up your sleeve,
> too?
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jul 20, 2015, at 11:27 PM, Jeffrey Arnold <jeffrey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Nice. I've found the forward-backwards type algorithms marginalizing over latent states work pretty well with Stan, although I've found it challenging to extend to greater than 2 discrete states. You can also use the backwards sampling algorithm in the generated quantities block to sample the discrete states. Together, I am almost certain that these constitute a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler. Here's an example of a general HMM model with Poisson observations (https://github.com/jrnold/ssmodels-in-stan/blob/master/stan/foo.R) applied to the earthquakes model in Zucchini and MacDonald, Hidden Markov Models for R (https://github.com/jrnold/ssmodels-in-stan/blob/master/stan/foo.R).
> >
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Jul 20, 2015 at 2:47 PM, jonny230774 <jonny_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Daniel,
> >
> > Very happy for this to be shared however you see fit.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> > Jon.
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 8:45:50 AM UTC+12, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > Thanks! Mind if we put it in the example models repository?
> >
> > There are a couple weird things going on with an element of prob_grp being NaN, but otherwise, nicely done!
> >
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> > P.S. I like your warning.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Sunday, June 21, 2015 at 8:06:43 PM UTC-4, jonny230774 wrote:
> > Hello All,
> >
> > I have recently implemented an unsupervised HMM in Stan very successfully.  In the manual a fully unsupervised HMM is not discussed except to say that the posterior is typically very multi-modal.  Having read this I am surprised I got it to work so well.  I am writing this post for three reasons:
> >
> > 1) If anyone is interested in the model then an example is attached
> > 2) To get feedback on whether other more experienced Stan users and better statisticians than myself are surprised I got it to work - is there something about my case that makes it work?
> > 3) To get feedback on the model in general - is there anything I could do to make it more efficient
> >
> > I ran my model using rstan in R.  I attach the R script.  The script is completely self-contained.  The model is running on simulated data.
> >
> > My data is a large number (1000) of short timeseries (length=10).  I have two latent groups.  The data emitted at each timestep is normal with different parameters for the two groups.  I have specified time invariant transition probabilities.  I am interested in estimates of the model parameters (likelihood parameters, transition probabilities and prior for the first timestep) and group membership for each timestep of each timeseries.
> >
> > My strategy is to embed the forward-backward algorithm in the transformed parameters block.  From this block I keep the estimates of group membership (because I am interested in them) and the one-step prediction probabilities from the forward algorithm (which I need to increment the log_probability).
> >
> > Hopefully this is clear.  I suspect my coding of the forward-backward algorithm might be a bit non-standard.  It certainly could be made more general (e.g. I have hard-coded in two groups which is all I will ever need for this project).
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > Jon.

> > On Jul 28, 2015, at 11:52 AM, Raghu Naik <naik....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Daniel / Jonah:
> >
> > Thanks for the quick replies. Very helpful.
> >
> > It seems that in these declarations the vector[N] / row_vector[N] component is guiding the output matrix shape and we are not making any shape assumption of the b[M] array. For that reason
> >
> > row_vector[N] b[M];
> >
> > is matrix[M,N]  and
> >
> > vector[N] b[M];
> >
> > is  matrix[N,M].
>
> I can see how you could conclude that, but it's not at all how Stan
> actually works.  Analogies from R will not work.  We coded Stan directly
> in C++ so you need to develop your intuitions there.
>
> There's a whole chapter in the manual to help you get started.
> Here are the data types in Stan and what they are in C++:
>
>   matrix[M,N] a;   // Eigen:Matrix<T, Dynamic, Dynamic>
>
> is a matrix, with data stored contiguously in column-major order in
> the underlying C++ app.  It's also what you need for any matrix op.
>
>   real a[M,N];   // std::vector<std::vector<T> >
>
> is a 2D array, with data stored non-contiguously in row-major order.
>
> And finally
>
>   row_vector[N] a[M];  // std::vector<Eigen::Matrix<T, Dynamic, 1> >
>
> is a 1D array whose elements are rwo vectors.
>
> > If that is the case we may be  better off reading these statements as
> >         • a N dimensional row vector with M-dimensional columns as elements for the first declaration and
> >         • a N-dimensional column vector with M-dimensional rows as elements for the second declaration.
> > Instead, for example,  if I read the second declaration as a M dimensional array with N dimensional vectors as elements, I do not get a clue about the output structure ?
>
> The I/O is all encapsulated w.r.t. R.   When you go to the dump
> format, we use R's dump ordering.  For JSON in Python, it's done
> differently.
>
> > of this declaration. Is it a rbind or a cbind of the M vectors in b? That was my problem in the first place that got me looking up the group threads.
>
> Stan's written in C++, not R, so there are no rbind or cbind things going on anywhere.
>
> - Bob
>

> On Jul 28, 2015, at 8:04 PM, MT <micha...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all, I've done some more reading of related stan google group threads, tried out a naive implementation, and wanted to provide my synthesized understanding of what needs to be operationalized.
>
> A quick summary of the STAN, operations
>
> 1) The user specified Stan Model defines a log posterior ignoring the normalizing constant.
> 2) With the log posterior, the gradients wrt to the model parameters are computed with auto-diff (relying on closed form functions)

Almost --- there are some iterative algorithms in there, so it's
not all closed form in the traditional sense.
But the set of built-in functions that can be autodiffed is
finite (but includes all of the C++ built-ins, cmath, and a
ton of extensions.

> 3) HMC is run (using the gradient information)
>
> The bottleneck with empirical likelihood is step 2. Stan CANNOT auto-diff the log posterior, specifically, the log empirical likelihood.
> This is because the log empirical likelihood is a non-closed form function of the model parameters. The log empirical likelihood is defined as a nonlinear function involving lagrange multipliers.
> See annotation 2 in my attached image.
>
> I've come to the above from reading threads and also trying a naive implementation below.
>
> 1) I solved for the lagrange multipliers in [R], (annotation 3)
> 2) fed it into stan in the data{} block,
> 3) Used the lagrange multipliers to define a new quantity in the transformed parameters block {} ( The w in the annotated image, annotation 2 )
> 4) Used increment_log_prob in the model{} block using the new quantity w
>
> I got nonsensical results of the basic regression parameter I simulated (annotation 1).
> Y = 1 + 10X + noise
>
> Doing some searching I found a recent related thread, where Ben Goodrich pointed out that this type of approach is incorrect.
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/emplik/stan-users/k58zmli1QJc/mMNpc5XKtkIJ
>
> I understand Ben's comment as "the lagrange multiplier in the transformed quantity is an 'intermediate quantity' therefore this approach WILL NOT factor into the gradient calculations correctly, if you rely on autodiff."
>
> Theoretically, the lagrange multipliers are a function of the original model parameters of interest (intercept and slope) annotation 3 and annotation 4)
>
> Because of this, it seems the right approach would be to hand calculate the gradient of the log empirical likelihood (annotation 5) . This involves a simple jacobian matrix (annotation 7).
>
> I've found a thread that talks about this approach in a high level
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/andria$20dawson/stan-users/EDu4GLsc5Ik/HGGgms6UqFsJ
>
> However, near the end, Bob comments
> " As I said to the last poster who asked, it might be
> easier to just write a function that computes the
> derivatives and then plug that into the model directly
> rather than trying to manipulate the generated code,
> which is going to be hard to maintain under any minor
> changes. "
>
> I'm curious is that can be done here?
>
> If this is a reasonable approach, My open questions are
> 1) I think I need to still use increment_log_prob (w) with w defined in annotated section 2)
> 2a) I think I need to compile the model, dive into the compiled c program, manually hardcode the gradient in the appropriate section

If it wasn't clear from that quote above, what I'm suggesting
is instead writing a C++ function that does the autodiff, then
plugging that into the model.  That way, you have something you
can independently test and something you can plug into any model.

> 2b) Ignoring the 2a approach, how would we follow bob's advice of pluggin in the computed derivatives instead of manipulating the c program

I'll send you a paper off-list.  As soon as the final re-org to the
includes for the math library, we'll put it up on arXiv.

>
> 3) Optional - I've found the optimal lagrange multipliers outside of stan, in [R]. But to followup on some comments here on how to 'optimize' in stan, is there some good example of how to use the stan BFGS routine ?

There are examples in all the interface manuals and also
a description of what the parameters mean in the main language
manual.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: autodiff for empirical likelihood
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, July 28, 2015 at 8:04:21 PM UTC-4, MT wrote:
> The bottleneck with empirical likelihood is step 2. Stan CANNOT auto-diff the log posterior, specifically, the log empirical likelihood.
> This is because the log empirical likelihood is a non-closed form function of the model parameters. The log empirical likelihood is defined as a nonlinear function involving lagrange multipliers.

This is not quite right. Stan currently has no ability to even solve for lambda. In the rare cases where an explicit expression is known for lambda, Stan should work.

> I've come to the above from reading threads and also trying a naive implementation below.
>
> 1) I solved for the lagrange multipliers in [R], (annotation 3)
> 2) fed it into stan in the data{} block,
> 3) Used the lagrange multipliers to define a new quantity in the transformed parameters block {} ( The w in the annotated image, annotation 2 )
> 4) Used increment_log_prob in the model{} block using the new quantity w

I think it would be easier to see what you are doing from a .stan file than a picture of a whiteboard, but in general the values of the lagrange multipliers will depend on the proposals for the parameters (theta), in which case the lagrange multipliers are not fixed "data".

> I'm curious is that can be done here?

Not much. The options seem to be
Restrict the models to cases where lambda is an explicit function of theta
Write particular models in C++ where you use Boost to numerically solve for lambda and deal with the derivatives yourself
Implement numerical optimization within .stan programs like for integrate_ode and utilize implicit differentiation

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Has anyone successfully used this?

I tried to implement the example given here: http://www.cidlab.com/supp.php?o=wienerstan

The 'wiener.hpp' file states that "y should contain reaction times in seconds, with upper-boundary responses strictly positive and lower-boundary response times coded as strictly negative numbers."

My example code:

library(rstan)
library(RWiener)

# generate data using RWiener package
set.seed(0)
dat <- rwiener(n = 1000, alpha = 1, tau = 0.2, beta = 0.5, delta = 0.5)

standata <- list(y = ifelse(dat$resp == "upper", dat$q, -1 * dat$q),
                 N = length(dat$resp))

wiener_model <- "
data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    real y[N];
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0> a;
    real<lower=0> t;
    real<lower=0,upper=1> b;
    real v;
}
model {
    v ~ normal(0, 2);

    for (n in 1:N) {
        y[n] ~ wiener(1, 0.2, 0.5, v);
    }
}"

fit <- stan(model_code = wiener_model, data = standata)

I get the error message:
Rejecting initial value:

If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

According to the manual (p. 396), Stan returns the first passage time of the accumulation process over the upper boundary only. How do I deal with both decision boundaries, if I cannot pass in lower-boundary response times as negative numbers?

messages.subject: posterior predictive checks
messages.subject_clean: posterior predictive checks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working on a project involving Stan and I have a question I wanted to ask you regarding posterior predictive checks. The subject of my project is quantum mechanics and the purpose of my code is to estimate N operators (matrices) in the presence of noise, compared to known noiseless operators. Since I am performing a simulation, I know what the noisy operators should be.

I have a metric, called the trace distance, for comparing the closeness of two operators, which reduces the N estimated operators to N real numbers. So I see how close the estimated operators are to the known noisy operators. These real numbers not explicitly random variables, as they are a function of the estimated operators, and can be calculated in Stan.

I want to see if my estimates are better than assuming noiseless operators. From what I have read, posterior predictive checks seem to be the best approach to do this. Since I am working on self-taught knowledge, I wanted to ensure that my approach to a posterior predictive test makes sense: My idea is to extract the estimates for trace distance produced from the stan() function in R and observe what proportion of trace distances for my estimates are better than the trace distance for the known operators. Does this make sense?

Thanks

The subject of my project is quantum mechanics and the purpose of my code is to estimate N operators (matrices) in the presence of noise, compared to known noiseless operators. Since I am performing a simulation, I know what the noisy operators should be.

>

Since I am working on self-taught knowledge, I wanted to ensure that my approach to a posterior predictive test makes sense: My idea is to extract the estimates for trace distance produced from the stan() function in R and observe what proportion of trace distances for my estimates are better than the trace distance for the known operators. Does this make sense?

I just want to clarify here that when you say "estimates", you really
mean draws from the posterior.  That is, you want to evaluate this
expectation:

  E[f(theta)] = INTEGRAL_Theta f(theta) p(theta | y) d.theta

              approx 1/M SUM_{m in 1:M} f(theta^(m))

where theta^(m) is the m-th posterior draw from p(theta | y).

Any function of a random variable is a random variable, so if theta
is a vector of RVs, then f(theta) is also an RV.  Intro math stats
books are terrible at explaining all of this --- you really need the
measure-theoretic intros aimed at applied math and stats grad students.

There are a number of ways to do Bayesian point estimation, but the
most standard is posterior mean (i.e., plug in f(theta) = theta into
the above expectation calculation).  Some people use medians (which
minimize expected absolute error rather than the expected square error
minimized by the posterior mean).

- Bob

Is there a way to prevent variables from the parameters block from being reported in the output csv? I believe intermediate variables defined in the model block are ignored, but I think the model block isn't the place to define variables with constraints; I get the following message when I try
vector<lower=0>[5] forgetVar;
 in the model block:
SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER: require unconstrained. found range constraint.

Basically, I'm more interested in the hierarchical priors, and there are many space-consuming parameters that depend on these that I'm not interested in.

messages.subject: Re: Way to ignore variables
messages.subject_clean: Way to ignore variables
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 30, 2015 at 1:49:30 PM UTC-4, William Beard wrote:
> Is there a way to prevent variables from the parameters block from being reported in the output csv?

Not in CmdStan. In RStan, there is a pars argument that takes a character vector of parameter names and an include flag indicating whether to include or exclude the parameters named in pars from the output.

> I believe intermediate variables defined in the model block are ignored, but I think the model block isn't the place to define variables with constraints

The model block does not permit constraints (so you will get that parser error) but moreover, your Stan program is likely miswritten if you were trying to do that.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: A Wierd Softmax Regression Parameterization Issue
messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 29, 2015, at 2:58 PM, Cody Ross <ctr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
> Bob,
>
> I still don't quite understand your response. You use the plural "extra intercepts" and "them" but isn't there only a single extra intercept?

Sorry for the confusion.  I was speaking in generalities.

> What I have a regression model for each category of outcome. Each outcome has its own predictor variables that don't factor in to other categories. This is just like writing the model in standard notation (and including every predictor variable for every category of outcome) with the constraint that parameters are zero for all predictors other than those that correspond to the outcome of interest. As such, I think all of the predictors should be well identified.

It's the coefficients that get identified, and the usual problem
is multiple intercepts --- it's a natural feature (or problem) for
hierarchical models.  And it's even worse in something like IRT where
there's just obvious problems.
See the manual chapter on problematic posteriors.  The standard
hierarchical models are only only weakly identified.

  mu_beta ~ ...
  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, mu_sigma);
  ...
  y_hat <- x[n] * beta

Because it's identical to having

  mu_beta ~ ...
  beta_raw ~ normal(0, mu_sigma);

  ...

>  The only remaining issue should be that I have K intercepts. Setting one of these to a constant, should be enough to identify the model right?

I'd think so.  But I don't have time to trace through the whole
model to check.  If it's not identified, you'll know in the posterior
through high correlations of variables.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] uniform prior on a matrix?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] uniform prior on a matrix?
messages.body_plain:
No.  There are lots of ways you can constrain it to be proper.

You can draw a random N x N correlation matrix uniformly.  And then
you can draw N scales (std deviations) and generate a random matrix.
Or you can use something like a Wishart prior.  You can read up on
how the Wishart is based on randomly generating matrices from normal
random vectors:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wishart_distribution#Definition

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ESS confusion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ESS confusion
messages.body_plain:
Sebastian, if I understand your question correctly, you shouldn't have to worry about thinning based on ESS; Instead, just calculate your quantity of interest in the generated quantities block (or after the fact in R) and use it however you would any other set of parameter draws--you can then directly assess the ESS of this generated quantity, check Rhat, etc...

Seth

messages.subject: Re: ESS confusion
messages.subject_clean: ESS confusion
messages.body_plain:
>
> For follow up analyses (of the prediction) I thin down the sample to it's effective sample size.

In addition to others comments, even if you are examining one quantity, note that if you were going to select ESS number of draws from the whole sample, then the effective sample size for the thinned set is likely to be smaller than the original ESS as the thinning throws away information. If you want to thin to get almost independent draws to simplify the follow up analysis, you need to look at the autocorrelations and not ESS.

Aki
